The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Naturality means that for an open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow M$ with restricted orientation, $D_M e=i_*D_U$, where $e$ is extension of compact supports. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;R)=H^p(M;R)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$. For arbitrary $M$ the isomorphism is the direct sum of those on its components. AC is used in the countable coordinate-neighborhood selection for exhaustion and in the local universal-coefficient proof.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Let
$$0\to A^\bullet\to B^\bullet\to C^\bullet\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of cochain complexes in an abelian category. Then
there is a natural exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^n(A)\to H^n(B)\to H^n(C)\xrightarrow{\partial^n}H^{n+1}(A)\to H^{n+1}(B)\to H^{n+1}(C)\to\cdots.$$

Let $Y$ be a closed oriented $3$-manifold and let $x,y\in\operatorname{Tor}H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$. For choices of an integer $n>0$ and an integral $2$-chain $C$ with $\partial C=nx$, the bounding-chain expression is $(C\cdot y)/n\bmod\mathbb Z\in\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$, where $C$ and $y$ are placed transversely and intersection signs use the orientation of $Y$. This expression is the torsion linking pairing when its independence of the choices is established.

derivations.claim: Since $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ is finite, $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q)=0$ by [F2], and $H^2(Y;\mathbb Q)=0$ by [F1]. Exactness of the coefficient sequence in [F3] makes $\beta:H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ an isomorphism. Composing it with [F1] identifies $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ isomorphically with $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$.

By [F2], $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ is the full character group of $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$. The isomorphism of step 1.1 therefore says that the adjoint of the pairing in [F4] is an isomorphism, proving nonsingularity.

For torsion classes $x,y$, choose $n,m>0$ and chains $C,D$ with $\partial C=nx$ and $\partial D=my$. Put the chains and cycles in general position. Their intersection $C\cap D$ is a $1$-chain; its oriented boundary is the signed sum of $nx\cap D$ and $C\cap my$. The boundary has total algebraic count zero, so $n(x\cdot D)=m(C\cdot y)$ with the boundary-orientation convention. Dividing and reducing modulo $\mathbb Z$ gives $(C\cdot y)/n=(D\cdot x)/m$, hence $\lambda_Y(x,y)=\lambda_Y(y,x)$.

citations.quote: Let $X$ be a path-connected CW space. The oriented bordism set $\Omega_n^{SO}(X)$ consists of classes of pairs $(M,f)$, where $M$ is a closed smooth oriented $n$-manifold and $f:M\to X$. Two pairs are bordant when there is a compact oriented $(n+1)$-manifold $W$ with $\partial W=M_0\sqcup(-M_1)$ and a map $F:W\to X$ restricting to $f_0$ and $f_1$ on the boundary. Disjoint union defines the operation. For a group $G$, $K(G,1)$ denotes a connected CW space with fundamental group $G$ and contractible universal cover.

derivations.claim: The sum is well-defined: if $F_i:W_i\to X$ are bordisms witnessing equivalences of pairs for $i=0,1$, then $W_0\sqcup W_1$ with map $F_0\sqcup F_1$ is a bordism witnessing the equivalence of the disjoint unions. Boundary orientations are inherited componentwise.

Disjoint union is associative and commutative up to the orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms that rebracket or permute its components; composing the maps with these diffeomorphisms preserves the bordism classes. The empty manifold with its unique map is a two-sided identity.

The cylinder $M\times[0,1]$ with map $f\circ\operatorname{pr}_M$ has boundary $(M,f)\sqcup(-M,f)$ under the product orientation convention. Thus $(-M,f)$ is a two-sided inverse of $(M,f)$, so the operation is an abelian group operation.

be a short exact sequence of cochain complexes in an abelian category. Then

derivations.claim: The rational homology-pair sequence and [F1], with $H_i(W;\mathbb Q)=0$ for $i>0$, give $H_1(Y;\mathbb Q)=H_2(Y;\mathbb Q)=0$; connectedness gives $H_0(Y;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$, and orientation gives $H_3(Y;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$. Thus $Y$ is a rational homology sphere. By [F4] and [A1], both $W$ and its smooth boundary $Y$ have finite CW type, so their integral homology groups are finitely generated; their positive-degree rationalizations vanish and are therefore finite.

Put $A=H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$, $B=H_1(W;\mathbb Z)$, and $C=H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$. Since $A$ is finite by step 1.1, the universal coefficient sequence [F3] gives $H^1(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$; [F7] then gives $H_2(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$. Also $H_3(W;\mathbb Z)=0$: [F1] identifies $H_4(W,Y)$ with $H^0(W)=\mathbb Z$, and its fundamental-class boundary maps to the generator of $H_3(Y)=\mathbb Z$; since $H_3(W,Y)\cong H^1(W)=0$, exactness forces $H_3(W)=0$.

By [F3], $H^2(W;\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{Ext}(B,\mathbb Z)$ and $H^3(W;\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{Ext}(C,\mathbb Z)$, because $B,C$ are finite and $H_3(W)=0$. Their orders are $|B|$ and $|C|$. Under [F1], these are the orders of $H_2(W,Y)$ and $H_1(W,Y)$, respectively. The pair sequence [F2] shows that $P=\ker(A\to B)$ is the cokernel of the injective map $H_2(W)\to H_2(W,Y)$, while $B\to H_1(W,Y)$ is onto because the next map $H_0(Y)\to H_0(W)$ is an isomorphism. Hence $|P|=|B|/|C|$ and $|A/P|=|B|/|C|$, so $|A|=|P|^2$.

To prove isotropy, [F2] and the naturality in [F7] identify $P$ under Poincaré duality with the image of $H^2(W;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$. For $x,y\in P$, choose lifts $\widetilde x,\widetilde y\in H^2(W;\mathbb Z)$. Since $W$ is a rational homology ball, the coefficient Bockstein $H^1(W;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(W;\mathbb Z)$ is onto by [F8]: the adjacent groups $H^1(W;\mathbb Q)$ and $H^2(W;\mathbb Q)$ vanish. Choose $\gamma\in H^1(W;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ with Bockstein $\widetilde y$. By [F5], $\lambda_Y(x,y)$ is the evaluation on $[Y]$ of the restriction of $\gamma\smile\widetilde x$. This class extends over $W$, and the inclusion sends $[Y]$ to zero in $H_3(W)$ because $Y=\partial W$. Thus $\lambda_Y(x,y)=0$.
The isotropy from step 3.2 gives $P\subseteq P^\perp$. Nonsingularity [F5] implies $|P^\perp|=|A|/|P|=|P|$ by step 3.1. Therefore $P=P^\perp$, so $P$ is a metabolizer by [F6].

Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk with boundary $K\subset S^3$. Choose a closed tubular neighborhood $N(D)\cong D^2\times D^2$ meeting $S^3$ in $\partial D\times D^2$, and let $X_D$ be the closure of $B^4\setminus\operatorname{int}N(D)$, with corners rounded. The positive meridian is the oriented circle $\{x\}\times\partial D^2$ in the overlap $D^2\times S^1$, oriented by the ambient and disk orientations.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

derivations.claim: Both $B^4$ and $N(D)$ are contractible, and $N(D)\cap X_D$ is connected and homotopy equivalent to $S^1$ by [F1]. The reduced degree-zero part of Mayer–Vietoris [F2] therefore gives $\widetilde H_0(X_D;\mathbb Z)=0$, so $X_D$ is connected.

In degree one, the sequence has $H_2(B^4)=0$, then $H_1(N(D)\cap X_D)\cong\mathbb Z$, then $H_1(N(D))\oplus H_1(X_D)$, then $H_1(B^4)=0$. Since $H_1(N(D))=0$, the inclusion of the overlap induces an isomorphism $H_1(N(D)\cap X_D)\to H_1(X_D)$. Its generator is the positive meridian by [F1].
For every $i\ge2$, the adjacent groups $H_i(N(D)\cap X_D)$, $H_i(N(D))$, and $H_i(B^4)$ vanish. Exactness of [F2] then forces $H_i(X_D)=0$. This proves the asserted homology in all degrees.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ and $B=K(C_d\times\mathbb Z,1)$. For geometric oriented **smooth** bordism of maps,
$$\Omega^{SO}_3(B)\cong\mathbb Z/d.$$

$$d\bigl([Z,f]-[Z,\mathrm{constant}]\bigr)=0\quad\hbox{in }\Omega^{SO}_4(B).$$

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to the specified prime-power integer $d$. Its explicit cyclic resolution works for all $d$ without assuming $d$ prime, and its geometric skeletal comparison uses the same smooth bordism convention [F1]. It gives the isomorphism $\Omega^{SO}_3(K(G,1))\cong\mathbb Z/d$.

The group $\mathbb Z/d$ has $d$ elements and is finite, including every exponent in a prime power. This proves the assertion under the stated AC convention, rather than inferring the prime-power calculation from its prime-order special case.

Its boundary is a degree-one longitude curve, hence represents the preferred longitude by [F3]. Each element of $\pi_1(F_0)$ has a smooth loop representative. Each lifted copy has one boundary component over the preferred longitude, proving that every lifted longitude is nullhomologous in $E_q$.

The latter bounds a meridian disk in the attached solid torus and the former maps to its core generator. The Mayer–Vietoris cokernel in [F6] therefore eliminates the core generator and gives $H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(E_q;\mathbb Z)/\langle[\widetilde\lambda]\rangle$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot bounding a smooth proper disk $D\subset B^4$, and let $q\ge2$. Write $X_D$ for the compact disk exterior and let the positive meridian induce $\pi_1(X_D)\to H_1(X_D;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q$. Let $X_{D,q}$ be the connected cover classified by the kernel of this map. Attach $D^2\times D^2$ to $X_{D,q}$ along the connected cover of $D^2\times S^1$ using the normal-disk map $z\mapsto z^q$. The resulting compact oriented $4$-manifold $W_{D,q}$ is the $q$-fold cyclic cover of $B^4$ branched along $D$; its boundary is $\Sigma_q(K)$, and the local branched model is $(x,z)\mapsto(x,z^q)$.

Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk, let $p$ be prime, and let $q=p^k$ with $k\ge1$. The $q$-fold cyclic cover $W_{D,q}$ of $B^4$ branched along $D$ is a compact connected oriented $4$-manifold with $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=0$ for every $i>0$ and boundary $\Sigma_q(\partial D)$.

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a compact connected smooth oriented $4$-manifold with rational homology of a point and connected boundary $Y$. Then $Y$ is a rational homology sphere, and $P=\ker(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(W;\mathbb Z))$ is a metabolizer for the torsion linking form $\lambda_Y$.

Assume AC. If $Y$ is a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold with finite $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$, then the bounding-chain torsion linking pairing $\lambda_Y$ is symmetric and nonsingular: its adjoint $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\to\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere and let $B^4$ be the standard four-ball with boundary $S^3$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable locally flat topologically properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. For each such surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. Define the smooth slice genus and the locally flat topological slice genus by

$$
g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K),\qquad g_4^{\mathrm{top}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K).
$$

A finite nonsingular linking form is a pair $(A,\lambda)$, where $A$ is a finite abelian group and $\lambda:A\times A\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is symmetric and induces an isomorphism $A\to\operatorname{Hom}(A,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$. For $P\le A$, put $P^\perp=\{a\in A:\lambda(a,p)=0\text{ for every }p\in P\}$. A metabolizer is a subgroup $P$ with $P=P^\perp$; equivalently, $\lambda$ vanishes on $P\times P$ and $|P|^2=|A|$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the boundary of $W_{D,q}$ is the rational homology sphere $\Sigma_q(K)$, and both are compact connected oriented manifolds with the required boundary identification. The kernel of its boundary inclusion is exactly the subgroup $P_D$ displayed in the statement.

Apply [F2] to $W_{D,q}$ and its boundary. The kernel identified in step 1.1 is self-annihilating for the boundary linking form; [F3] supplies nonsingularity and [F5] the metabolizer convention. Therefore $P_D$ is a metabolizer.

Assume AC. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ and $q\ge2$, the first homology of the $q$-fold cyclic cover $M_{0,q}$ of zero surgery has an isomorphism of abelian groups
$$H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z,$$
where the free summand is generated by $\widetilde\mu$, the closed lift of the $q$-fold meridian loop $\mu^q$.
Assume AC, as in the smooth Casson–Gordon bordism convention. For every prime-power integer $d$ and $G=\mathbb Z/d\oplus\mathbb Z$, the oriented bordism group $\Omega_3^{SO}(K(G,1))$ is finite.

Let $X$ be a path-connected CW space. The oriented bordism set $\Omega_n^{SO}(X)$ consists of classes of pairs $(M,f)$, where $M$ is a closed smooth oriented $n$-manifold and $f:M\to X$. Two pairs are bordant when there is a compact oriented $(n+1)$-manifold $W$ with $\partial W=M_0\sqcup(-M_1)$ and a map $F:W\to X$ restricting to $f_0$ and $f_1$ on the boundary. Disjoint union defines the operation. For a group $G$, $K(G,1)$ denotes a connected CW space with fundamental group $G$ and contractible universal cover.

For every path-connected CW space $X$, disjoint union makes $\Omega_n^{SO}(X)$ an abelian group with identity the empty manifold with its unique map to $X$ and inverse of $(M,f)$ represented by $(-M,f)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

derivations.claim: On [F1]'s branched-cover summand send a class to its character value, identifying its cyclic image with $C_d$; send $\widetilde\mu$ to zero in that factor. In the other factor use the integral free projection. This is the stated homomorphism $\eta$ on actual integral homology and hence on the fundamental group. It is represented by a continuous map to the specified $K(G,1)$: on a finite CW presentation send each one-cell to a loop with the assigned group image, fill each two-cell because its relation has trivial image, and extend over higher cells because the target's higher homotopy groups vanish. The extensions agree on cell boundaries; their finite pasting is continuous. AC permits these finite choices, and changing them alters the map only within its homotopy class by the same cell-by-cell argument.

Its geometric class belongs to [F2]'s finite group. Some positive integer $r$ kills that element (indeed the explicit calculation permits $r=d$). By [F3], zero means that the disjoint union of those $r$ actual marked copies bounds a compact smooth oriented four-manifold with a map to $K(G,1)$ restricting to their maps. This is exactly the required bordism datum, with the positive orientations and both prescribed character coordinates unchanged.

Assume AC. If a smooth oriented knot $K$ bounds a smooth proper disk $D$ in $B^4$ and $q$ is a prime power, then
$$P_D=\ker\bigl(H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\to H_1(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)\bigr)$$
is a metabolizer for the torsion linking form of $\Sigma_q(K)$.

Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk, let $p$ be prime, and let $q=p^k$ with $k\ge1$. The $q$-fold cyclic cover $W_{D,q}$ of $B^4$ branched along $D$ is a compact connected oriented $4$-manifold with $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=0$ for every $i>0$ and boundary $\Sigma_q(\partial D)$.

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $q\ge2$, and let $M=\Sigma_q(K)$ be its $q$-fold cyclic branched cover. A character is a homomorphism $\chi:H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$. Its order is its order in $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(M;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$; it is finite-order when this order is finite and has prime-power order when its order is $p^e$ for a prime $p$ and $e\ge1$. It vanishes on a subgroup $P$ when $\chi(x)=0$ for every $x\in P$.

derivations.claim: If $\chi$ extends to $\widetilde\chi:H_1(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$, then for every $x\in P_D$ one has $i(x)=0$, so $\chi(x)=\widetilde\chi(i(x))=0$. The extension has finite image because its domain is finite.

Conversely, suppose $\chi(P_D)=0$. Then $\chi$ factors uniquely through the subgroup $I=i(H_1(\Sigma_q(\partial D)))$ of the finite group $B=H_1(W_{D,q})$. Let $p$ be the prime underlying the order of $\chi$ as in [F2]. Every element of order coprime to $p$ maps to zero, since its image is killed both by a power of $p$ and by an integer coprime to $p$. Thus the factored map restricts to the $p$-primary subgroup $I_p\le B_p$.

A homomorphism from a subgroup $J$ of a finite abelian $p$-group $B_p$ into $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z[p^\infty]$ extends when one adjoins one element $b\in B_p$: if $p^k$ is the order of $b+J$, choose $c\in\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z[p^\infty]$ with $p^kc=f(p^kb)$, which exists because multiplication by $p^k$ is surjective on this Prüfer group. Set $f'(j+rb)=f(j)+rc$. If $j+rb=j'+r'b$, then $(r-r')b\in J$, so $r-r'$ is divisible by $p^k$; the chosen equation makes the two values equal. The extension is therefore well-defined. Repeating this finite step extends the character from $I_p$ to $B_p$.

Set the extension to zero on the complementary primary summand of $B$ and combine it with the extension on $B_p$. The resulting character on $B$ extends $\chi$ and has finite $p$-power image because $B$ is finite and the values are $p$-primary. This proves the reverse implication.

citations.quote: Assume AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, $q\ge2$, and $M=\Sigma_q(K)$ oriented as the boundary of the positive-meridian branched cover. When $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)$ is finite, its torsion linking form is the oriented pairing $\lambda_M:H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ given by $\lambda_M(x,y)=(C\cdot y)/n\bmod\mathbb Z$ for any integer $n>0$ and integral $2$-chain $C$ in $M$ with $\partial C=nx$; reversing the orientation negates $\lambda_M$. For a prime-power-order character $\chi$ of order $d$, the standard splitting $H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z\langle\widetilde\mu\rangle$ of the $q$-fold cyclic cover $M_{0,q}$ of zero surgery extends $\chi$ to $\eta:H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z/d\oplus\mathbb Z$ by identifying its cyclic image with $\mathbb Z/d$ and using the free-summand projection in the second factor. A Casson–Gordon bordism datum is a positive integer $r$ and a compact oriented $4$-manifold $W$ with a map to $K(\mathbb Z/d\oplus\mathbb Z,1)$ whose boundary represents $r$ copies of $(M_{0,q},\eta)$.

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $q$ be a prime power, and let $\chi:H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ have prime-power order $d$. Under the standard splitting $H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z\langle\widetilde\mu\rangle$, the character extends to $\eta:H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z/d\oplus\mathbb Z$ by identifying its cyclic image with $\mathbb Z/d$ and using the free-summand projection in the second factor. Some positive multiple of $(M_{0,q},\eta)$ bounds a compact oriented $4$-manifold with an extending map to $K(\mathbb Z/d\oplus\mathbb Z,1)$.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a smooth knot exterior or the exterior of a smooth proper disk in the standard four-ball. Its meridian-coordinate homomorphism is $\ell:\pi_1X\to\mathbb Z$. Let $X_q$ be its connected $q$-fold cyclic cover, for any $q\ge1$, and put $\psi=\ell/q$ on its group. For any homomorphism $c:\pi_1X_q\to C_{p^a}$, where $p$ is prime and $a\ge1$, give $\mathbb C(t)$ the rank-one unitary coefficient system
$$\rho(g)=\zeta_{p^a}^{c(g)}t^{\psi(g)},\qquad \bar t=t^{-1}.$$
Then $H_*(X_q;\mathbb C(t)_\rho)=0$. The same conclusion holds for a trivial finite character.

If $M_{0,q}$ is the $q$-fold cover of zero surgery on a smooth knot, and $c$ is any prime-power-order character on its first homology, the same conclusion holds on $M_{0,q}$ with its meridian free coordinate. In particular every smooth four-bordism whose boundary consists of such data has a nonsingular twisted middle Hermitian form, with no change to its absolute twisted $H_2$. The regular $C_{p^a}\times\mathbb Z$ cover in this assertion is generally infinite; the assertion concerns its specified rank-one localization.

Assume AC. Let $F$ be a commutative field of characteristic different from two with involution, and supply a rank-one unitary $F$ local system on each smooth compact oriented manifold in question, with one compatible system on each gluing or bordism. Give its finite-dimensional local homology the usual Hermitian cap-intersection form.

For a four-manifold $W$, the radical of its absolute middle form is exactly the image of $H_2(\partial W;F)$; denote its nonsingular quotient form by $Q_F(W)$. If $\partial W$ is $F$-acyclic, this is the absolute middle form itself. If two four-manifolds with the same entire marked boundary are glued with opposite boundary orientations, giving a closed $Z=W_0\cup_{\partial}(-W_1)$, then
$$[Q_F(Z)]=[Q_F(W_0)]-[Q_F(W_1)]\quad\text{in }W(F).$$
The nonsingular middle form of the boundary of any compact oriented smooth five-manifold with extending coefficients is metabolic, hence zero in $W(F)$. All assertions commute with extension of involutive fields, disjoint union, orientation reversal and coefficient-compatible marked identifications. In particular, the untwisted form used for a manifold with boundary is its nonsingular image form, not an unsupported assertion that its entire ordinary $H_2$ has nonsingular intersection form.

derivations.claim: The deck group $G=C_d\times\mathbb Z$ includes an infinite cyclic factor. Thus its regular cover $Y$ is not a finite-sheeted cover: the free coordinate takes the boundary meridian to one and gives arbitrarily many different sheets. Use the regular cover and the rank-one character projection followed by Laurent-field localization specified in [F2]. Its exactness identifies the module in the Statement with $H_2(W;F)$.

By [F2], $H_i(\partial W;F)=0$ in every degree. The actual pair sequence therefore identifies $H_2(W;F)$ with $H_2(W,\partial W;F)$. By [F3] the latter is its conjugate dual, with this map exactly the intersection pairing. It follows that the pairing is nonsingular. The involution in [F2] is precisely complex conjugation with $t\mapsto t^{-1}$, so the pairing is Hermitian in the stated convention.

To spell out the boundary cap, split each finite-dimensional boundary chain group into its cycles and a complement; the differential on that complement is an isomorphism to the preceding boundary space. Its inverses give a contraction of the acyclic boundary complex. The quotient from absolute to relative chains consequently has contractible kernel and preserves the absolute middle homology. This algebraic Poincare cap is enough for the Witt construction; it changes neither its module nor its pairing. The ordinary form, which need not be nonsingular on all ordinary $H_2$, instead uses [F3]'s quotient by its boundary radical. These are distinct operations, and no nonexistent finite $G$-cover or geometric attachment preserving a singular ordinary form has been assumed.

Let $X$ be a path-connected CW space. The oriented bordism set $\Omega_n^{SO}(X)$ consists of classes of pairs $(M,f)$, where $M$ is a closed smooth oriented $n$-manifold and $f:M\to X$. Two pairs are bordant when there is a compact oriented $(n+1)$-manifold $W$ with $\partial W=M_0\sqcup(-M_1)$ and a map $F:W\to X$ restricting to $f_0$ and $f_1$ on the boundary. Disjoint union defines the operation. For a group $G$, $K(G,1)$ denotes a connected CW space with fundamental group $G$ and contractible universal cover.

For every path-connected CW space $X$, disjoint union makes $\Omega_n^{SO}(X)$ an abelian group with identity the empty manifold with its unique map to $X$ and inverse of $(M,f)$ represented by $(-M,f)$.

> (Choice function).

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

Hence on closed four-manifolds their difference is a homomorphism from $\Omega_4^{SO}(B)$ to $W(F)$. For a constant map the two coefficient systems are the same constant $F$ system, so $D(Z,\mathrm{constant})=0$.

Applying that homomorphism to [F2] gives $dD(Z,f)=0$ for every closed $Z$ over $B$. In particular every closed ambiguity has torsion Witt difference and becomes zero after tensoring with $\mathbb Q$. This conclusion concerns the entire Witt class, not just its signature. No arbitrary-group analytic index theorem is required.

If the bounding multiplicities are $r_0,r_1$, take $r_1$ disjoint copies of $W_0$ and $r_0$ copies of $W_1$. Their whole marked boundaries are the same $r_0r_1$ copies. Glue them, reversing the second orientation, with the same boundary character maps. Whole-boundary Witt gluing [F3] gives $$D(Z)=r_1D(W_0)-r_0D(W_1).$$ This uses the ordinary nonsingular quotient even when the ordinary absolute form has a radical. The twisted boundary is acyclic by [F1], so that term uses precisely the absolute module of the Statement. By step 2.1 the left side is zero rationally. Dividing by $r_0r_1$ proves $D(W_0)/r_0=D(W_1)/r_1$. Disjoint union, repeated multiples and all marked gluing choices are therefore compatible.

We also record the target enlargement needed for a disk extension. Embed $C_d$ in $C_D$ for $d\mid D$ by $a\mapsto(D/d)a$, and keep the infinite coordinate unchanged. With positive roots of unity, $\zeta_D^{(D/d)a}=\zeta_d^a$, so the two rank-one $F$ coefficient systems and their forms are literally the same. Regard any original bounding datum as a datum over the larger target. Even if its boundary map is not onto that target, the proof of steps 1.1–3.1 still applies: [F2] and [F3] allow arbitrary continuous maps to $B$, and acyclicity concerns the actual coefficient system. One may use the induced principal cover, which can be disconnected; its local coefficient module is unchanged. Thus a smooth filling over the larger finite cyclic target computes the same rational class.

Finally the specified one-sided signature is a well-defined homomorphism on this rational Witt group. The entries of a Hermitian rational matrix, its nonzero determinant, and a rational change-of-basis matrix have only finitely many zeros and poles on the unit circle unless the relevant function is identically zero. For a nonsingular representative choose a short interval $0<\theta<\epsilon$ avoiding those finite exceptional sets. Its evaluations are nonsingular Hermitian matrices, and their eigenvalue signs cannot change without a zero determinant, so the signature is constant there. Congruent representatives have congruent evaluations on a common such interval. A hyperbolic form evaluates to a hyperbolic form and has zero signature. Direct sums add signatures, and rationalization extends this homomorphism by rational linearity. citations.quote: Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk, let $p$ be prime, and let $q=p^k$ with $k\ge1$. The $q$-fold cyclic cover $W_{D,q}$ of $B^4$ branched along $D$ is a compact connected oriented $4$-manifold with $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=0$ for every $i>0$ and boundary $\Sigma_q(\partial D)$.

Assume AC. If a smooth oriented knot $K$ bounds a smooth proper disk $D$ in $B^4$ and $q$ is a prime power, then
$$P_D=\ker\bigl(H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\to H_1(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)\bigr)$$
is a metabolizer for the torsion linking form of $\Sigma_q(K)$.

Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk with boundary K, let q be a prime power, and let $W_{D,q}$ be its branched cover. Put
$$P_D=\ker\bigl(H_1(\Sigma_q(\partial D);\mathbb Z)\to H_1(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)\bigr).$$
If $\chi:H_1(\Sigma_q(\partial D);\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ has prime-power order, then $\chi$ vanishes on $P_D$ if and only if it extends to a character of prime-power order on $H_1(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)$.

Assume AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot bounding a smooth proper disk $D\subset B^4$, and let $q\ge2$. Write $X_D$ for the compact disk exterior and let the positive meridian induce $\pi_1(X_D)\to H_1(X_D;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q$. Let $X_{D,q}$ be the connected cover classified by the kernel of this map. Attach $D^2\times D^2$ to $X_{D,q}$ along the connected cover of $D^2\times S^1$ using the normal-disk map $z\mapsto z^q$. The resulting compact oriented $4$-manifold $W_{D,q}$ is the $q$-fold cyclic cover of $B^4$ branched along $D$; its boundary is $\Sigma_q(K)$, and the local branched model is $(x,z)\mapsto(x,z^q)$.

Assume AC. Let $X_D$ be the exterior of a smooth proper disk, with positive-meridian isomorphism $H_1(X_D;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Let $X_{D,\infty}$ be the connected cover classified by the kernel of $\pi_1(X_D)\to H_1(X_D;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$, and let $t$ denote the deck transformation represented by the positive meridian. For $q\ge2$, define $X_{D,q}=X_{D,\infty}/\langle t^q\rangle$.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a smooth knot exterior or the exterior of a smooth proper disk in the standard four-ball. Its meridian-coordinate homomorphism is $\ell:\pi_1X\to\mathbb Z$. Let $X_q$ be its connected $q$-fold cyclic cover, for any $q\ge1$, and put $\psi=\ell/q$ on its group. For any homomorphism $c:\pi_1X_q\to C_{p^a}$, where $p$ is prime and $a\ge1$, give $\mathbb C(t)$ the rank-one unitary coefficient system
$$\rho(g)=\zeta_{p^a}^{c(g)}t^{\psi(g)},\qquad \bar t=t^{-1}.$$
Then $H_*(X_q;\mathbb C(t)_\rho)=0$. The same conclusion holds for a trivial finite character.

If $M_{0,q}$ is the $q$-fold cover of zero surgery on a smooth knot, and $c$ is any prime-power-order character on its first homology, the same conclusion holds on $M_{0,q}$ with its meridian free coordinate. In particular every smooth four-bordism whose boundary consists of such data has a nonsingular twisted middle Hermitian form, with no change to its absolute twisted $H_2$. The regular $C_{p^a}\times\mathbb Z$ cover in this assertion is generally infinite; the assertion concerns its specified rank-one localization.

Assume AC. For a fixed prime-power cover degree and prime-power order character, the rationalized difference between the twisted and untwisted Casson–Gordon intersection-form Witt classes, divided by the bounding multiplicity $r$, is independent of the chosen multiple and bounding pair. It defines a class in $W(\mathbb C(t))\otimes\mathbb Q$.

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $q$ be a prime power, and let $\chi:H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ have prime-power order $d$. Choose a Casson–Gordon bordism datum $(M_{0,q},\eta,r,W)$. Write $G=\mathbb Z/d\oplus\mathbb Z$, let $Y\to W$ be the regular cover determined by $\eta$, and give $\mathbb C(t)$ the $G$-action $(a,n)z=\exp(2\pi ia/d)t^n z$ and involution $\overline{t}=t^{-1}$ with complex conjugation on constants. Define
$$H_2^t(W;\mathbb C)=H_2(Y;\mathbb C)\otimes_{\mathbb C[G]}\mathbb C(t).$$
The Casson–Gordon Witt class is
$$\tau(\Sigma_q(K),\chi)=\frac{1}{r}\bigl([H_2^t(W;\mathbb C)]-[Q_0(W)\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C(t)]\bigr)\in W(\mathbb C(t))\otimes\mathbb Q,$$
using the nonsingular twisted form and the ordinary nonsingular image form. Precisely, put $Q_0(W)=H_2(W;\mathbb C)/\operatorname{rad}(\lambda_W)$ with its induced form; the untwisted term in the display is understood as $Q_0(W)\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C(t)$. The twisted boundary complex is acyclic, so its algebraic Poincare cap preserves the absolute twisted module. This does not assert that an arbitrary ordinary absolute intersection form is nonsingular. Here $W(\mathbb C(t))$ is the Witt group of nonsingular Hermitian forms over the field with involution, modulo hyperbolic forms. Its signature defect is $\sigma(K,\chi)=\sigma_1(\tau(\Sigma_q(K),\chi))$, where $\sigma_1$ evaluates a Hermitian representative at $t=e^{i\theta}$ and takes the one-sided limit as $\theta\to0^+$. This is the specified Casson–Gordon invariant and signature homomorphism; it is not an arbitrary rho invariant or an unspecified difference of signatures.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere and let $B^4$ be the standard four-ball with boundary $S^3$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable locally flat topologically properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. For each such surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. Define the smooth slice genus and the locally flat topological slice genus by

$$
g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K),\qquad g_4^{\mathrm{top}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K).
$$

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an extending character $\widetilde\chi$ on the branched disk cover, and write its exact order as $D=p^a$. If the original nontrivial character has order $d=p^b$, then $d\mid D$. Restrict $\widetilde\chi$ to $H_1(X_{D,q})$ and pair it with $\ell/q$. Its finite coordinate vanishes on the lifted meridian because that circle bounds the branch-tube disk in the filled cover. Its infinite coordinate takes that circle to one. On the exterior of the boundary knot the finite coordinate is the original $\chi$; on the zero-filling solid torus it is zero. Thus its boundary is precisely the original $\eta$ followed by the inclusion $C_d\times\mathbb Z\to C_D\times\mathbb Z$, with the root representation unchanged.

The actual oriented boundary of $X_{D,q}$ is $M_{0,q}$. Indeed the product disk tube at the base disk gives a longitude filling of the knot exterior: its framing is zero, since a parallel disk is disjoint and its boundary has linking zero with $K$. Passing to the meridional $q$-cover lifts the same longitude slope, while its normal circle is the closed lift of $\mu^q$. These are the zero-surgery cover coordinates in [F2], with the positive boundary orientation retained. Mayer–Vietoris in the rational homology ball $W_{D,q}=X_{D,q}\cup(D^2\times D^2)$, whose overlap is $D^2\times S^1$, gives $H_2(X_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=0$ and $H_1(X_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$ on that overlap circle. The higher groups vanish as well. In particular its ordinary middle nonsingular image form is zero.

The character in step 1.1 is of prime-power order on the actual exterior cover. Hence [F3] gives $H_2(X_{D,q};\mathbb C(t))=0$, so its twisted form is also zero. The difference of the two Witt forms of this actual single-boundary smooth filling is therefore zero. By [F4]'s larger-target comparison it computes the original rationalized class even when $D>d$: compare any original multiple bounding datum, viewed over $C_D\times\mathbb Z$, with the same number of copies of this filling and use the closed fourth-bordism ambiguity calculation. Thus $\tau(\Sigma_q(K),\chi)=0$ in $W(\mathbb C(t))\otimes\mathbb Q$. Applying the specified one-sided signature homomorphism gives $\sigma(K,\chi)=0$, as claimed. This proves the full prime-power extension case rather than assuming extension with unchanged finite order.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $F$ be a connected compact oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and let $V$ be its positive-push Seifert matrix in an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Write $\Delta_K(t)$ for the Alexander polynomial normalized up to multiplication by $\pm t^k$, and let $q\ge2$ with $\zeta_q$ a primitive $q$-th root of unity. Then $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)$ is finite if and only if $\Delta_K(\zeta_q^j)\ne0$ for every $1\le j<q$, and, when it is finite,
$$
|H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)|=\prod_{j=1}^{q-1}|\Delta_K(\zeta_q^j)|.
$$
The same criterion and order hold when $\Delta_K(t)$ is replaced by $\det(V-tV^T)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$.

For every $n\ge1$ the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_n$
([[def-cyclotomic-polynomial]]) is irreducible in $\mathbb Q[t]$
([[def-irreducible-and-prime-elements-in-a-domain]]).

Assume AC. If $Y$ is a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold with finite $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$, then the bounding-chain torsion linking pairing $\lambda_Y$ is symmetric and nonsingular: its adjoint $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\to\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
right $R$-modules, and $G$ a left $R$-module. Then naturally in $C,G$,
$0\to H_n(C)\otimes_RG\to H_n(C\otimes_RG)\to\operatorname{Tor}^R_1(H_{n-1}(C),G)\to0$
is exact.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Naturality means that for an open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow M$ with restricted orientation, $D_M e=i_*D_U$, where $e$ is extension of compact supports. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;R)=H^p(M;R)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$. For arbitrary $M$ the isomorphism is the direct sum of those on its components. AC is used in the countable coordinate-neighborhood selection for exhaustion and in the local universal-coefficient proof.

derivations.claim: Suppose a nontrivial $q$-th root of unity $\omega$ were a zero of $D$. Its order is $p^s$ for some $1\le s\le k$. By [F3], the minimal polynomial $\Phi_{p^s}$ divides $D$ in $\mathbb Q[t]$. Since $\Phi_{p^s}$ is monic and both polynomials have integer coefficients, polynomial long division gives an integer-coefficient quotient with zero remainder. Thus $p=\Phi_{p^s}(1)$ divides $D(1)$.
This contradicts $D(1)=\pm1$ from [F2]. Therefore $D$ has no zero at any nontrivial $q$-th root of unity. The criterion [F1] gives finiteness of $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)$.
By [F5], the finite first homology from step 2.1 makes $\Sigma_q(K)$ a rational homology sphere. Its torsion linking form is nonsingular by [F4], which proves the final assertion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

citations.quote:
Let $S$ be a nonempty connected boundaryless topological $2$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]). Let $K$ be a finite abstract
simplicial complex ([[def-abstract-simplicial-complex]]) whose simplices all
have dimension at most $2$, let $h:|K|\to S$ be a homeomorphism, and suppose
that:

1. every $1$-simplex of $K$ is contained in exactly two $2$-simplices of $K$;
2. for every vertex $v$ of $K$ the **link graph** $\operatorname{lk}(v)$ — with
   one vertex for each $1$-simplex $\{v,w\}$ of $K$ and one edge $\{x,y\}$ for
   each $2$-simplex $\{v,x,y\}$ of $K$ — is a cycle.

Then there is a polygonal schema with exactly one polygon
([[def-polygonal-schema-and-edge-pairing]]) whose realization $Y$ is
homeomorphic to $S$.

The construction selects only from finite collections and uses no choice
principle.

For one-polygon surface schemas
([[def-polygonal-schema-and-edge-pairing]]), each of the following operations
preserves the quotient homeomorphism type:

1. subdividing a paired side into two sides (edge subdivision);
2. cyclically rotating the boundary word, or reversing the polygon
   orientation and inverting every letter;
3. cancelling an adjacent inverse pair $a\,a^{-1}$ in the boundary word when another paired letter remains; the sole $aa^{-1}$ bigon is the terminal sphere schema and its empty reduced word is notation only;
4. cutting the polygon along an embedded polygonal diagonal whose interior
   lies in the polygon interior, and regluing the two new boundary sides to
   each other (a $(P2)$ split), as well as the inverse operation of gluing two
   faces along a paired pair of sides.

The resulting finite cut-and-paste identities move two same-direction
occurrences of a letter together as a crosscap block $bb$, extract an
interlaced pair pattern $a\,U\,b\,V\,a^{-1}X\,b^{-1}Y$ as a commutator handle
block $c\,d\,c^{-1}d^{-1}YX\,VU$, and replace one handle plus one crosscap by
three crosscaps. Each move preserves the surface link condition, and no choice
axiom is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The bounded region of a smooth embedded
circle in the oriented plane, together with its boundary, is a smooth manifold
with boundary diffeomorphic to the closed standard disk. Let $D_0,D_1$ be two
such closed regions. Every orientation-preserving smooth boundary
diffeomorphism $b:\partial D_0\to\partial D_1$ extends to an
orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $B:D_0\to D_1$. More precisely, for
specified smooth inward collars $c_i:\partial D_i\times[0,\epsilon)\to D_i$
with $c_i(p,0)=p$, the extension may be required to satisfy
$B(c_0(p,r))=c_1(b(p),r)$ for every sufficiently small $r\ge0$. In addition, given interior points $p_i\in D_i$ and an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $q$ from a neighborhood of $p_0$ onto a neighborhood of $p_1$, the extension can agree with $q$ near $p_0$ while retaining the prescribed boundary collars.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $N$ be a connected smooth $n$-manifold with
nonempty boundary and let $D\subseteq\partial N$ be an embedded closed disk.
Then the boundary connected sum $N\natural D^n$, obtained by gluing an $n$-disk
along $D$, is diffeomorphic to $N$ by a diffeomorphism equal to the identity
outside a collar neighbourhood of $D$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $V$ be a compact
smooth $n$-manifold with boundary and let $N$ be a smooth $n$-manifold without
boundary ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $F:V\times I\to N$ be a smooth map such
that $F_t:=F(\cdot,t)$ is a smooth embedding for every $t\in I$
([[def-smooth-embedding]]), and suppose $F$ is constant near the ends: for some
$\varepsilon\in(0,\tfrac12)$ one has $F(x,t)=F(x,0)$ for $t\le\varepsilon$ and
$F(x,t)=F(x,1)$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon$, for all $x\in V$.

Then for every open neighbourhood $W\subseteq N$ of the compact image
$F(V\times I)$ there is a smooth map $H:N\times I\to N$ such that
$H_0=\operatorname{id}_N$, every $H_t$ is a diffeomorphism of $N$
([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
$$H_t\circ F_0=F_t\quad\text{for every }t\in I,$$
$H_t=\operatorname{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, $H_t=\operatorname{id}_N$
for $t\le\varepsilon/2$, and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.

derivations.claim: We first record the smooth finite neighborhood version of the polygon construction. Choose small smooth disks at every supplied vertex and thin edge rectangles along its edges, with corner roundings in the triangle coordinates. This gives a ribbon neighborhood of the finite one-skeleton, with cyclic orders fixed by orientation. A free-triangle collapse can be realized on such rounded neighborhoods by deleting a smooth disk bulge along one boundary interval: in the reference triangle retain thin strips of its other two sides, a rounded disk at their common vertex, and small disks at its other vertices. The removed middle sector has one attaching interval along those strips. It is a rounded convex triangle, hence a standard disk by radial parametrization. Its collar and the retained collars are the same normal coordinates on both sides. Consequently [F3] implements the collapse by a smooth diffeomorphism relative to all unrelated boundary intervals. A finite dual tree rooted at the exterior collapses a boundary surface to a finite graph, as follows directly from the interval/circular links: each triangle has a free edge when its parent has already been removed. Reversing these finitely many disk bulges identifies the actual surface smoothly with a rounded ribbon neighborhood of that graph. This is a statement about neighborhoods, not a diffeomorphism collapsing an edge or face to a lower-dimensional set.

The combinatorial normal-form operations in [F1] also have smooth ribbon-neighborhood realizations. Merging two vertex disks joined by a tree band replaces their union by one disk: absorb the band and one vertex disk along its boundary interval using [F3]. Match every other incident band interval by its boundary parameter and apply [F2] with those parameters and collars; they retain their cyclic order. A diagonal split is made by a smooth embedded arc in one disk interior, transverse to its boundary at its two distinct endpoints; cutting its product strip and then identifying its two banks recovers the SAME smooth neighborhood. In an inverse merge two such disks join along that strip. Boundary-side subdivision only adds a marked point to its parameter. For an inverse-pair cancellation, its two successive boundary occurrences of the same band and intervening disk strip form a disk bulge, handled by step1.1. The three split/merge operations of the interlaced-handle extraction in [F1] are performed with these same smooth arc strips. At every new vertex use a small disk with its incident strip endpoints in their cyclic order; [F2] matches its boundary arcs and their product collars. Thus the seam maps agree on whole collars and the resulting finite pasting is a smooth map with smooth inverse, including at the vertices. No map that collapses a tree to a point is used as a diffeomorphism.

Cap every boundary component by a parametrized smooth disk, using its supplied collar and a finite fan triangulation, and round the finite presentation seams in their signed collars. This supplies a closed smooth surface and finite face presentation. The finite [F1] reduction, implemented on rounded neighborhoods as in step2.1, identifies it smoothly with a sphere or a fixed standard genus-$g$ commutator model. One may retain a small disk in a face throughout the procedure, do the ribbon construction on its complement, and finally extend across that retained disk by [F2]; this avoids treating a closed surface as a neighborhood of its one-skeleton alone. In an oriented reduced one-vertex word, an unprocessed opposite pair must interlace another, unless the terminal sphere digon is reached: otherwise its two sides separate the remaining vertex germs. Extract such a pair by the explicit handle move in [F1] and repeat. This is a finite decreasing word procedure. Its final cell counts give $\chi(\widehat S)=2-2g$, whereas capping the $b$ boundary components added $b$ disk faces and gives $\chi(\widehat S)=\chi(S)+b$. Hence the two capped surfaces have the same $g$ and are smoothly identified by their constructions. The capped disk images are actual smooth embedded disks in that common closed model.

In a connected closed smooth surface any two ordered finite disjoint families of smoothly parametrized embedded disks can be matched by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism. Here is the required finite construction. Choose finitely many distinct parking points outside the TARGET disk family; its complement is a nonempty open set, since finitely many disjoint closed disks cannot equal a connected closed surface. Choose a center in each source disk avoiding those finitely many points. First shrink each source disk into a small disk about that center using its parametrization and a radial shrinking isotopy of that compact disk, and extend it by [F3] with support near that disk. Take the shrunken images small enough to miss every chosen parking point. No assertion that the complements of the two ORIGINAL disk families intersect is needed. Join successive disk centers to their assigned parking points, and then to their assigned target centers, by paths missing the other parked small disks. Such paths exist: a path in a connected surface can be covered by finitely many disk charts, replaced there by polygonal subpaths, and any segment entering one of the finitely many forbidden small disks can be routed along its circle collar instead. Subdivide into finitely many chart segments, shrink the moving disk if necessary, and extend the translation isotopy of a small coordinate disk along each segment by [F3]. All supports miss the other parked disks. A final expansion, the inverse target shrinking, matches each entire disk. Orientation of the transported parametrization can be adjusted by an interior coordinate rotation and a positive linear path. Thus apply this construction in step3.1 to send the capped disks to their prescribed paired capped disks. Restricting to their complements gives a preliminary oriented diffeomorphism $S_0\to S_1$ with the desired boundary-component correspondence.

Correct its circle maps and collar germs separately in the disjoint boundary neighborhoods. The difference between its circle map and the prescribed one has a smooth increasing lift $h(\theta)$ with $h(\theta+2\pi)=h(\theta)+2\pi$. The lift interpolation $(1-t)\theta+t h(\theta)$ has positive angular derivative. Multiply its parameter by a normal cutoff, equal to one at the boundary and zero beyond a collar; its angular derivative remains positive, so this gives the required supported boundary-map correction. To correct the collar germ use the exact collar interpolation construction in [F2]: a relative collar map has coordinates $(\theta,r)\mapsto(H(\theta,r),R(\theta,r))$, with $H(\theta,0)=\theta$, $R(\theta,0)=0$, $R_r(\theta,0)>0$. Interpolation with the identity is an embedding on one uniformly narrow two-sided annulus, since the boundary Jacobian is triangular with positive diagonal; compactness and the local inverse exclude collisions after a common shrink. Extend this compact annular isotopy by [F3] in the double or capped surface. It fixes the boundary pointwise and preserves its two sides. Restricting back realizes exactly the prescribed collars on a common smaller width.

Finally match optional distinct interior points by the same finite parking and path construction in the interior, with supports away from all boundary collars. To realize each specified germ at its now matched point, use the germ-extension construction of [F2] on a small coordinate disk. Explicitly the rescalings $q_t(z)=q(tz)/t$ extend smoothly at $t=0$ to $Dq(0)$ by the integral derivative formula; the latter positive matrix joins the identity by rotation and positive-matrix interpolation. This yields a compact-source disk isotopy on one common small disk. Apply [F3] with support in a small target disk disjoint from all other matched points. Its final map agrees with the required relative germ there and is the identity near every other prescription. Perform the finitely many operations successively. All initial choices, cuts, graph reductions, parking paths and compositions were finite; the stated Countable Choice is used only in the actual smooth extension suppliers [F2]–[F3]. This proves the full prescribed matching without assuming a general smoothing theorem for an arbitrary homeomorphism.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice as required by the chosen tubular-neighborhood and peripheral-system data. Let K be a smooth oriented knot with compact exterior E_K, positive meridian mu_K, and preferred longitude lambda_K on the boundary torus. The zero-framed surgery manifold M(K) is the closed oriented 3-manifold obtained by gluing D²×S¹ to E_K so that the meridian boundary circle of D²×{1} is identified with lambda_K and the core {0}×S¹ is identified with mu_K. The orientation extends the orientation of E_K across the filling. Thus the filling slope is the preferred zero-linking longitude; the definition asserts no 4-manifold bounded by M(K).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $S_0,S_1$ be compact connected oriented smooth surfaces with nonempty smooth boundary. Supply finite smooth triangle presentations: face-to-face triangular disks, with circular interior vertex links and interval boundary links, whose parametrizations are smooth nonsingular maps in surface charts through each closed triangle. Suppose the two presentations have the same Euler characteristic and the same positive number $b$ of boundary components.

For any bijection of their boundary components, any orientation-preserving smooth circle maps on the paired components, and any prescribed inward collar germs, there is an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $B:S_0\to S_1$ realizing those circle maps and their collar identifications. In particular one may prescribe one marked point on each boundary circle. The diffeomorphism can additionally agree with finitely many prescribed orientation-preserving interior diffeomorphism germs at distinct points with distinct target points, while retaining the boundary collars.

All surface presentations are supplied finite data. No triangulation-existence, arbitrary topological smoothing, three-dimensional smoothing or unproved smooth classification result is assumed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology:
$$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically,
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$
If a basepoint and one oriented lift of each cell outside $A$ are supplied on every component, the $n$th group is the direct sum of the corresponding coefficient fibers, and its boundary is the signed $R[\pi]$ incidence matrix acting through monodromy.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $n$-manifold and let $A=\partial M$; let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and $\mathcal L$ an $R$-module local system on $M$. Cap with the canonical relative twisted fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $k$,
$$H^k(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M,A;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L),\qquad H^k(M,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L).$$
Here $\mathcal O_M^R$ is the collar extension of the interior orientation system. The statement is for the actual boundary $A$, not an arbitrary subspace of $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

derivations.claim: Work in an inward collar $S^3\times[0,\epsilon)$ of the standard ball. Push $F$ to the graph of a smooth positive interior depth function, zero on its boundary and with positive inward derivative there. Such a function is obtained from the supplied finite band and disk charts and positive finite bump sums, retaining the prescribed boundary collar. Round its finitely many seams in those charts. Denote this neat pushed surface by $F'$, and remove the interior of a small product normal disk neighborhood. The result $V_F$ is a compact smooth manifold after the displayed corner roundings. Its boundary is the knot exterior $E_K$ glued to $F\times S^1$ along their common torus: a normal disk to $F'$ has boundary the positive meridian, and the surface boundary direction is the preferred zero-linking longitude. This already fixes the peripheral marking, before any new handle is attached.

Here is a useful cut model, including why its chamber is a ball. The trace of the inward push gives a three-dimensional sheet from $F'$ back to its original position in $S^3$. Cut $V_F$ open along the portion of this sheet outside the removed normal neighborhood. The two banks are copies of a thickening of $F$, and the resulting chamber $Q$ is a ball with these marked banks. This last assertion has a collar construction. In each normal two-plane the removed disk and the cut trace are a rounded slit reaching the outside boundary. Cutting the slit opens it into an indentation attached to that boundary. Over a small three-dimensional neighborhood of $F$ in $S^3$, straighten that indentation to a depth graph $s=h(x)$; the graph has support in that neighborhood. The straightening in a normal section is the increasing reparametrization between two rounded intervals, and agrees with the identity at the outer section endpoints. The product coordinates along $F$ paste these reparametrizations; at its boundary use the supplied half-disk collar, so the slit endpoint is the same rounded half-section on both sides. All widths can be chosen common over the finitely many compact disk/band pieces. For a collar of depth $L>\max h$, the formula $(x,s)\mapsto(x,h(x)+(L-h(x))s/L)$ is a diffeomorphism from the original collar onto the graph indentation, agrees with the unchanged interior along a smaller interpolated collar, and has strictly positive normal derivative. It is identity outside the graph support. Undoing this indentation identifies $Q$ with the standard ball. The banks retain precisely the positive and negative normal push copies of $F$ in its boundary. This is a cut-and-collar parameterization, not a claim that an arbitrary smooth four-ball is standard.

We now change the boundary to actual zero surgery. Let $H$ be a smooth genus-$g$ handlebody whose oriented boundary is the union of a copy of $F$ and a disk along $\partial F$. Such a marked handlebody is supplied by the finite standard disk with $2g$ bands on the boundary of the standard genus-$g$ three-dimensional handlebody. The given disk-band surface has a finite smooth triangle presentation by subdividing its finitely many rectangles and disks in their coordinates. Both surfaces have Euler characteristic $1-2g$ and one boundary, so [F2] matches them with the exact given boundary map and collar. This transfers the handlebody parameter to the given $F$. Glue $H\times S^1$ to $V_F$ along $F\times S^1$, using the normal circle as the second factor and opposite boundary orientations. Round the product corners in those same collars, and call the result $W_F$. The remaining boundary is exactly $E_K\cup(D^2\times S^1)$, where the disk meridian is the actual preferred longitude and the circle core is the actual positive meridian. Its orientation restricts to the original oriented exterior. Therefore the boundary identification is the oriented [F1] zero surgery, rather than a homology-equivalent substitute. Equivalently, this gluing attaches the $g$ round handles which compress $F$ to the displayed disk. It is not the simply connected two-handle trace of zero surgery.

Form the infinite cyclic cut space by taking chambers $Q_k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, and identifying the positive bank of $Q_k$ with the negative bank of $Q_{k-1}$. Fix the indexing so the positive meridian crosses to the next chamber; its deck motion is $T$. Finite consecutive unions of chambers are simply connected by [F3]: each chamber is a ball and each joining thickened $F$ is connected, so the tree of trivial vertex groups has trivial pushout. A compact loop or homotopy meets only finitely many chambers, since the chamber pattern is locally finite. Hence the full cut space is simply connected and is the universal cover, with deck group generated by $T$. Thus $\pi_1(V_F)=\mathbb Z$, generated by the actual positive meridian. The cover's Mayer–Vietoris sequence, or its degreewise short exact small-chain sequence, has the form of the mapping cone of the difference of the two bank inclusions, from $C_*(F)\otimes\Lambda$ to $C_*(Q)\otimes\Lambda$. The same assertion holds directly with a specified character in place of $\Lambda$: coefficients are trivial within each bank and chamber, and the second bank map has the character factor. Since $Q$ is a ball and $F$ has one boundary component, it gives $$H_2(V_F;\Lambda)\cong H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\otimes\Lambda,\qquad H_3(V_F;\Lambda)=0.$$ On degree-zero homology the difference map is $1-t$ up to its invertible sign/deck factor. For every $z\ne1$ this factor is invertible, while the degree-one chamber homology is zero. Directly using the character small-chain sequence therefore gives $H_2(V_F;\mathbb C_z)\cong H_1(F;\mathbb C)$, without a possibly nonflat specialization argument.

We calculate the ordinary part separately over $\mathbb R$. Mayer–Vietoris for the original decomposition of the ball into $V_F$ and $F\times D^2$ identifies the rim-torus map $$H_1(F)\otimes H_1(S^1)=H_2(F\times S^1)\longrightarrow H_2(V_F)$$ as an isomorphism: its adjacent ball homology groups vanish and $H_2(F\times D^2)=0$. It also gives $H_1(V_F)=\mathbb R$, generated by the meridian, since the other degree-one summand is $H_1(F)$ and the overlap map to it is the identity. One has $H_3(V_F)=0$ since the adjacent degree-three product group and ball groups are zero. For $W_F=V_F\cup(H\times S^1)$ the degree-two overlap map is $(\mathrm{id},j_*)$ in this rim identification, where $j_*:H_1(F)\to H_1(H)$ is onto of ranks $2g\to g$. Its cokernel has dimension $g$. The degree-one overlap map is $$(x,n)\longmapsto(n,j_*x,n)\in H_1(V_F)\oplus H_1(H)\oplus H_1(S^1),$$ with an immaterial minus sign on one gluing summand. Its kernel has dimension $g$. Exactness therefore gives $\dim H_2(W_F)=2g$. The image of $H_2(H\times S^1)$ is injective: the graph image $(x,j_*x)$ meets $0\oplus H_2(H\times S^1)$ only in zero. It has dimension $g$. Choose the $g$ disjoint framed longitude curves of the explicit three-dimensional handlebody. Their products with $S^1$ are disjoint embedded tori with disjoint normal pushes. They represent this image, so it is isotropic.

We calculate the form with its signs. Represent the finitely many basis cycles by oriented smooth one-cycles on $F$, with transverse intersections, and choose independent normal levels for any coinciding pieces. For $a_i$ take a cap of its positive push in $Q_1$ and a cap of its negative push with reversed orientation in $Q_0$. Their union across the banks is an oriented smooth two-cycle $\Sigma_i$ representing the connecting class in step3.1. Caps can be obtained by coning a smooth cycle in the supplied ball parameter and smoothing the cone as a map relative to its boundary; immersion is unnecessary. For intersection counts take two independent copies. Cover their compact interior overlap by finitely many coordinate charts, add coordinate-vector perturbations with supported bumps, and apply [F5] to the product evaluation map and the diagonal of the product ball. Its derivative in those independent target-translation parameters spans the normal to the diagonal. Thus a sufficiently small parameter makes the two maps transverse, while their already separated boundary collars remain fixed. The intersection points are finite, and self-intersections of either separate map do not affect the resulting intersection of cycles. The ordinary intersection number of two such caps in a ball is the linking number of their boundary cycles: choose a spanning two-chain for one boundary in the boundary three-sphere and push its interior inward, where its intersections with the other cap are exactly the signed crossings defining linking. Changing either cap adds a closed two-cycle in the ball and hence changes the count by zero. At each transverse intersection its chart orientation sign is exactly the local orientation evaluation in cap duality, so this geometric count is the homological intersection form of [F4]. Thus the same rule applies to these cycle representatives and to an independent copy for a self-pairing.

Every loop of $F$ is trivial in $\pi_1(V_F)$: its pushed bank copy lies in the ball $Q$. The map $\pi_1(F)\to\pi_1(H)$ is onto, as is seen in the standard handlebody by its $g$ longitude curves on the punctured boundary. Its kernel kills only these boundary relations. Applying [F3] to $V_F\cup(H\times S^1)$ therefore kills all of the free handlebody group and identifies its circle factor with the positive meridian of $V_F$. No relation kills any power of that meridian: the maps to $\mathbb Z$ which are zero on $\pi_1(H)$ and one on the circle and meridian agree on the overlap. Hence $\pi_1(W_F)=\mathbb Z$ with exactly the specified generator. Reduction modulo $d$ gives the claimed extensions on the actual boundary.

For completeness the four cap pairings give the following finite table, in our first-positive-push convention: $$\begin{array}{c|c}k&\Sigma_i\mathbin{\cdot}T^k\Sigma_j\\\hline 0&V_{ij}+V_{ji}\\ 1&-V_{ij}\\ -1&-V_{ji}\\ |k|>1&0. \end{array}$$ Indeed the two same-chamber upper-upper and lower-lower boundary pairings are respectively $\operatorname{lk}(a_i,a_j^+)=V_{ji}$ and $\operatorname{lk}(a_j,a_i^+)=V_{ij}$, by moving the two chosen normal levels simultaneously without crossing either curve. The lower cap has opposite boundary orientation; at a neighboring chamber exactly one of the two caps is lower, giving the minus sign. The positive neighboring translate pairs the positive push of $a_i$ with $a_j$, and the negative neighboring translate pairs the opposite order. Nonneighboring chamber interiors are disjoint. This also proves the diagonal entries by using an independent parallel cycle before taking the same class. Hence the table sums to $(1-t)V+(1-t^{-1})V^T$. It is Hermitian for $t^*=t^{-1}$. With this displayed pairing, $\lambda(Tx,y)=t\lambda(x,y)$ and $\lambda(x,Ty)=t^{-1}\lambda(x,y)$ by shifting the summation index, explicitly fixing the coefficient convention.

For coefficients with $1-t$ invertible, the complexes of both $F\times S^1$ and $H\times S^1$ are contractible. Explicitly the cellular circle complex is $0\to R\xrightarrow{t-1}R\to0$ (or its inverse-deck version, differing by a unit); its contraction sends degree zero to degree one by $(t-1)^{-1}$. In the product total complex the contraction is $(-1)^p$ times this map on a degree-$p$ base chain; direct substitution in the total differential gives $ds+sd=1$. The finite product cells on $F,H$ give the same result for local singular homology by subdivision and their ordinary cellular comparison. The same calculation works directly for each $z\ne1$, with $(z-1)^{-1}$, including every singular Alexander root. Mayer–Vietoris in [F3] now makes $H_2(V_F)\to H_2(W_F)$ an isomorphism for these coefficients. The cycles of the cap calculation can be pushed into the interior of $V_F$, so their intersections computed in $W_F$ have exactly the same orientation and signs. This proves the localized and every nontrivial-character form assertions. Nothing here divides by $\det H(z)$.

The ordinary first homology of $M_K$ is one-dimensional, generated by the meridian. One can compute this with the same supplied exterior/tube: Mayer–Vietoris for $S^3=E_K\cup(S^1\times D^2)$ says that the torus first homology maps isomorphically to the direct sum of the two first homologies, because $H_2(S^3)=H_1(S^3)=0$. The tube kills the meridian, so the exterior homology is generated by it; its kernel slope is the preferred longitude since $F$ bounds it in the exterior. The zero filling kills precisely that longitude and retains the meridian. By step4.2 the map $H_1(M_K)\to H_1(W_F)$ is consequently an isomorphism. The pair exact sequence and [F4] then show that $H_2(W_F)\to H_2(W_F,M_K)$ is onto between vector spaces of equal dimension, hence an isomorphism. Its intersection form is therefore nonsingular. Its $g$-dimensional isotropic subspace from step3.2 has half its dimension. This establishes the ordinary part without substituting $t=1$ into the localized basis, which would be invalid.
