Assume full AC, matching the chosen finite twisted-chain and maximal-abelian-cover conventions. Let K be a smooth oriented knot, M(K) its preferred-longitude zero-framed surgery, W a compact connected oriented smooth 4-manifold with boundary M(K), and π=π₁(W). Put π^(0)=π and π^(j+1)=[π^(j),π^(j)]. A right Zπ-chain complex with coefficients in a left Z[π/π^(j)]-module is formed by tensoring over Zπ with that module.

For n≥0, W is an integral n-solution for K when H₁(M(K);Z)→H₁(W;Z) is an isomorphism, H₂(W;Z) is free of rank 2r for some finite r, and there are classes x₁,…,x_r,y₁,…,y_r in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n)]) whose equivariant intersection pairings satisfy λ_n(x_i,x_j)=0 and λ_n(x_i,y_j)=δ_ij. It is an integral (n+1/2)-solution when, in addition, each x_i is the image of a class x̃_i in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n+1)]) and λ_{n+1}(x̃_i,x̃_j)=0 for all i,j. Here λ_j is the equivariant intersection pairing induced by the orientation of W.

For a commutative ring R with 1≠0, a group G belongs to Strebel's class D(R) if every homomorphism between projective RG-modules is injective whenever its tensor with the trivial G-module R is injective. In this page R is Q or F_p for a prime p. For a countable discrete group G, its group von Neumann algebra N G is the weak-operator closure of CG in the left regular representation on ℓ²(G), with trace τ_G(T)=⟨Tδ_e,δ_e⟩. The von Neumann dimension of a finitely generated projective N G-module represented by a projection E is τ_G(E); for an arbitrary module it is the supremum of the dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules.

For a compact oriented 4-manifold W with boundary, sign(W) is the inertia difference of the symmetric intersection form on H₂(W;R) modulo its radical (the subspace pairing to zero with every class), equivalently on the image of H₂(W;R)→H₂(W,∂W;R). Given a closed oriented 3-manifold M, a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G, a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G of φ, the L²-signature sign_G^(2)(W,ψ) is the von Neumann signature of the nonsingular part of the N G-coefficient intersection form. When such a W and extension exist, the signature defect is sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is called the rho invariant of (M,φ) only after its independence of the bounding data is established by a separate bordism argument.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology:
$$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically,
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$
If a basepoint and one oriented lift of each cell outside $A$ are supplied on every component, the $n$th group is the direct sum of the corresponding coefficient fibers, and its boundary is the signed $R[\pi]$ incidence matrix acting through monodromy.

derivations.claim: Denote by $t$ the cyclic shift on the standard orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C[G]$. Its powers $1,t,\ldots,t^{d-1}$ are linearly independent, since their values on $\delta_e$ are the distinct basis vectors, and they span a finite-dimensional unital star algebra, hence a strongly closed algebra. Thus $\mathcal N G=\mathbb C[G]$. Put $$e_r=\frac1d\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\zeta^{-rk}t^k.$$ The geometric sum is $d$ if its exponent is divisible by $d$, and zero otherwise, by multiplying it by $1-\zeta^j$. Consequently $e_re_s=\delta_{rs}e_r$, $\sum_re_r=1$, $e_r^*=e_r$ and $te_r=\zeta^re_r$. Each $e_r$ has one-dimensional range on the regular representation and trace $1/d$, its identity coefficient. This includes $d=1$. Hence $\mathcal N G\cong\bigoplus_r\mathbb C e_r$ as a traced star algebra, with trace $d^{-1}\sum_r$.

Lift the finitely many cells of the supplied pair to the cover. Their translates identify its complex cellular chains with the finite free $\mathbb C[G]$ chains of $W$. Multiplying by the finitely many $e_r$ gives a direct sum of complexes; on the $r$th summand every monodromy matrix is evaluated at $t=\zeta^r$. This is precisely the character cellular complex. Projection and inclusion commute with the differential, so kernels and images split in these summands. All the spaces have finite complex dimension, so every image is closed; reduced Hilbert homology and ordinary homology agree, including in relative degrees. Thus the actual middle homology splits as the sum of the character homologies, without a flatness or tensor-exactness assumption.

The intersection pairing respects this splitting. Its sesquilinearity gives, in the linear-first convention, $$\lambda(e_rx,e_sy)=e_r\lambda(x,y)e_s,$$ since $e_s^*=e_s$; this is zero for $r\ne s$. Within one summand its value is its scalar character form times $e_r$. This can also be seen directly on cells: lift one relative orientation chain from $W$ and add all its translates to get the orientation chain of the cover. Cup, cap, boundary and evaluation are finite linear formulas commuting with the central projections. The coefficient-at-identity pairing on a basis of lifted chains counts exactly their ordinary intersections in the cover. For Fourier-projected lift cycles $P_rx=d^{-1}\sum_k\zeta^{-rk}T^kx$, the ordinary cover pairing is the scalar character pairing divided by $d$; expand the two sums and put $j=b-a$ to get $$ I(P_rx,P_ry)=\frac1d\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}(x\mathbin{\cdot}T^jy)\zeta^{rj}.$$ Here $I$ is the ordinary real cover intersection form extended complex linearly in its first argument and conjugate linearly in its second. Thus all normalizations differ only by the positive scalar $d^{-1}$ on a character component. If the alternate inverse-deck convention is used it interchanges $r$ and $d-r$, which leaves the finite sum unchanged.

In any character block choose a basis of middle homology. Its form matrix is Hermitian; its radical is exactly its kernel. By [F2] the positive and negative spectral spaces have dimensions $n_+(\lambda_r),n_-(\lambda_r)$, and the zero eigenspace is its radical. These dimensions do not depend on the chosen basis: a maximal positive subspace has dimension $n_+$, since projection to the positive spectral space is injective on any positive subspace, and that spectral space itself is positive. An invertible basis change bijects positive subspaces; repeat with the negative form for $n_-$. The same argument applies to a positive scalar multiple and to a transpose by complex conjugation. In the direct sum of step2 the full radical is the direct sum of these kernels, because all cross blocks vanish. No component is removed by assuming that a determinant is nonzero.

On a finite $\mathcal N G$ module, a projection whose character ranks are $q_r$ has trace $\sum_rq_r/d$: represent it on a finite free module using step1, apply the ordinary matrix trace in each component, and sum the diagonal identity coefficients. Applied to the positive and negative homology projections of step4 this yields $$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W,\psi)=\frac1d\sum_r(n_+(\lambda_r)-n_-(\lambda_r)).$$ The ordinary cover form is the orthogonal sum of the same finite character blocks, with the positive normalization of step3, so its signature is the sum of their signatures. This proves both equalities, with every radical and the trivial character retained. The argument was for this actual finite cover and finite complex, and used neither a closed-signature index theorem nor a bordism-independence assertion.

$(\mathbb{Q}, +, \cdot, 0, 1)$ with the operations of [[def-rat-operations]]
is a field: a commutative ring with $1 \ne 0$ in which every nonzero element
has a multiplicative inverse.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with additive identity $0_F$, multiplicative
identity $1_F$, and the field axioms as stated there. A **vector space over $F$**,
also called an **$F$-vector space**, consists of

- a set $V$, whose elements are called **vectors**;
- a binary operation $+ : V \times V \to V$ on $V$ ([[def-binary-operation]]),
  the **vector addition**;
- an element $0_V \in V$, the **zero vector**;
- a map $\cdot \,:\, F \times V \to V$, the **scalar multiplication**, written
  $\lambda v := \cdot(\lambda, v)$;

subject to the following axioms, in which $u, v \in V$ and $\lambda, \mu \in F$
are arbitrary.

- **(V1)** $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]): $+$ is associative
  and commutative, $0_V$ is a two-sided identity for $+$
  ([[def-identity-element]]), and every $v \in V$ has an additive inverse
  ([[def-invertible-element]]).
- **(V2)** $\lambda(u + v) = \lambda u + \lambda v$.
- **(V3)** $(\lambda + \mu)v = \lambda v + \mu v$.
- **(V4)** $(\lambda\mu)v = \lambda(\mu v)$.
- **(V5)** $1_F v = v$.

The elements of $F$ are called **scalars**. When several vector spaces are in
play we write $0_V$ for the zero of $V$, and we write $-v$ for the additive
inverse of $v$ and $u - v := u + (-v)$.

**The notation $0_V$ and $-v$ is legitimate.** Axiom (V1) asserts only that some
two-sided identity and some additive inverses exist. That there is at most one
two-sided identity for $+$ is [[lem-identity-unique]], and that an invertible
element of a monoid has exactly one inverse is [[lem-inverse-unique]]; both are
proved before [[def-group]] and are inherited here with the group structure. So
$0_V$ and $-v$ denote well-defined elements, and nothing below re-derives them.

**What (V1) buys, and why it is not restated.** Associativity, commutativity, the
identity law $v + 0_V = v = 0_V + v$, the inverse law $v + (-v) = 0_V$,
cancellation ([[lem-group-cancellation]]) and the inverse identities
([[lem-group-inverse-laws]]) are facts about abelian groups. They are quoted from
the group page wherever they are used and are never proved again for vectors.

Write $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for the embedding of
[[lem-nat-embeds-int]], and for $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ put

$$g\mathbb{Z} \;:=\; \{\, gk \;:\; k \in \mathbb{Z} \,\} .$$

Then $(\mathbb{Z},+,0)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), $g\mathbb{Z}$ is the
cyclic subgroup $\langle g \rangle$ generated by $g$
([[def-generated-subgroup]]) for every $g$, and:

**every subgroup $H \le (\mathbb{Z},+)$ ([[def-subgroup]]) equals
$\iota(n)\mathbb{Z} = \langle \iota(n) \rangle$ for exactly one natural number
$n$.** When $H = \{0\}$ that natural number is $0$; otherwise it is the natural
number whose image is the least positive element of $H$.

In particular every subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ is cyclic.

derivations.claim: On pairs $(a,n)$ with $a\in A$ and positive integer $n$, put $(a,n)\sim(b,m)$ when $ma=nb$. This is an equivalence relation. Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate. If $ma=nb$ and $pb=mc$, then $m(pa-nc)=0$, so torsion-freeness gives $pa=nc$, proving transitivity. Denote the class of $(a,n)$ by $[a,n]$ and its quotient set by $V$. Define $[a,n]+[b,m]=[ma+nb,nm]$, $-[a,n]=[-a,n]$, $0=[0,1]$, and $(r/s)[a,n]=[ra,sn]$ for integer $r$ and positive integer $s$. These are independent of representatives: if $n'a=na'$ and $m'b=mb'$, multiplying the first relation by $mm'$ and the second by $nn'$ gives the cross-multiplied equality for the two proposed sums. If also $r/s=r'/s'$, then $rs'=r's$ and $s'n'ra=snr'a'$, which gives the scalar equality. Negation and zero respect the relation as well.

For completeness, every subgroup $H\le\mathbb Z^d$ is free on at most $d$ elements, by induction on the finite integer $d$. The case $d=0$ has the empty basis. For $d>0$, project to the first coordinate. Its image is $c\mathbb Z$ by [F2]. The kernel is identified by the remaining coordinates with a subgroup of $\mathbb Z^{d-1}$, so the induction hypothesis gives it a basis of at most $d-1$ elements. If $c=0$, this kernel is all of $H$. If $c>0$, take one element $h\in H$ with first coordinate $c$. Every $x\in H$ has first coordinate $nc$ for a unique integer $n$, and $x-nh$ is in the kernel. Hence the kernel basis together with $h$ generates $H$. It is independent, because the first coordinate of a relation first forces the coefficient of $h$ to be zero, and then independence of the kernel basis forces all remaining coefficients to be zero. This proves the induction step for every subgroup, without assuming it is finitely generated in advance.

The operations make $V$ a rational vector space. Addition is commutative because $ma+nb=nb+ma$, and both associations of a three-term sum have representative $[mpa+npb+nmc,nmp]$ for inputs $[a,n],[b,m],[c,p]$. Zero is an identity and the negative sums to $[0,n^2]=[0,1]$. The identities $(r/s)([a,n]+[b,m])=(r/s)[a,n]+(r/s)[b,m]$ and $(r/s+t/u)[a,n]=(r/s)[a,n]+(t/u)[a,n]$ follow by cross multiplication, reducing respectively to $r(ma+nb)=mra+nrb$ and $(ru+ts)a=rua+tsa$. Scalar associativity follows from $[rta,sun]$ for $(r/s)(t/u)[a,n]$, and scalar $1$ acts as the identity. These are all axioms in [F1]. The map $\eta:A\to V$, $\eta(a)=[a,1]$, is additive and injective, since $[a,1]=[0,1]$ forces $a=0$. Every $[a,n]$ equals $(1/n)\eta(a)$, so $V$ is spanned over $\mathbb Q$ by the fixed finite list $\eta(a_1),\ldots,\eta(a_m)$.

Process that finite spanning list in its given order, retaining a vector exactly when it does not belong to the span of those previously retained. The resulting list $b_1,\ldots,b_r$ spans $V$, because each discarded vector was already in the span of an earlier retained sublist. It is independent: in a nonzero finite relation, the last vector with nonzero coefficient would belong to the span of the earlier ones, contrary to its retention rule. Thus it is a basis, constructed by a finite recursion rather than by an arbitrary basis-selection theorem. Each $\eta(a_j)$ has unique rational coordinates in this basis. Take $D>0$ to be the product of the positive denominators of the finitely many coordinates, using $D=1$ for the empty product. For $a\in A$, define $\Phi(a)$ as $D$ times the coordinate vector of $\eta(a)$. Every $a$ is an integer linear combination of the $a_j$, so $\Phi(a)\in\mathbb Z^r$. The map $\Phi:A\to\mathbb Z^r$ is additive and injective, since $D\ne0$, coordinates are unique and $\eta$ is injective.

Apply step 1.2 to $H=\Phi(A)\le\mathbb Z^r$. Its finite basis and the injective map in step 3.1 identify $A$ with $\mathbb Z^t$ for some $t\le r$, giving the asserted finite freeness (rename $t$ to $r$ in the first assertion). The only selections were a single finite generating list, finitely many unique coordinate tuples, and at most one lift at each of finitely many integer-coordinate induction stages. Existence of such finitely many witnesses does not require any choice axiom. The explicit rationalization and integer-subgroup proof used no general PID structure or factorization theorem.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) and let $G$ be a group
([[def-group]]). The **group ring** $R[G]$ is the free left $R$-module on the
set $G$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]).

For each $g \in G$, write $[g] \in R[G]$ for the standard basis vector indexed
by $g$. Thus every element of $R[G]$ has a unique expression
$$\sum_{g \in F} r_g [g]$$
with $F \subseteq G$ finite and $r_g \in R$.

The notation is deliberately that of **formal** finite sums: at this stage
$R[G]$ is only the underlying free $R$-module with its distinguished basis. The
multiplication satisfying
$$[g][h]=[gh]$$
and the resulting $R$-algebra structure are constructed in
[[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $G$ be a group. Write $[g] \in R[G]$ for
the basis vector of [[def-group-ring]] indexed by $g \in G$.

There is a unique $R$-bilinear multiplication on $R[G]$ satisfying
$$[g][h]=[gh]\qquad(g,h\in G).$$
With this product, $R[G]$ is a unital $R$-algebra whose underlying
$R$-module has basis $\{[g]:g\in G\}$. Its identity is $[e]$, where $e$ is the
identity of $G$, and every basis element $[g]$ is a unit with inverse
$[g^{-1}]$.

Every finitely generated torsion-free abelian group $A$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^r$ for some finite integer $r\ge0$. Here torsion-free means $na=0$ with $n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$ implies $a=0$. More precisely, a fixed finite generating list yields an embedding of $A$ into a finite-rank integer lattice, and every subgroup of $\mathbb Z^r$ has a basis of at most $r$ elements. These conclusions require no form of the Axiom of Choice and no general PID factorization or structure theorem.

derivations.claim: Let $B$ be the subgroup of $A$ generated by the images of the finite supports of $f$ and $g$. It is finitely generated, torsion-free and abelian, so [F2] identifies it with $\mathbb Z^r$. Transport the lexicographic order from $\mathbb Z^r$ to $B$. This is a total order invariant under addition. No order on the whole quotient or on $G$ is needed. Let $X,Y\subseteq B$ be the finite quotient supports of $f,g$. Choose lifts $t_x\in G$ for the finitely many elements of $X\cup Y\cup(X+Y)$, using the same lift for any repeated element. By grouping terms in each coset, [F1] gives unique expressions $f=\sum_{x\in X}r_xt_x$ and $g=\sum_{y\in Y}s_yt_y$ with $0\ne r_x,s_y\in k[H]$. Distinct cosets have disjoint group bases, so these grouped coefficients are nonzero.

For these lifts put $\alpha_x(s)=t_xst_x^{-1}$ on $k[H]$ and $h_{x,y}=t_xt_yt_{x+y}^{-1}\in H$. Normality makes $\alpha_x$ a ring automorphism, with inverse conjugation by $t_x^{-1}$. Direct multiplication gives $(r_xt_x)(s_yt_y)=r_x\alpha_x(s_y)h_{x,y}t_{x+y}$. This is the crossed-product multiplication on the finite supports. The factor $h_{x,y}$ is retained and is a unit; it is not assumed to be $1$. Its compatibility with iterated multiplication is inherited from associativity in $G$. Thus the calculation applies to a nonsplit extension.

Let $x_0=\max X$ and $y_0=\max Y$. Every other pair $(x,y)$ satisfies $x+y<x_0+y_0$: if $x<x_0$, then $x+y\le x+y_0<x_0+y_0$, and if $x=x_0$ but $y<y_0$, addition invariance gives the same strict inequality. Hence the coefficient of $t_{x_0+y_0}$ in $fg$ is the single term $r_{x_0}\alpha_{x_0}(s_{y_0})h_{x_0,y_0}$. It is nonzero by [A1], invertibility of $h_{x_0,y_0}$ and injectivity of $\alpha_{x_0}$. By disjointness of coset bases, $fg\ne0$. Since $f,g$ were arbitrary, $k[G]$ has no zero divisors. Only finitely many lifts were chosen, so the proof introduces no choice axiom.

Let $G$ be a group, let $S\subseteq G$ be finite, and let $\varepsilon>0$. A
finite nonempty subset $F\subseteq G$ is an **$(S,\varepsilon)$-Folner set** if

$$|sF\triangle F|<\varepsilon|F|\qquad\text{for every }s\in S.$$

The group $G$ satisfies the **Folner condition** if for every finite
$S\subseteq G$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists an $(S,\varepsilon)$-Folner
set.

Every finitely generated torsion-free abelian group $A$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^r$ for some finite integer $r\ge0$. Here torsion-free means $na=0$ with $n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$ implies $a=0$. More precisely, a fixed finite generating list yields an embedding of $A$ into a finite-rank integer lattice, and every subgroup of $\mathbb Z^r$ has a basis of at most $r$ elements. These conclusions require no form of the Axiom of Choice and no general PID factorization or structure theorem.

A group G is poly-torsion-free abelian (PTFA) if it admits a finite subnormal series
1=G_0 ◁ G_1 ◁ ⋯ ◁ G_m=G
in which every quotient G_{j+1}/G_j is torsion-free abelian. The trivial group is PTFA, using the length-zero series. The term “subnormal” means each G_j is normal in G_{j+1}; normality in all of G is not required.

derivations.claim: A torsion-free abelian group satisfies [F1]. Indeed the subgroup generated by a finite test set is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^r$ by [F2]. For $r=0$ use the singleton identity set. For $r>0$ bound every test vector's coordinates in absolute value by $M\ge0$ and take the integer cube $E_n=[-n,n]^r\cap\mathbb Z^r$, with $n\ge M$. A translate by any test vector has intersection with $E_n$ of cardinality at least $(2n+1-M)^r$, whereas both sets have cardinality $(2n+1)^r$. Thus its relative symmetric difference is at most $2[1-(1-M/(2n+1))^r]$, which tends to zero. The transported cube witnesses the required condition in the original group. All choices concern a single finitely generated subgroup and a finite test set.

Suppose $1\to H\to G\xrightarrow{\pi}Q\to1$ is any group extension and both $H,Q$ satisfy [F1]. Fix finite $S\subseteq G$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Choose a finite nonempty $(\pi(S),\varepsilon/2)$-Folner set $E\subseteq Q$. For the finite set $E\cup\pi(S)E$, choose lifts $t_q\in G$. For each $s\in S$ and $q\in E$ with $\pi(s)q\in E$, put $h_{s,q}=t_{\pi(s)q}^{-1}st_q\in H$. This is a finite collection of elements of $H$. Choose a finite nonempty set $B\subseteq H$ with $|h_{s,q}B\triangle B|<(\varepsilon/2)|B|$ for all of them, and let $F=\bigcup_{q\in E}t_qB$. Its cosets are disjoint, so $|F|=|E||B|$.

For $s\in S$, the cosets present in exactly one of $sF,F$ contribute $|\pi(s)E\triangle E||B|$ elements to the symmetric difference. On a common coset indexed by $\pi(s)q$, the two subsets are $t_{\pi(s)q}h_{s,q}B$ and $t_{\pi(s)q}B$, whose difference has cardinality $|h_{s,q}B\triangle B|$. There are at most $|E|$ common cosets. Therefore $|sF\triangle F|\le|\pi(s)E\triangle E||B|+\sum_{q\in E,\,\pi(s)q\in E}|h_{s,q}B\triangle B|<\varepsilon|E||B|=\varepsilon|F|$. This proves the extension assertion for an arbitrary extension; the lifts were not required to form a homomorphism or a global transversal.

The trivial group satisfies [F1] using its singleton set. Induct up the given finite subnormal series. At each stage the kernel is the previous subgroup and the quotient is torsion-free abelian, so step 1.1 supplies the quotient condition and step 2.1 supplies the extension condition. This proves [F1] for every PTFA group in the full subnormal convention of [F3]. The construction uses only finitely many witnesses at each of finitely many stages. It constructs finite sets directly, without invariant means, ultrafilters or simultaneous choices over a family of tests, and hence adds no choice hypothesis.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) and let $G$ be a group
([[def-group]]). The **group ring** $R[G]$ is the free left $R$-module on the
set $G$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]).

For each $g \in G$, write $[g] \in R[G]$ for the standard basis vector indexed
by $g$. Thus every element of $R[G]$ has a unique expression
$$\sum_{g \in F} r_g [g]$$
with $F \subseteq G$ finite and $r_g \in R$.

The notation is deliberately that of **formal** finite sums: at this stage
$R[G]$ is only the underlying free $R$-module with its distinguished basis. The
multiplication satisfying
$$[g][h]=[gh]$$
and the resulting $R$-algebra structure are constructed in
[[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $G$ be a group. Write $[g] \in R[G]$ for
the basis vector of [[def-group-ring]] indexed by $g \in G$.

There is a unique $R$-bilinear multiplication on $R[G]$ satisfying
$$[g][h]=[gh]\qquad(g,h\in G).$$
With this product, $R[G]$ is a unital $R$-algebra whose underlying
$R$-module has basis $\{[g]:g\in G\}$. Its identity is $[e]$, where $e$ is the
identity of $G$, and every basis element $[g]$ is a unit with inverse
$[g^{-1}]$.

Let $G$ be a group, let $S\subseteq G$ be finite, and let $\varepsilon>0$. A
finite nonempty subset $F\subseteq G$ is an **$(S,\varepsilon)$-Folner set** if

$$|sF\triangle F|<\varepsilon|F|\qquad\text{for every }s\in S.$$

The group $G$ satisfies the **Folner condition** if for every finite
$S\subseteq G$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists an $(S,\varepsilon)$-Folner
set.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

A **ring** is a set $R$ carrying two binary operations ([[def-binary-operation]]),
addition $+$ and multiplication $\cdot$, and two distinguished elements $0$ and
$1$ of $R$, such that

- **(R1)** $(R, +, 0)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]): addition is
  associative and commutative, $0 + x = x = x + 0$ for every $x \in R$, and every
  $x \in R$ has an additive inverse;
- **(R2)** $(R, \cdot, 1)$ is a monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]):
  multiplication is associative and $1 \cdot x = x = x \cdot 1$ for every
  $x \in R$;
- **(R3)** multiplication distributes over addition **on both sides**: for all
  $x, y, z \in R$,

$$x \cdot (y + z) \;=\; x \cdot y + x \cdot z, \qquad (y + z) \cdot x \;=\; y \cdot x + z \cdot x .$$

We write $xy$ for $x \cdot y$, call $0$ the **zero** and $1$ the **identity** (or
**unity**) of $R$, write $-x$ for the additive inverse of $x$, and abbreviate
$x - y := x + (-y)$.

**Why "the" zero, "the" identity and "the" additive inverse are legitimate.**
Each of $0$ and $1$ is a two-sided identity for its own operation, and a binary
operation has at most one two-sided identity ([[lem-identity-unique]],
[[def-identity-element]]), so each is determined by the operation and the
notation is single-valued. An additive inverse of $x$ is an inverse in the
monoid $(R,+,0)$ ([[def-invertible-element]]), and in a monoid an element has at
most one inverse ([[lem-inverse-unique]]); so $-x$ names one element, and a
single equation $y + x = 0$ already forces $y = -x$.

**Convention: a ring has an identity.** Axiom (R2) asks for a *monoid*, so the
existence of $1$ is part of the definition and is not an extra hypothesis to be
carried around. This is the convention used throughout this library. A structure
satisfying (R1), (R3) and the associativity half of (R2), but not required to
have a multiplicative identity, is called a **non-unital ring** (also *rng*); it
is not called a ring here, and where such a structure occurs it is named as a
non-unital ring in as many words. The distinction has content: the companion
page exhibits a subset of $\mathbb{Z}$ that is closed under addition, additive
inverses and multiplication and is not a subring, precisely because it misses
the identity.

Nothing above requires $1 \ne 0$. A ring in which $1 = 0$ has exactly one
element; the companion page records it as the **zero ring**. Definitions that
need $1 \ne 0$ — integral domain, division ring, field — say so explicitly.

A **division ring** (also **skew field**) is a ring $D$ ([[def-ring]]) such that

- **(V1)** $1 \ne 0$ in $D$;
- **(V2)** every $x \in D$ with $x \ne 0$ is a unit, that is, has a two-sided
  multiplicative inverse ([[def-invertible-element]],
  [[lem-ring-units-form-a-group]]).

Equivalently, $D^{\times} = D \setminus \{0\}$: by (V2) every nonzero element is
a unit, and by (V1) together with [[lem-ring-units-form-a-group]] the element
$0$ is not a unit, since $0$ is a unit only when $1 = 0$. Consequently
$(D \setminus \{0\}, \cdot, 1)$ is a group ([[lem-ring-units-form-a-group]]); in
particular $D \setminus \{0\}$ is closed under multiplication, so a division
ring has no zero divisors.

A **commutative division ring** is a division ring whose multiplication is
commutative. Those are exactly the fields
([[lem-commutative-division-ring-is-a-field]],
[[lem-field-is-a-commutative-ring]]).

e s\in I$, $0

e0$ but $0
e t\in\ker f$, choose $0
e su=tv$ by the right Ore condition; here $u
e0$. Right linearity gives $f(s)u=f(t)v=0$, contradicting absence of zero divisors.

Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate, and transitivity follows by intersecting the two nonzero agreement ideals using step 2.2. This defines a quotient set $D$. Denote the class of a map by $[f]$. The class is zero exactly when its map is identically zero: a nonzero map is injective by step 2.2 and cannot vanish on a nonzero ideal. Define addition by the sum on the intersection of domains, and define $[f][g]=[f\circ g]$ on $g^{-1}(I)$ if $I$ is the domain of $f$ and $J$ is the domain of $g$. That preimage is a right ideal. It is nonzero if $g=0$, when it is all $J$; otherwise choose $t\in J$ with $g(t)\ne0$ and a nonzero element $g(t)r\in g(t)R\cap I$. Then $tr\ne0$ belongs to the preimage. Thus multiplication is always represented on a nonzero right ideal.

These operations are independent of representatives. For addition, intersect the two agreement ideals and all relevant domains. For multiplication, if $f=f'$ on a nonzero ideal $U$ and $g=g'$ on a nonzero ideal $V$, restrict to $V\cap g^{-1}(U)$. This is nonzero by step 2.2 and the preimage argument of step 3.1, and both composites agree there. Zero maps cause no exception: they may be represented by the zero map on all $R$, and equivalent maps representing zero are actually zero on their domains. Thus addition and multiplication are well-defined. The additive zero is the zero map on $R$, additive inverse is $-f$, and the multiplicative identity is the identity map on $R$.

The ring identities hold on nonzero common restriction ideals, hence in $D$. For addition and its commutativity and associativity, use the intersection of all three domains and the ordinary additive identities of $R$. For multiplication of nonzero representatives $f,g,h$, the two associative composites agree on the nonzero ideal of those $x$ for which $h(x)$ lies in the domain of $g$ and $g(h(x))$ lies in the domain of $f$; successive preimages are nonzero because the maps are injective and the preimage argument of step 3.1 applies. If a representative is zero, both composites are zero. For $f(g+h)=fg+fh$, restrict first to the common domain of $g,h$, then to the intersection of the preimages of the domain of $f$ under each nonzero one of $g,h$. These are nonzero ideals and their intersection is nonzero; zero summands impose no restriction. Both $g(x),h(x)$ and their sum then lie in the domain of $f$, and additivity of $f$ proves equality there. For $(f+g)h=fh+gh$, restrict to the preimage under $h$ of the intersection of the domains of $f,g$; the same argument applies. Identity and zero laws hold by their defining maps. This verifies every unital ring axiom without a formal-fraction associativity assumption.

Map $r\in R$ to the class of left multiplication $L_r:R\to R$, $L_r(x)=rx$. This is a unital ring homomorphism, since $L_r+L_s=L_{r+s}$ and $L_r\circ L_s=L_{rs}$. It is injective: for $r\ne0$, its restriction to every nonzero ideal is nonzero by absence of zero divisors, so its class is not zero by step 3.1. In particular $1\ne0$ in $D$. For a nonzero class $[f]$, the representative $f:I\to R$ is injective by step 2.2 and its image $f(I)$ is a nonzero right ideal. The inverse function $f^{-1}:f(I)\to I\subseteq R$ is right-linear. Its two composites with $f$ are the identity maps on $I$ and $f(I)$ respectively, hence represent $1$ in $D$. Thus every nonzero class has a two-sided inverse, and [F3] makes $D$ a division ring.

Finally choose $0\ne s\in I$ for a representative $f:I\to R$ and put $a=f(s)$. The composite $f\circ L_s$ is defined on all $R$, because $sR\subseteq I$, and sends $x$ to $ax$. Thus $[f]L_s=L_a$, and in the embedded-ring notation $[f]=as^{-1}$. Every element of $D$ is therefore a right fraction and every nonzero original denominator is invertible. The only selections were finitely many elements in individual nonempty sets at each proof step; no choice function on an infinite family was used. Together with steps 1.1 and 2.1 this proves every assertion.

The positive normal is determined by the surface and ambient orientations. Use the preferred longitude and positive meridian of this actual surface and tube in the zero-surgery manifold $M_K$.

A finite smooth construction gives a compact connected oriented four-manifold $W_F$ with its actual oriented boundary identified with $M_K$, and an isomorphism $\pi_1(W_F)\cong\mathbb Z$ taking the positive meridian to $1$. Thus the positive meridian map $\pi_1(M_K)\to\mathbb Z/d$ extends over $W_F$ for every positive integer $d$. The ordinary intersection form of $W_F$ is nonsingular over $\mathbb R$, has dimension $2g$, contains an isotropic subspace of dimension $g$, and has signature zero.

More precisely, put $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$ and $R=\Lambda[(1-t)^{-1}]$. The positive deck generator is denoted $T$. With the equivariant pairing **linear in the first variable**
$$\lambda(x,y)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(x\mathbin{\cdot}T^ky)t^k,$$
the localized second homology has a basis of size $2g$ and matrix
$$H(t)=(1-t)V+(1-t^{-1})V^T.$$
For every unit complex number $z\ne1$, the corresponding character component has actual second homology of dimension $2g$ and intersection matrix $H(z)$, up to a positive scalar if Fourier-projected lift cycles are used as basis. This assertion includes singular matrices $H(z)$: no Alexander-polynomial nonvanishing is required. Equivalently, in the conjugate-first convention the matrix is the transpose, with the same signature. The trivial-character component is the ordinary metabolic form just described; the zero matrix $H(1)$ is not asserted to be its homology-basis matrix.

Use the standing AC and canonical-trace convention of the $L^2$ signature definition. Let $W$ be a compact oriented four-manifold with a supplied finite CW pair model for its boundary and a surjection $\psi:\pi_1(W)\to G=\mathbb Z/d$, $d\ge1$. Let $\widetilde W_\psi$ be its actual degree-$d$ cover, and write $\zeta=\exp(2\pi i/d)$. For $0\le r<d$, let $\lambda_r$ be the character intersection form for the character sending the specified positive generator of $G$ to $\zeta^r$. Then, allowing arbitrary radicals,
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W,\psi)=\frac{\operatorname{sign}(\widetilde W_\psi)}d=\frac1d\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}\operatorname{sign}(\lambda_r).$$
Here the ordinary cover signature, like each character signature, means positive inertia minus negative inertia with the kernel discarded. Changing consistently from linear-first to conjugate-first pairings transposes the character matrices and does not change the formula. No independence of a bounding manifold, no infinite-cyclic integration and no arbitrary-group index assertion is part of this statement.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite

relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary

Let $M$ be a closed oriented three-manifold with a specified coefficient homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(M_j)\to\Gamma$ on each component, where $\Gamma$ is PTFA. The integral coefficient ring is $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$ with its fraction division ring $K\Gamma$. More generally let $k$ be $\mathbb Z$ or a commutative field, let $K$ be the fraction division ring of $k[\Gamma]$, and let $k[\Gamma]\subseteq R\subseteq K$ be an involution-stable unital intermediate ring. The involution fixes $k$ and sends $g$ to $g^{-1}$; on fractions it is the involutive anti-automorphism extending this formula. Taking $k=\mathbb Z$ and $R=\Lambda$ recovers the integral convention.

If $H_1(M;K)=0$, the coefficient Bockstein, oriented Poincaré duality and evaluation define the Blanchfield linking pairing
$$B_{M,\phi,R}:TH_1(M;R)\times TH_1(M;R)\longrightarrow K/R.$$
Here $T$ denotes the submodule of elements with a nonzero right annihilator, the first variable is conjugate-linear, and the second is right-linear. Nonsingularity means that the adjoint
$$\overline{TH_1(M;R)}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_R(TH_1(M;R),K/R)$$
is an isomorphism of left $R$-modules, where $r\cdot\bar x=\overline{x\bar r}$ on the conjugate module. This is equivalent to the conjugate-dual formulation in the right-module convention. For $\Gamma=\mathbb Z$ with generator $t$, $R=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ and $K=\mathbb Q(t)$ give the classical coefficient convention. Nonsingularity is a separate property of the defined pairing, with its coefficient hypotheses supplied by the nonsingularity theorem.

For a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G over a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, define the signature defect by ρ(M,φ;W,ψ)=sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is an invariant of (M,φ) only when a separate bordism-independence theorem applies.

derivations.claim: Choose finitely many line-bundle trivializing charts with smaller precompact subcharts covering $X$. In each larger chart choose a smooth nonnegative Euclidean bump $\rho_i$, supported inside it and positive on the smaller closure. Their sum is positive, so divide by the sum to make $\sum_i\rho_i=1$. A local nonzero frame $v_i$ defines a global smooth section $s_i=\rho_i v_i$ by zero extension; the support is strictly inside its frame chart. At every point some $s_i$ is nonzero. Thus $s=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)$ is a nowherezero section of $L^{\oplus m}$. A Hermitian metric on $L$ is constructed by the same finite positive weighted sum of local squared frame norms, which is positive on every nonzero fiber vector. Normalize $s$ in the induced direct-sum metric. Its span is a trivial smooth line subbundle, and the smooth orthogonal projection $u\mapsto\langle u,s\rangle s$ exhibits a smooth complementary bundle $Q$ (in a local frame, extend the nonzero vector to a frame using a nonzero coordinate minor). Hence $L^{\oplus m}\cong\mathbf1\oplus Q$. For empty $X$ take $m=1$ and the zero bundle ring.

For actual bundles define $\lambda_{-1}(E)=\sum_{k=0}^{\operatorname{rank}E}(-1)^k[\bigwedge^kE]$, componentwise if necessary. The fiberwise map which wedges an $i$-fold wedge from $E$ before a $j$-fold wedge from $F$ gives the smooth isomorphism $\bigwedge^k(E\oplus F)\cong\bigoplus_{i+j=k}\bigwedge^iE\otimes\bigwedge^jF$. Local basis wedges prove bijectivity and respect transitions, so finite distributivity gives $\lambda_{-1}(E\oplus F)=\lambda_{-1}(E)\lambda_{-1}(F)$. For a line $\lambda_{-1}(L)=1-[L]$ and $\lambda_{-1}(\mathbf1)=0$. Apply this actual-bundle identity to step1.1 to obtain $(1-[L])^m=\lambda_{-1}(L^{\oplus m})=\lambda_{-1}(\mathbf1\oplus Q)=0$. No exterior-power operation on virtual differences or splitting principle is used.

Put $x=[L]-1$ in the commutative ring of [F1]. The given tensor-power isomorphism implies $(1+x)^d=1$. Expanding the finite binomial gives $dx=-x^2q(x)$, where $q(x)=\sum_{j=2}^d\binom djx^{j-2}$ (zero if $d=1$). Induction then gives $d^k x=(-1)^k x^{k+1}q(x)^k$ for every nonnegative integer $k$: multiply the preceding identity by $d$ and substitute $dx=-x^2q(x)$, using commutativity. Step2.1 says $x^m=0$, so taking $k=m-1$ gives $d^{m-1}x=0$, including $m=1$. This is an actual integer annihilator, not just a rational equality.

Applying an additive $I$ to step3.1 gives $d^{m-1}(I([L])-I(1))=0$ in $\mathbb Z$. The coefficient is a positive integer, so the difference is zero. All charts, sections, bundle splittings, powers and sums used above were finite; no triangulation, classification of line bundles, Chern character or infinite-dimensional operator argument entered the assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold without boundary of real dimension $n\ge2$, equipped with a smooth positive density, and $E\to M$ a finite-rank real Euclidean or complex Hermitian smooth vector bundle. Let $P$ be a smooth-coefficient second-order differential operator on $E$, formally symmetric for the density and metric, whose positive-frequency principal symbol is
$$\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=a_x(\xi,\xi)I_{E_x},$$
where $a$ is a smooth positive-definite real quadratic form on cotangent vectors. Thus in any local frame $P=-a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+B^j\partial_j+C$, with scalar real positive-definite $a^{ij}$ and matrix-valued lower coefficients. Nonnegativity of $P$ is not needed here.

For nonnegative integers $k$, define $H^k(M,E)$ by requiring the coefficients of each member of a finite smooth partition of unity times the section, in precompact bundle charts and extended by zero, to lie in $H^k(\mathbb R^n)$; the norm is the square root of the sum of these component Sobolev norms squared. Different such choices give equivalent norms. The following hold.

1. These are Hilbert spaces, smooth sections are dense, $H^0=L^2$ with equivalent norms, $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^k$ is compact, and $H^k\hookrightarrow C^r$ continuously whenever $k>r+n/2$.
2. If $u\in H^1$ and $Pu=f\in H^k$ distributionally, then $u\in H^{k+2}$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|u\|_{L^2}).$$
In particular smooth data give smooth weak solutions. The same estimate holds for all $u\in H^{k+2}$.
3. For sufficiently large real $\lambda>0$, $P+\lambda:H^2\to L^2$ is a bounded bijection with bounded inverse $B:L^2\to H^2$. As an operator on $L^2$, $B$ is compact, injective and selfadjoint, has dense range $H^2$, and the unbounded operator $P$ with domain exactly $H^2$ is selfadjoint. The map $B:H^k\to H^{k+2}$ is bounded for every nonnegative integer $k$ and preserves smooth sections.
4. It supplies two-sided parametrices **modulo compact operators**:
$$PB=I-\lambda B\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad BP=I-\lambda B\quad\hbox{on }H^2.$$
Here on the second space $B$ denotes its restriction after inclusion $H^2\hookrightarrow L^2$; it is compact on $H^2$. No assertion concerning arbitrary-order elliptic operators, or pseudodifferential symbol classes, is part of this theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach
spaces over the same scalar field and let $T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is Fredholm
([[def-fredholm-operator-cokernel-and-index]]) if and only if there is a bounded
linear $S:Y\to X$ such that both $ST-I_X$ and $TS-I_Y$ are compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach
spaces over the same scalar field, let $T:X\to Y$ be a Fredholm operator and let
$K:X\to Y$ be compact ([[def-fredholm-operator-cokernel-and-index]],
[[def-compact-linear-operator]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Then $T+K$
is Fredholm and $\operatorname{ind}(T+K)=\operatorname{ind}T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold without boundary, of real dimension at least two. Its metric defines the $L^2$ pairing on forms by the Riemannian density; orientation is unnecessary. Let $d^*$ denote the formal adjoint of $d$, and $\Delta=dd^*+d^*d$ on total real forms, or on their complexification. With domain $H^2$ the operator is nonnegative and selfadjoint. Its degreewise smooth kernels $\mathcal H^k$ are finite dimensional, and there is an orthogonal smooth decomposition
$$\Omega^k(M)=\mathcal H^k\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}d\Omega^{k-1}(M)\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}d^*\Omega^{k+1}(M).$$
The map $h\mapsto[h]$ is an isomorphism $\mathcal H^k\to H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)$, over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ as appropriate.

More generally let $X$ be a compact complex manifold of complex dimension $m\ge1$ with a smooth Hermitian metric. Let $E$ be a holomorphic bundle of finite rank with a smooth Hermitian metric. The holomorphic bundle structure supplies frames with holomorphic invertible transition matrices; the Hermitian metric is separate smooth positive-definite pairing data. On $E$-valued $(p,q)$ forms, define $\bar\partial_E$ by the coefficientwise Dolbeault operator in holomorphic bundle charts and let $\bar\partial_E^*$ be its formal adjoint. For each fixed $p$, $\Delta_{\bar\partial_E}=\bar\partial_E\bar\partial_E^*+\bar\partial_E^*\bar\partial_E$ on the sum over $q$ is nonnegative and selfadjoint on $H^2$; its smooth harmonic spaces $\mathcal H_E^{p,q}$ are finite dimensional and
$$\Omega^{p,q}(X,E)=\mathcal H_E^{p,q}\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\bar\partial_E\Omega^{p,q-1}(X,E)\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\bar\partial_E^*\Omega^{p,q+1}(X,E).$$
In particular harmonic forms represent the smooth Dolbeault quotient
$$H_{\bar\partial}^{p,q}(X,E):=\ker\bar\partial_E/\operatorname{im}\bar\partial_E$$
uniquely. Terms outside the degree range are zero. This asserts smooth Dolbeault cohomology; an identification with sheaf cohomology requires a separate Dolbeault-resolution comparison theorem.

For either complex write $D=d$ or $D=\bar\partial_E$, $P=DD^*+D^*D$, and let $\Pi,G$ be the preceding Green projection and inverse. They preserve degree, $G$ preserves smooth forms, and on smooth forms
$$DG=GD,\qquad D^*G=GD^*,\qquad D\Pi=\Pi D=D^*\Pi=\Pi D^*=0.$$
Every closed smooth $u$ satisfies $u=\Pi u+D(D^*Gu)$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, integration on smooth simplices followed by the inverse of restriction from continuous to smooth singular cohomology gives a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras
$$J_M:H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R).$$
The source product is wedge of form classes, the target product is the front/back singular cup product, and both stars denote direct sums of the homogeneous groups. Naturality is for smooth maps. No compactness assumption is imposed.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $n$-manifold and let $A=\partial M$; let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and $\mathcal L$ an $R$-module local system on $M$. Cap with the canonical relative twisted fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $k$,
$$H^k(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M,A;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L),\qquad H^k(M,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L).$$
Here $\mathcal O_M^R$ is the collar extension of the interior orientation system. The statement is for the actual boundary $A$, not an arbitrary subspace of $M$.

the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second

and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner

Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary

Let $X$ be a compact smooth manifold and $L\to X$ a smooth complex line bundle with a specified isomorphism $L^{\otimes d}\cong\mathbf1$ for a positive integer $d$. Let $K^0_{\mathrm{sm}}(X)$ denote the Grothendieck ring of finite-rank smooth complex vector bundles, with direct sum as addition, tensor product as multiplication and the trivial complex line as unit. Then $[L]-1$ is torsion in its additive group. Explicitly, a finite construction gives an integer $m\ge1$ for which
$$(1-[L])^m=0,\qquad d^{m-1}([L]-1)=0.$$
Consequently every additive homomorphism $I:K^0_{\mathrm{sm}}(X)\to\mathbb Z$ satisfies $I([L])=I(1)$. No stable triviality of $L$, rational characteristic-class formula or index theorem is assumed.

derivations.claim:
Smooth bundle metrics and unitary connections needed for every bundle exist by finite formulas. Choose finitely many precompact trivializations and smooth nonnegative bumps with positive sum, normalize the bumps, and sum the local positive metrics. Gram–Schmidt on the finitely many local frames gives smooth unitary frames: all denominators are positive smooth square roots. The ordinary derivative in each such frame defines a local unitary connection. Their finite weighted sum is a global connection, since the weights sum to one in the Leibniz rule; metric compatibility is retained by the same sum. Thus this construction applies to arbitrary finite-rank smooth bundles, including every auxiliary complement occurring in a Grothendieck relation, not only flat lines. A difference of two connections is a smooth endomorphism-valued one-form. The formal adjoint identity on a closed oriented four-manifold is $d_
abla^*=-*d_
abla*$, obtained by integrating $d\langle u\wedge *vangle$ and using unitarity and Stokes. It does not require $
abla^2=0$.

In an oriented orthonormal coframe, $*$ sends a basis wedge to its complementary wedge with the permutation sign, so it is an isometry and $*^2=(-1)^{k(4-k)}$ on $k$-forms. The coefficients of $\tau$ in degrees $0,1,2,3,4$ are $(-1,-1,1,1,-1)$ times $*$; substitution gives $\tau^2=1$, hence self-adjointness. Using step1.1, the identities $a_{k+1}=(-1)^ka_k$ and $a_{k-1}(-1)^k=-a_k$ for this coefficient list give $D_E\tau+\tau D_E=0$ on every degree, including the zero endpoint terms. The $\pm1$ projection ranges are smooth bundles, since $(1\pm\tau)/2$ are smooth projections of constant rank on each component. The principal symbol of $d_\nabla$ is exterior multiplication $\varepsilon(\xi)$ and that of its formal adjoint in the differential-symbol convention is $-\iota_{\xi^\sharp}$. The wedge/deletion identity $\varepsilon(\xi)\iota_{\xi^\sharp}+\iota_{\xi^\sharp}\varepsilon(\xi)=|\xi|^2$ shows that $P=D_E^2$ has positive-frequency symbol $|\xi|^2I$. Curvature terms and connection coefficients are lower order. This $P$ is formally symmetric and nonnegative, since $(Pu,u)=\|D_Eu\|^2$ on smooth forms. It preserves the two chirality bundles. Therefore [F1] applies to $P_+$ and $P_-$, with one common sufficiently large $\lambda$.

Put $B_\pm=(P_\pm+\lambda)^{-1}$. On smooth sections, $D_E$ commutes with $P$, so uniqueness of the shifted inverses gives $B_-D_E^+=D_E^+B_+$, and the analogous reversed identity. Let $Q=D_E^-B_-:L^2(\Omega^-)\to H^1(\Omega^+)$. This is bounded by [F1] and the local first-order coefficient estimates. Direct multiplication first on smooth sections gives $D_E^+Q=I-\lambda B_-$ on $L^2(\Omega^-)$ and $QD_E^+=I-\lambda B_+$ on $H^1(\Omega^+)$. Smooth density extends them to those spaces. The errors are compact: $B_-:L^2\to H^2$ followed by inclusion into $L^2$ is compact, and $B_+:H^1\to H^3$ followed by inclusion into $H^1$ is compact. Hence [F2] proves that the displayed first-order map is Fredholm with exactly the claimed domain and target.

Give a finite principal cover $Y\to X$ with its specified group of order $h$ the pullback metric and orientation. It is a compact closed smooth manifold: finitely many smaller evenly covered neighborhoods with compact closures cover $X$, and their finitely many compact lift closures cover $Y$. Each deck map is an orientation-preserving isometry, so commutes with $d,d^*,*,D,\tau$ and the uniquely characterized harmonic projection of [F3]. For a character $\chi$, projection $h^{-1}\sum_{g}\overline{\chi(g)}g^*$, where $h$ is also the covering degree, therefore splits all these complexes and harmonic spaces. It also splits their cohomology: a projected closed form or primitive represents exactly the corresponding cohomology eigenspace. Forms in this eigenspace are sections of a flat line bundle with locally constant unitary transition scalars among the character values, by choosing one sheet on each evenly covered chart. With the convention $g^*\omega=\chi(g)\omega$ its holonomy is the inverse character: changing the chosen sheet multiplies the coefficient by $\chi(g)$, and parallel transport around the loop compares the endpoint sheet by the inverse. Either way its finite tensor power is canonically trivial, because all transition scalars have that finite order. The local differential, adjoint and chirality are precisely those already used for that flat bundle; covering integration multiplies both the $L^2$ pairing and middle intersection pairing by the same positive integer $h$. Thus kernel dimensions and all inertia signs agree in the two descriptions. This also works for a disconnected principal cover, since its finitely many sheets and components enter the same finite projection.

We need an actual regularity check for its cokernel, not an assumed first-order domain theorem. If $v\in L^2$ and $Pv=f\in L^2$ distributionally, put $w=B(f+\lambda v)\in H^2$. Then $u=v-w\in L^2$ satisfies $(P+\lambda)u=0$ distributionally. For any smooth $h$, $\phi=Bh$ is smooth and $(P+\lambda)\phi=h$; formal symmetry therefore gives $(u,h)=0$. Smooth density implies $u=0$, so $v\in H^2$, and higher regularity makes it smooth if $f$ is smooth. In particular a distributional $L^2$ solution of $D_E^-v=0$ satisfies $P_-v=0$ and is smooth. A vector annihilates the range of $D_E^+:H^1\to L^2$ exactly when it solves that distributional equation, by testing on smooth sections and using density. Its cokernel is thus its smooth opposite-chirality kernel. The same argument applies to its kernel. Consequently its index is the finite number $\dim\ker(D_E|_{\Omega^+})-\dim\ker(D_E|_{\Omega^-})$.

For fixed bundle, two unitary connections, even for different smooth Hermitian metrics, have exterior covariant derivatives differing by a smooth zeroth-order wedge map. Their adjoints both have the formula of step1.1, so the two total $D_E$ operators also differ by a smooth zeroth-order map. Viewed from $H^1$ to $L^2$ this difference is compact by [F1]'s compact inclusion; all smooth positive fiber metrics give equivalent norms on these spaces by finite compact chart bounds. The chirality uses only the fixed base metric. Thus [F2] gives equal indices without a curvature-zero premise or a uniform family regularity assertion. A smooth bundle isomorphism, with transported metric and connection, conjugates the operators by bounded invertible maps on $H^1$ and $L^2$ and preserves the dimensions of kernel and cokernel. Connection/metric independence removes the transported choices. Direct sums give block-sum operators and the direct sums of their kernels and cokernels, so indices add. The explicit pair relations defining $K^0_{\mathrm{sm}}(X)$ now give a well-defined additive map: a witnessing stable bundle isomorphism gives equality after adding the same integer index, which can be cancelled in $\mathbb Z$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). A complex-linear functional $\tau:M\to\mathbb C$ is **positive** if $\tau(P)\in[0,+\infty)$ for every positive operator $P\in M$ ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]), a **state** if it is positive and $\tau(I_H)=1$, **normal** if its restriction to the operator-norm unit ball of $M$ is continuous for the relative weak-operator topology ([[def-strong-and-weak-operator-topologies]], [[def-operator-norm]]), **tracial** if $\tau(ST)=\tau(TS)$ for all $S,T\in M$, and **faithful** if $\tau(T^*T)=0$ implies $T=0$. A **faithful normal tracial state** is a positive normalized trace that is both normal and faithful. In particular, $(M,\tau)$ is a **finite tracial von Neumann algebra** when $\tau$ is a faithful normal tracial state. If $H=\{0\}$ then $M=\{0\}$ and has no state, since $I_H=0$.

For a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space $K$, the normalized matrix trace $\operatorname{tr}_K/\dim K$ is a faithful normal tracial state on $\mathcal B(K)$, and it is the unique tracial state.

For a discrete group $\Gamma$ equipped with the discrete topology, let $H_\Gamma=\ell^2(\Gamma,\mathbb C)$, whose Hilbert-space structure under AC is established in the proof. Define the left and right regular operators by
$$
(\lambda_\Gamma(g)f)(h)=f(g^{-1}h),\qquad (\rho_\Gamma(g)f)(h)=f(hg)\qquad(g,h\in\Gamma).
$$
Put $L(\Gamma):=W^*(\lambda_\Gamma(\Gamma))$ using the concrete generated von Neumann algebra of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]]. Then
$$
\tau_\Gamma(T):=\langle T\delta_e,\delta_e\rangle\qquad(T\in L(\Gamma))
$$
is a faithful normal tracial state on $L(\Gamma)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a unital $*$-subalgebra closed in the weak operator topology. Then $M''=M$, and $M$ is also closed in the strong operator topology. Consequently the concrete von Neumann algebras of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]] are exactly the unital $*$-subalgebras that are closed in either of these topologies. For an arbitrary set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ one has $W^*(\mathcal S)''=W^*(\mathcal S)$.

Assume AC. Let $T$ be a bounded normal operator on a nonzero complex Hilbert
space $H$, with operator spectrum $\sigma(T)$
([[def-spectrum-and-resolvent-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then:

1. there is a unique regular projection valued measure $E$ on the Borel
   $\sigma$-algebra of the nonempty compact set $\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb C$
   such that $\int z\,dE(z)=T$ and, equivalently,
   $$\Phi_E(f)=f(T)\qquad\text{for every continuous }f:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C,$$
   where $f(T)$ is the continuous functional calculus of
   [[thm-continuous-functional-calculus-for-bounded-normal-operators]] and
   $\Phi_E$ is the bounded Borel integral of the projection valued measure $E$;
   this $E$ is the **spectral projection valued measure** of $T$;
2. conversely, if $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb C$ is nonempty and compact and $E$ is
   a regular projection valued measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of
   $\Lambda$, then $T_E:=\int z\,dE(z)=\Phi_E(z)$ is a bounded normal operator
   with $\sigma(T_E)\subseteq\Lambda$ and $\|T_E\|\le\max_{z\in\Lambda}|z|$.

Assume AC. Every bounded operator $T$ on a nonzero complex Hilbert space has a unique partial isometry $U$ with $T=U|T|$ and $\ker U=\ker T$; its initial space is $\overline{\operatorname{ran}|T|}$ and its final space is $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: A spectral projection of a self-adjoint matrix over $A$ belongs to the same matrix von Neumann algebra: it commutes with every element of that algebra's commutant by [F3], so belongs to its double commutant by [F2]. In the rectangular case apply this observation to $B^*B$ and $BB^*$; the polar partial isometry is the strong limit of $B(B^*B+\varepsilon I)^{-1/2}$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, and belongs to the rectangular matrix algebra by [F2]–[F4]. Thus kernel, initial and final projections are matrices over $A$. The equality $\tau_s(v^*v)=\tau_r(vv^*)$, obtained by summing the trace identity for the matrix entries of $v$, gives the displayed rank-nullity formula. The algebraic kernel is exactly $P_{\ker B}A^s$, and $B$ maps $(I-P_{\ker B})A^s$ bijectively onto its algebraic image.

Every finite projective module has the form $eA^r$ for an idempotent $e$. Its Hilbert range is closed because $e^2=e$. Let $p$ be its orthogonal range projection, which lies in $M_r(A)$ by step 1.1. Since $ep=p$ and $pe=e$, one has $eA^r=pA^r$. Every module map between two such projection modules is given by a rectangular matrix: extend it to the ambient finite free module by composing with the source projection. If the algebraic map is injective, its Hilbert kernel projection is zero, since a nonzero kernel projection has a nonzero column in the algebraic kernel. Polar decomposition then implies that the source projection trace is at most the target projection trace. Applying this to an isomorphism and its inverse proves invariance of projective dimension.

For finitely many vectors of $L$, let $B$ have those vectors as columns. The corresponding range projection $q_B$ lies in $M_r(A)$ by step 1.1. As the finite subsets increase, the ranges increase, and their union has Hilbert closure equal to the closure of $L$: a vector $x\in A^r$ gives its Hilbert representative by applying its entries to $\delta_e$, while right translates of those representatives are also representatives of vectors of $L$. Their closed span contains the range of each column operator, because the coordinate vectors span $\ell^2(G)$ densely. The increasing projections converge strongly to their supremum $q\in M_r(A)$ by [F2]. Their ranges lie in the range of $p$, so $q\le p$.

For each such $B$, let $q_{B,\varepsilon}=\mathbf1_{[\varepsilon,\infty)}(BB^*)$ for $\varepsilon>0$. Then $q_{B,\varepsilon}\le q_B$ and $q_{B,\varepsilon}\uparrow q_B$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The bounded Borel function $f_\varepsilon(t)=t^{-1}\mathbf1_{[\varepsilon,\infty)}(t)$ gives $q_{B,\varepsilon}=BB^*f_\varepsilon(BB^*)$. Hence every column of $q_{B,\varepsilon}$ is a right $A$-linear combination of columns of $B$, and $q_{B,\varepsilon}A^r\subseteq L$. Normality of the trace first lets these traces approach $\tau_r(q_B)$ and then, over finite subsets, $\tau_r(q)$. Conversely any finite projective submodule of $L$ embeds in $qA^r$, so step 2.1 bounds its dimension by $\tau_r(q)$. Taking suprema proves $\dim_A L=\tau_r(q)$.

The module $(p-q)A^r$ embeds in $pA^r/L$, giving lower dimension bound $\tau_r(p)-\tau_r(q)$. For the reverse bound let a finite projective $P$ embed in that quotient. Projectivity lifts this map to a map $f:P\to pA^r$. For each projection $q_{B,\varepsilon}$ from step 3.1, the map $(p-q_{B,\varepsilon})f$ is injective: its kernel maps under $f$ into $q_{B,\varepsilon}A^r\subseteq L$, and therefore has zero image under the given embedding of $P$ into the quotient. Step 2.1 yields $\dim_A P\le\tau_r(p)-\tau_r(q_{B,\varepsilon})$. Taking the projection traces arbitrarily close to $\tau_r(q)$ proves the quotient formula.

Submodules of a zero-dimensional module are zero-dimensional by the defining supremum. If a finite projective embeds in a quotient of a zero-dimensional module, projectivity lifts it to an injective map into the original module; hence its dimension is zero, proving quotient closure. For an exact sequence $0\to U\to V\to W\to0$ with $U,W$ zero-dimensional, take any finite projective $P\subseteq V$. Its kernel $K=P\cap U$ and its image $P/K\subseteq W$ are zero-dimensional. Apply steps 3.1 and 4.1 inside a projection representation of $P$: those formulas give $\dim_A P=\dim_A K+\dim_A(P/K)=0$. Thus $V$ is zero-dimensional. Finally, each image of a zero-dimensional module in a filtered colimit is zero-dimensional by quotient closure; these images form a directed family. Every finite set of generators of a finite projective submodule of the colimit lies in one member, so that projective has dimension zero. This proves filtered-colimit closure.

Assume AC. Let $G$ be a discrete group, let $A=\mathcal N G\subseteq\mathcal B(\ell^2(G))$ have its canonical faithful normal trace $\tau$, and give matrices the unnormalized trace $\tau_r((a_{ij}))=\sum_{i=1}^r\tau(a_{ii})$. For a projection $p\in M_r(A)$ put $\dim_A(pA^r)=\tau_r(p)$; for any right $A$-module take the supremum of dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules. These dimensions are independent of the projective representation. If $L\subseteq pA^r$ is any submodule and $q$ is the projection onto its Hilbert closure in $p\ell^2(G)^r$, then $q\in M_r(A)$, $q\le p$, and
$$\dim_A L=\tau_r(q),\qquad \dim_A(pA^r/L)=\tau_r(p)-\tau_r(q).$$
In particular a Hilbert-dense submodule has dimension-zero quotient. Modules of dimension zero are closed under submodules, quotients, extensions and filtered colimits. For any matrix $B\in M_{r,s}(A)$, its kernel and Hilbert-closed image are projection modules, its algebraic image is isomorphic to its support projection module, and
$$\tau_s(P_{\ker B})+\tau_r(P_{\overline{\operatorname{im}B}})=s.$$

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology:
$$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically,
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$
If a basepoint and one oriented lift of each cell outside $A$ are supplied on every component, the $n$th group is the direct sum of the corresponding coefficient fibers, and its boundary is the signed $R[\pi]$ incidence matrix acting through monodromy.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. On a compact collared triad $(W;M_0,M_1)$, every adapted excellent Morse function determines a finite handle decomposition relative to $M_0$, with one handle of index $\operatorname{ind}(p)$ per critical point. Given an adapted field, the attaching sphere is the boundary of its local unstable disk transported to the lower regular level. Conversely every finite handle decomposition relative to $M_0$ is realized by an adapted excellent Morse function with one critical point per handle, of the same index, ordered by the prescribed handle order.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $n$-manifold and let $A=\partial M$; let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and $\mathcal L$ an $R$-module local system on $M$. Cap with the canonical relative twisted fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $k$,
$$H^k(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M,A;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L),\qquad H^k(M,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(M;\mathcal O_M^R\otimes_R\mathcal L).$$
Here $\mathcal O_M^R$ is the collar extension of the interior orientation system. The statement is for the actual boundary $A$, not an arbitrary subspace of $M$.

derivations.claim: For a finite matrix differential $d_i$, its algebraic kernel over $A$ is exactly $p_Z A^{n_i}$, where $p_Z$ projects onto its Hilbert kernel: the matrix equality $d_i p_Z=0$ gives one inclusion, and applying $p_Z$ to each column gives the other. Let $p_B$ project onto the closure of the image of $d_{i+1}$. Then $p_B\le p_Z$. Orthogonal projection onto the algebraic module $P_i=(p_Z-p_B)A^{n_i}$ induces a surjection from algebraic homology $H_i^{\mathrm{alg}}$, with kernel $T_i=p_B A^{n_i}/\operatorname{im}d_{i+1}$. This kernel has dimension zero by [F1]. The target $P_i$ is projective, so the surjection splits algebraically; in fact inclusion of the harmonic projection module into cycles gives a splitting. Thus $H_i^{\mathrm{alg}}\cong P_i\oplus T_i$. Separately, $P_i$ embeds in the Hilbert module $\mathscr H_i=(p_Z-p_B)\ell^2(G)^{n_i}$ by applying its columns to $\delta_e$. This embedding is injective, since a group von Neumann operator annihilating $\delta_e$ annihilates all its right translates. Its image is dense because it contains $(p_Z-p_B)(\mathbb CG)^{n_i}\delta_e$. Consequently the natural map from $H_i^{\mathrm{alg}}$ to $\mathscr H_i$ has image this dense $P_i$, not necessarily all of $\mathscr H_i$. The same dictionary applies to the dual finite matrix complex.

The cellular cap map in [F3] is represented by a map between finite free $R$ complexes, using the dual cellular decomposition or a finite common subdivision. Its homology maps are isomorphisms: apply [F3] to the regular $R$ fiber as a complex local system; all the constructions commute with right multiplication by $R$. Cellular cochains here are the finite dual matrix complex: on each relative cell the local-coefficient cochain is its freely specified fiber value, and induction over the finite cellular filtration gives the cochain comparison, just as for the cellular chain comparison in [F2]. The cap map's cone is therefore a bounded acyclic complex of finite free $R$ modules. Such a complex is contractible: start at its lowest nonzero degree, split the surjection onto that projective term, remove the resulting two-term identity complex, and continue over the finitely many degrees. All splittings are maps between finite projective summands of finite free modules and hence are finite matrices of elements of $R$. Every such matrix acts boundedly on $\ell^2(G)$. The cap map and its chain homotopy inverse consequently extend to bounded chain homotopy equivalences after completion.

Consider three consecutive terms of an algebraically exact homology sequence in [F2], and decompose each as $P\oplus T$ by step 1.1. Every map from $T$ to a finite algebraic projection module vanishes: its image has dimension zero, whereas every nonzero element in a finite projection module generates a positive-dimensional submodule by the spectral quotient formula and faithfulness in [F1]. Hence the sequence induces maps $f_P,g_P$ on the algebraic projective reduced parts. These are restrictions of bounded maps on their Hilbert completions: restriction and inclusion come from finite cellular matrices, and connecting maps can be computed using the degreewise free splittings of the relative or cellular union chain sequence, again by finite matrices followed by harmonic projections. Let $K_A=\ker g_P$, a finite algebraic projection module whose Hilbert closure is the kernel $K_H$ of the completed map, by the same matrix-kernel argument as in step 1.1. View $K_A$ inside the middle algebraic homology using its harmonic-cycle splitting. Its image under the actual second homology map lies in the target $T$, so $K_A/\ker(g|_{K_A})$ has dimension zero. The quotient formula in [F1] makes $\ker(g|_{K_A})$ Hilbert-dense in $K_H$. Exactness identifies each of its elements with an actual preceding image; projecting that preimage off its $T$ summand does not change its projected image. Thus $\ker(g|_{K_A})\subseteq\operatorname{im}f_P\subseteq K_A$. The completed preceding image consequently has closure $K_H$. This proves weak exactness on completed reduced homology without identifying $P$ with its Hilbert completion.

Bounded chain homotopies descend to completed reduced homology, because differentials and all maps are bounded and therefore preserve closures of boundaries. Thus the maps in step 1.2 induce bounded mutually inverse maps on the Hilbert completions $\mathscr H_i$ of step 1.1. Orthogonal projection identifies completed reduced cohomology of the finite dual matrix complex with the Hilbert dual of completed reduced homology: both are the orthogonal complement of boundaries within cycles, and the involution on $R$ identifies the adjoint matrices. On a closed manifold the intersection map is exactly cap duality followed by this Riesz identification; it is therefore bounded and invertible. Its usual symmetry sign follows from the cellular cup/cap identity.

The cellular identity $\partial(c\cap z)=\pm((\delta c)\cap z)\pm c\cap\partial z$ proves compatibility with boundary and restriction before completion. The cup/cap and intersection identities likewise hold on cellular cycles, by their defining evaluation on the dual cells. Any chain homotopies involved are finite matrices, hence remain bounded after completion by step 1.2. They vanish on reduced homology, and every relevant map is continuous. The identities therefore persist on reduced homology with the same orientation signs. Together with steps 1.1, 2.1 and 2.2 this proves all assertions.

derivations.claim: The positive spectral subspace of $J$ is strictly positive for its quadratic form: integrating the positive spectral variable gives a positive number for every nonzero vector there. If a closed module subspace $U$ is strictly positive, its projection into that positive spectral subspace is injective, because a vector with no positive spectral part has nonpositive quadratic form. Polar rank-nullity in [F1] therefore bounds $\dim_A U$ by the trace of the positive spectral projection. This proves the positive characterization, and applying it to $-J$ proves the negative one.

For two projections $p,q$ on a common finite module, rank-nullity for $(I-q):pH\to(I-q)H$ gives $\tau(p\wedge q)\ge\tau(p)-\tau(I-q)$; its kernel is exactly their closed range intersection. If $T$ is injective with dense image, let $q_\varepsilon=\mathbf1_{[\varepsilon,\infty)}(TT^*)$. The traces $\tau(q_\varepsilon)$ tend to $\dim_A H_1$ by [F1], and $q_\varepsilon H_1$ lies in the image of $T$ with a bounded module inverse on it. Intersect this range with a positive spectral subspace $p_\delta H_1=\mathbf1_{[\delta,\infty)}(J)H_1$. Its trace tends to $\tau(p_\delta)$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ by the intersection inequality. Pulling it back by the bounded inverse of $T$ gives a closed positive subspace for $T^*JT$ of the same dimension. Step 1.1 and then $\delta\downarrow0$ show that the positive inertia of $T^*JT$ is at least that of $J$. Conversely, on every closed positive subspace for $T^*JT$, project $T$ into the positive spectral subspace of $J$; this map is injective, giving the reverse inequality by [F1]. Repeat with $-J$.

Assume $J$ is invertible and put $L=V^{\perp_J}\subseteq V$, $K=V\cap L^\perp$ and $Q=V^\perp$, where unmarked orthogonals use the underlying Hilbert product. These are closed module subspaces and $H=L\oplus K\oplus Q$. The identity $L=J^{-1}Q$ says that $J|_L:L\to Q$ is a bounded isomorphism. In this decomposition the matrix of $J$ is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0&B\\0&C&E\\B^*&E^*&F\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, where $B^*:L\to Q$ is invertible. Replace $k\in K$ by $k-(B^*)^{-1}E^*k$. This bounded invertible triangular change makes $K$ orthogonal, for the form, to both $L$ and $Q$, leaving its form $C$ unchanged. In the remaining $L\oplus Q$ block, replace $l$ by $l-\tfrac12(B^*)^{-1}Fq$ to obtain $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&B\\B^*&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Conjugation by $\operatorname{diag}(I_L,-I_Q)$ negates this last form; its positive and negative spectral projections consequently have the same trace, so its signature is zero. Step 2.1 applies to the bounded invertible changes just used, proving that the original signature is the signature of $C$.

The restriction of the form to $V=L\oplus K$ is $0\oplus C$, so it too has signature equal to that of $C$. This proves coisotropic reduction. For a map with a kernel, its pullback form vanishes on that kernel and has no cross terms with it; discard the kernel and use step 2.1 on its orthogonal complement whenever the remaining image is dense. For the trivial group, projection traces are ordinary complex dimensions; complexifying a real symmetric form preserves its real positive and negative dimensions by diagonalizing the finite real form. Thus the ordinary case is included.
