Assume full AC, matching the chosen finite twisted-chain and maximal-abelian-cover conventions. Let K be a smooth oriented knot, M(K) its preferred-longitude zero-framed surgery, W a compact connected oriented smooth 4-manifold with boundary M(K), and π=π₁(W). Put π^(0)=π and π^(j+1)=[π^(j),π^(j)]. A right Zπ-chain complex with coefficients in a left Z[π/π^(j)]-module is formed by tensoring over Zπ with that module.

For n≥0, W is an integral n-solution for K when H₁(M(K);Z)→H₁(W;Z) is an isomorphism, H₂(W;Z) is free of rank 2r for some finite r, and there are classes x₁,…,x_r,y₁,…,y_r in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n)]) whose equivariant intersection pairings satisfy λ_n(x_i,x_j)=0 and λ_n(x_i,y_j)=δ_ij. It is an integral (n+1/2)-solution when, in addition, each x_i is the image of a class x̃_i in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n+1)]) and λ_{n+1}(x̃_i,x̃_j)=0 for all i,j. Here λ_j is the equivariant intersection pairing induced by the orientation of W.

For a commutative ring R with 1≠0, a group G belongs to Strebel's class D(R) if every homomorphism between projective RG-modules is injective whenever its tensor with the trivial G-module R is injective. In this page R is Q or F_p for a prime p. For a countable discrete group G, its group von Neumann algebra N G is the weak-operator closure of CG in the left regular representation on ℓ²(G), with trace τ_G(T)=⟨Tδ_e,δ_e⟩. The von Neumann dimension of a finitely generated projective N G-module represented by a projection E is τ_G(E); for an arbitrary module it is the supremum of the dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules.

For a compact oriented 4-manifold W with boundary, sign(W) is the inertia difference of the symmetric intersection form on H₂(W;R) modulo its radical (the subspace pairing to zero with every class), equivalently on the image of H₂(W;R)→H₂(W,∂W;R). Given a closed oriented 3-manifold M, a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G, a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G of φ, the L²-signature sign_G^(2)(W,ψ) is the von Neumann signature of the nonsingular part of the N G-coefficient intersection form. When such a W and extension exist, the signature defect is sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is called the rho invariant of (M,φ) only after its independence of the bounding data is established by a separate bordism argument.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the nondegeneracy of the
middle form. Let $M$ be a closed oriented smooth manifold of dimension $4k$,
$k\ge0$, and let $Q_M$ be its middle-dimensional intersection form on
$H^{2k}(M;\mathbb R)$ ([[def-middle-dimensional-intersection-form]],
[[lem-middle-dimensional-intersection-form-is-symmetric-and-nondegenerate]]).
Let $(p,q,z)$ be the inertia data of the symmetric form $Q_M$
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]): $p$ the
maximal dimension of a positive-definite subspace, $q$ the maximal dimension of
a negative-definite subspace, and $z$ the dimension of the radical. By
Sylvester's law of inertia ([[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]]) these integers
are intrinsic to $Q_M$ and $p+q+z=\dim_{\mathbb R}H^{2k}(M;\mathbb R)$. The
**signature** of $M$ is
$$\sigma(M):=p-q\in\mathbb Z.$$

The middle form is nondegenerate by
[[lem-middle-dimensional-intersection-form-is-symmetric-and-nondegenerate]], so
$z=0$ and $p+q=\dim_{\mathbb R}H^{2k}(M;\mathbb R)$; the signature can
equivalently be read as the difference of the numbers of positive and negative
diagonal entries in any basis diagonalizing $Q_M$. For $k=0$ the group
$H^0(M;\mathbb R)$ is free on the components of $M$ and the pairing is the
signed count of components, so $\sigma(M^0)$ is the number of positively
oriented components minus the number of negatively oriented components, and
$\sigma(\varnothing)=0$.

The signature is defined by this item only for dimensions divisible by four; no
value is assigned in other dimensions (see the closing bookkeeping remark on
this page). The value is independent of the chosen diagonalizing basis and of
reading the form over $\mathbb Q$ or over $\mathbb R$ by
[[lem-signature-is-independent-of-basis-and-field-extension-from-rationals-to-reals]],
the lemma named in `justified_by`.

Assume the standing full AC convention. Give compact oriented smooth manifolds finite cellular models, and give their cellular complexes the local regular coefficients of any discrete group $G$. Put $A=\mathcal N G$. For each degree, let $p_Z$ and $p_B$ be the Hilbert projections onto cycles and the closure of boundaries after completion in $\ell^2(G)$. The algebraic reduced part is the finite projective $A$-module $P=(p_Z-p_B)A^n$, whereas completed reduced homology is the Hilbert module $H=(p_Z-p_B)\ell^2(G)^n$. Algebraic homology with $A$ coefficients surjects onto $P$ with zero-dimensional kernel; its natural map into $H$ has dense image $P$ under $x\mapsto x\delta_e$, and need not be surjective onto $H$. The Hilbert completion of $P$ in this embedding is $H$. Pair and Mayer–Vietoris sequences become weakly exact on completed reduced homology: the closure of each image is the next kernel. Poincaré–Lefschetz cap duality induces bounded invertible maps on completed reduced homology and cohomology. In particular, the middle intersection operator of a closed oriented even-dimensional manifold is invertible. The cap boundary identity and the intersection/cup identities persist on these completed modules, with their ordinary orientation signs.

Work under the standing AC convention for finite von Neumann modules. Let $A=\mathcal N G$ with its finite trace, and let all Hilbert modules below be ranges of projections on finite sums of $\ell^2(G)$. For a bounded self-adjoint module operator $J$ define its positive and negative inertia by the traces of $\mathbf1_{(0,\infty)}(J)$ and $\mathbf1_{(-\infty,0)}(J)$, and its signature by their difference. Each inertia is the supremum of dimensions of closed module subspaces on which the form $\langle Jx,x\rangle$ is strictly positive or strictly negative, respectively. If $T:H_0\to H_1$ is bounded, injective and has dense image, then $T^*JT$ and $J$ have the same inertia. If $J$ is invertible, $V\subseteq H$ is closed, and $V^{\perp_J}\subseteq V$, then the form on $H$ and its restriction to $V$ have equal signatures. Kernels contribute zero. These statements include ordinary real signatures by complexification and the trivial-group trace.

derivations.claim: Van Kampen gives the glued homomorphism to $\Gamma$ from the matching restrictions. Let $j:H_2^{(2)}(W_0)\oplus H_2^{(2)}(W_1)\to H$ be the sum of the inclusion maps, and let $V=\overline{\operatorname{im}j}$. The closed intersection operator $J$ on $H$ is invertible by [F2]. Under Poincaré duality, the annihilator $V^{\perp_J}$ identifies with the kernel of restriction $H^2_{(2)}(X)\to H^2_{(2)}(W_0)\oplus H^2_{(2)}(W_1)$: evaluation on each piece is exactly the pairing with its inclusion in $X$.

Weak cohomology Mayer–Vietoris exactness identifies that kernel with the closure of the image of the connecting map $H^1_{(2)}(M)\to H^2_{(2)}(X)$. Cap boundary naturality in [F2] identifies this connecting map, up to its harmless orientation sign, with $H_2^{(2)}(M)\to H_2^{(2)}(X)$ after cap duality on $M$ and $X$. Cap duality is a bounded isomorphism, so it preserves these closures. Hence $V^{\perp_J}$ is the closure of this last image. The inclusion $M\to X$ factors through either piece, so this image lies in $V$. Thus $V$ is coisotropic.

The pullback form $j^*Jj$ is the orthogonal sum of the intersection forms on $W_0$ and $-W_1$. Indeed the same-piece term is the absolute-to-relative intersection pairing by cap naturality; cross terms vanish because representative cellular chains can be pushed into the respective collar interiors, which are disjoint. This can be checked on the finite dual cellular chains before completion: each intersection contribution comes from a cell and its dual in the same piece, with its given group-ring coefficient, and there are no cross-piece intersections. The identity extends by boundedness to the reduced homology in [F2]. Reversing orientation on $W_1$ negates its form.

Discard $\ker j$; it is a null summand of the pullback form. The restriction of $j$ to its Hilbert orthogonal complement is injective with dense image in $V$. By [F3] its pullback has the signature of the restricted form on $V$. By the coisotropic conclusion of step 2.1, this is the signature of $J$ on $H$. Step 2.2 and additivity of spectral trace on an orthogonal sum give the asserted $L^2$ signature equality.

Apply the same argument to the trivial coefficient group. Reduced homology is ordinary finite-dimensional complex homology; its form is the complexification of the real intersection form. Complexification preserves both real inertia dimensions, as in [F3]. The resulting equality is the asserted ordinary signature equality.

Assume AC. Fix a compact closed oriented smooth four-manifold $X$ and a smooth Riemannian metric. For every finite-rank smooth complex Hermitian bundle $E\to X$ and every smooth unitary connection $\nabla$, let $d_\nabla$ be its exterior covariant derivative and put $D_E=d_\nabla+d_\nabla^*$. On $E$-valued $k$-forms set
$$\tau_k=-(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}*,$$
where the Hodge star is complex linear and acts only on the form factor. Then $\tau$ is a smooth self-adjoint involution and $D_E\tau=-\tau D_E$. The operator
$$D_E^+:H^1(\Omega^+(X,E))\longrightarrow L^2(\Omega^-(X,E))$$
is Fredholm. Its integer index is independent of the unitary connection and bundle metric, invariant under smooth bundle isomorphism, and additive under direct sum. It therefore defines an additive homomorphism
$$I_X:K^0_{\mathrm{sm}}(X)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z.$$

For a finite smooth principal cover $Y\to X$ with a specified finite group action free and transitive on each fiber, every unitary one-dimensional character of that specified group determines a smooth flat line bundle $L$. The index $I_X([L])$ is the signature of the corresponding middle character intersection form (in the inverse deck convention use the conjugate character, which has the same signature). Moreover
$$I_X([L])=I_X(1)=\operatorname{sign}(X).$$
This includes every character, the trivial character and finite covers with disconnected total space. This is a compact finite-order-character result, not a local curvature index formula, an arbitrary-group closed $L^2$ index theorem, or a boundary signature-operator assertion.

Use the standing AC and canonical-trace convention of the $L^2$ signature definition. Let $W$ be a compact oriented four-manifold with a supplied finite CW pair model for its boundary and a surjection $\psi:\pi_1(W)\to G=\mathbb Z/d$, $d\ge1$. Let $\widetilde W_\psi$ be its actual degree-$d$ cover, and write $\zeta=\exp(2\pi i/d)$. For $0\le r<d$, let $\lambda_r$ be the character intersection form for the character sending the specified positive generator of $G$ to $\zeta^r$. Then, allowing arbitrary radicals,
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W,\psi)=\frac{\operatorname{sign}(\widetilde W_\psi)}d=\frac1d\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}\operatorname{sign}(\lambda_r).$$
Here the ordinary cover signature, like each character signature, means positive inertia minus negative inertia with the kernel discarded. Changing consistently from linear-first to conjugate-first pairings transposes the character matrices and does not change the formula. No independence of a bounding manifold, no infinite-cyclic integration and no arbitrary-group index assertion is part of this statement.

Let W₀ and W₁ be compact oriented smooth 4-manifolds with a common identified boundary M, and let Γ be a discrete group. Suppose coefficient homomorphisms ψ_i:π₁(W_i)→Γ agree on π₁(M), and let X=W₀∪_M(−W₁) be the resulting closed oriented 4-manifold with its glued coefficient map. Then
sign(X)=sign(W₀)−sign(W₁)
and
sign_Γ^(2)(X)=sign_Γ^(2)(W₀,ψ₀)−sign_Γ^(2)(W₁,ψ₁).

Assume AC. For every supplied finite smooth oriented disk-band Seifert surface $F$ with one-boundary knot $K$, ordered homology basis and first-variable positive-push matrix $V$, let $W_F$ and its meridional extension $\psi_d:\pi_1(W_F)\to\mathbb Z/d$ be the actual construction of the finite disk-band bounding-manifold construction. For every positive integer $d$, set $\zeta_d=\exp(2\pi i/d)$ and
$$D_d(F)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_{\mathbb Z/d}(W_F,\psi_d)-\operatorname{sign}(W_F).$$
Then
$$D_d(F)=\frac1d\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}\operatorname{sign}\bigl((1-\zeta_d^r)V+(1-\zeta_d^{-r})V^T\bigr).$$
The sign is exactly the positive $L^2$ signature minus ordinary signature convention. The formula allows singular character forms and all $d$, including $d=1$ and even $d$. The term $r=0$ is defined by the zero Hermitian matrix and contributes zero; its equality to the trivial-character signature follows from the ordinary metabolic calculation, not from specialization of a localized homology basis.

The boundary is the actual oriented zero surgery and its positive meridian map, not the knot exterior or a simply connected trace. The displayed formula proves this **canonical bounding defect**. Whenever a separately proved applicable bordism-independence assertion identifies the rho invariant with the defect of this bounding extension, it consequently gives the same value for that rho invariant. No such general independence assertion, global signature invariance, rho identification, uniform bound, infinite-cyclic formula or arbitrary-group index theorem is asserted here.
Every nonempty path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected space has a universal covering space.

For a path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected base $B$, the deck group of a universal cover is isomorphic to $\pi_1(B,b_0)$. With the library's traversal-order path product the monodromy action is a right action, and the assignment carrying a loop class to the deck transformation that moves the chosen point of the fibre to the corresponding lifted endpoint is itself an isomorphism; no path reversal is inserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Over any simply connected coordinate ball choose one universal sheet; the quotient is that ball times the finite set $G$. These local identifications have locally constant sheet permutations, so define the smooth covering structure and orientation. At a chosen basepoint the lift of a loop $\gamma$ ends at $[\gamma\widetilde x,g]=[\widetilde x,\psi(\gamma)g]$, so this is the actual prescribed monodromy rather than its inverse. Its degree is exactly $d$, and its total space may be disconnected. It is compact by finitely many compact lift closures of smaller evenly covered charts. Pull back a Riemannian metric. A compact disconnected $X$ has finitely many components (its connected coordinate charts have a finite covering subfamily), so the subsequent construction applies on each and signatures add.

Kernels, images and middle homology split literally by these projections, and every image is closed. Sesquilinearity makes different components orthogonal, so the positive and negative projections have trace $d^{-1}$ times the sum of their component ranks; the same statement holds after removing each component's radical. This proves the character-mean formula also for the actual possibly disconnected principal cover, without silently applying [F2]'s surjectivity hypothesis in a larger scope. Hence the value is well-defined among all the supplied smooth extensions whenever at least one exists.

For the knot data, [F4] supplies an actual smooth bounding extension with the exact oriented zero-surgery boundary and positive meridional coefficient homomorphism. A **CW complex** is a Hausdorff space $X$ with a filtration
$$\varnothing=X^{-1}\subseteq X^0\subseteq X^1\subseteq\cdots,\qquad X=\bigcup_{n\geq0}X^n,$$
where $X^0$ is discrete and $X^n$ is obtained from $X^{n-1}$ by attaching a (possibly infinite) family of $n$-disks along maps $S^{n-1}\to X^{n-1}$ as in [[def-cell-attachment-by-a-characteristic-map]]. The images of the disk interiors are its **open $n$-cells** $e^n_\alpha$, and the disk maps are their characteristic maps. It moreover satisfies: (C) each closed cell $\overline {e^n_\alpha}$ meets only finitely many cells; and (W) $A\subseteq X$ is closed exactly when $A\cap\overline e$ is closed in $\overline e$ for every cell $e$. These are closure finiteness and the weak topology.

derivations.claim: Choose finitely many chart domains $V_i$ whose smaller concentric coordinate balls cover $M$, using compactness. For boundary charts use the relatively open unit half-ball $B^n_+=\{x:|x|<1,\ x_n\ge0\}$; for interior charts use the unit ball. Denote the chart by $\varphi_i$ and arrange that the radius-$1/3$ smaller balls cover. Choose the explicit radial bump $\rho_i$ equal to $1$ at radius at most $1/3$ and zero at radius at least $2/3$, interpolating linearly in between, and extend it by zero outside $V_i$. Its support is compact in $V_i$. Define $$e(x)=\bigl(\rho_i(x),\,\rho_i(x)\varphi_i(x)\bigr)_{i=1}^s\in\mathbb R^{s(n+1)},$$ with the vector entry zero outside $V_i$. Boundedness of the chart coordinates makes these extensions continuous. If $e(x)=e(y)$, choose an index with $\rho_i(x)>0$. The equal scalar and vector entries recover $\varphi_i(x)=\varphi_i(y)$ and hence $x=y$. A continuous injection of a compact space into the Hausdorff Euclidean space is an embedding. From now on identify $M$ with its image. All choices here form one finite list.

Write an ambient point in the $i$th block as $(t_i,z_i)$. On the open ambient set $O_i=\{t_i>0,\ |z_i/t_i|<1\}$ define $$q_i(t,z)=e\bigl(\varphi_i^{-1}(p_i(z_i/t_i))\bigr),$$ where $p_i$ is the identity for an interior chart and $p_i(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},\max(0,x_n))$ for a boundary chart. The latter decreases norm and retracts the unit ball onto its relative half-ball. Thus $q_i:O_i\to e(V_i)$ is continuous and $q_i(x)=x$ for every $x\in M\cap O_i$. The compact sets $K_i=e(\{\rho_i\ge1/2\})$ cover $M$ and lie in $O_i$. Choose a positive $\delta_i$ with the closed $\delta_i$ neighborhood of $K_i$ contained in $O_i$; such a number exists by compactness and the open cover by small ambient balls. Put $\beta_i(z)=\max(0,\delta_i-\operatorname{dist}(z,K_i))$. Its closed support $S_i$ is compact and contained in $O_i$, and $\sum_i\beta_i>0$ on $M$. Empty $K_i$ may simply be discarded. No nearest-point selection is made: distance means the infimum of the set of distances.

We construct successive continuous maps $r_j:D_j\to M$, where $D_j=U_j\cap\{\beta_1+\cdots+\beta_j>0\}$ and $U_j$ is an open neighborhood of $M$. In addition require the following controlled property even at points outside $D_j$: for every $x\in M$ and every neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $M$, there is an ambient neighborhood $A$ of $x$ with $r_j(A\cap D_j)\subseteq V$. Begin with $U_0=\mathbb R^N$ and the empty map. Suppose the property holds for $r_{j-1}$. There is an open neighborhood $U_j\subseteq U_{j-1}$ of $M$ such that $$r_{j-1}(U_j\cap S_j\cap D_{j-1})\subseteq e(V_j).$$ Indeed, at $x\in M\cap S_j$ the chart $e(V_j)$ is a neighborhood of $x$, so the controlled property supplies the required ambient neighborhood. At $x\in M\setminus S_j$ an ambient neighborhood avoids the closed set $S_j$. Take the union of all open subsets of $U_{j-1}$ satisfying the displayed containment. This union contains $M$ and itself satisfies that containment. Taking the union of all admissible neighborhoods avoids selecting one for every point.

On $D_j$ put $a=\beta_1+\cdots+\beta_{j-1}$ and $b=\beta_j$. Where $b=0$ use $r_j=r_{j-1}$; where $a=0$ use $r_j=q_j$. If $a,b>0$, both $r_{j-1}$ and $q_j$ lie in $e(V_j)$ by step 3.1, so define $$r_j(z)=e\varphi_j^{-1}\left(\frac{a}{a+b}\,\varphi_j e^{-1}r_{j-1}(z)+\frac{b}{a+b}\,\varphi_j e^{-1}q_j(z)\right).$$ The chart image is a bounded convex ball or half-ball, so the convex combination remains in it. This map is continuous where both weights are positive. At a point where $a=0,b>0$, the first coordinate vector is uniformly bounded in the unit ball and its coefficient tends to zero; the expression therefore tends to the $q_j$ value regardless of whether $r_{j-1}$ has a limit there. At $b=0,a>0$, either a neighborhood avoids $S_j$, or the point is in $S_j$ and the containment from step 3.1 puts $r_{j-1}$ in $e(V_j)$ there. Continuity of $r_{j-1},q_j$ and the bounded coordinate formula then gives the stated $r_{j-1}$ value. This proves continuity on all of $D_j$.

The controlled property also persists. At $x\notin S_j$ the map locally is the old map. At $x\in M\cap S_j$, choose a sufficiently small convex coordinate neighborhood of $\varphi_j(x)$ in the ball or half-ball whose inverse lies in a prescribed neighborhood of $x$. The old controlled property puts all defined old values in this neighborhood for ambient points sufficiently near $x$; continuity of $q_j$ and $q_j(x)=x$ puts the new values there too. Every convex blend, as well as each endpoint case, remains in that neighborhood. This proves the property at $x$. Whenever $r_j$ is defined at a point of $M$, all contributing maps have value that point, so $r_j|_{M\cap D_j}$ is the identity. Finite induction ends with $M\subset D_s$, since the sum of the weights is positive there. The continuous map $r_s:D_s\to M$ is therefore the required neighborhood retraction. The induction and neighborhood unions require no infinite selection.

By compactness, some positive $\varepsilon$ has the closed $\varepsilon$ neighborhood of $M$ contained in the open set $D_s$: finitely many ambient balls with doubled balls inside $D_s$ give a uniform positive minimum radius. Choose a rectangular grid with cube side less than $\varepsilon/\sqrt N$. There are only finitely many grid cubes meeting the bounded compact set $M$, and their union $L$ contains $M$ and lies in $D_s$, because each such cube has diameter less than $\varepsilon$. Include all cube faces. This is a finite CW complex by [F1], and the inclusion $M\hookrightarrow L$ followed by $r_s|_L$ is literally the identity on $M$. Empty $M$ is the empty retract. A compact zero-manifold is finite, and the same disjoint-neighborhood construction, or a finite set of points as $L$, handles that case without dividing by $\sqrt0$. For positive dimension the construction above applies to interior and boundary charts alike. Every noncanonical datum chosen in the proof belongs to a finite chart or parameter list. Thus the asserted embedding, retraction and finite domination hold without a choice axiom.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Every compact Hausdorff topological manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, admits an embedding $e:M\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^N$, an open neighborhood $U$ of $e(M)$ and a retraction $r:U\to e(M)$. Moreover there is a finite Euclidean cubical complex $L$ with $e(M)\subseteq L\subseteq U$, so that $r|_L$ makes $M$ an actual retract of a finite CW complex. No choice principle, smooth or PL structure, triangulation of $M$, or general locally contractible-space retraction theorem is assumed.

derivations.claim: Here the right-module singular complex is defined intrinsically: $C_n=\bigoplus_\sigma\mathcal R_{\sigma(v_0)}$, and on a coefficient $a$ its first face has coefficient $T_{01}a$ over $v_1$, while face $i>0$ has coefficient $(-1)^ia$ over $v_0$. The signs include the first face sign $+1$. The identities $d_id_j=d_{j-1}d_i$ pair and cancel faces for $i<j$; the only two potentially different transport composites are along edges $01,12$ and edge $02$, equal because their paths are homotopic in the simplex. Thus $d^2=0$ for arbitrary noncommutative $R$. The same formula on affine simplices defines $F_*$, and affine inclusion defines a chain map $J$. All formulas are right-linear. Choosing one basis in each of the finitely many vertex fibers makes each $F_n$ finite-free, and $F_n=0$ above the dimension of $L$.

Cover $L$ by its finitely many open vertex stars. A simplex is called small if its image lies in one of them. Apply [F1] to obtain the small chain complex $C_*^{\mathrm{sm}}$, inclusion $I$, map $\rho:C_*\to C_*^{\mathrm{sm}}$ and homotopy $D$. The proof of [F1] transports coefficients only along paths within the domain simplex; hence its face cancellations and least-integer subdivision formula apply to the right-module complex of step 1.1, or equivalently to its underlying abelian-group complex. In particular $\rho$ and $D$ are right-$R$ linear and preserve every subcomplex generated by simplices whose images lie in a specified subcomplex of $L$.

For a small singular simplex $\sigma$, let $A_\sigma$ be the finite subcomplex generated by the geometric simplices whose relative interiors meet its image. If $v$ is a vertex whose open star contains that image, every such geometric simplex contains $v$. Therefore $A_\sigma$ is a cone with apex $v$: joining $v$ to any of its faces remains in it. If $\tau$ is a face of $\sigma$, then $A_\tau\subseteq A_\sigma$. Choose as apex the least vertex whose open star contains the image. Both its simplicial chains and its singular chains have explicit augmented cone contractions: join to $v$, using straight segments in the geometric cone, and transport coefficients along those segments. For a simplex map $f$, the singular cone is $t_0v+(1-t_0)f(t_1/(1-t_0),\ldots)$, extended by $v$ at $t_0=1$; boundedness makes it continuous there. The boundary is the original chain minus the cone on its boundary, with the usual augmentation term in degree zero. The simplicial cone is the oriented join, zero when the vertex already occurs. These identities follow by the finite face cancellations. The coefficient system trivializes on the cone by its straight paths, so the identities apply to all its fibers without choosing trivializations independently at every point.

Define $S:C_*^{\mathrm{sm}}\to F_*$ by induction. For a point simplex, send its coefficient to the least apex vertex of its carrier along their straight segment. For degree $n>0$, the already defined $S(d\sigma)$ is a cycle in $A_\sigma$; in degree zero its transported augmentation is zero. Put $S\sigma$ equal to its simplicial cone at the chosen apex. The cone identity gives $dS\sigma=S(d\sigma)$. Images of all faces lie in their nested carriers, so each operation stays in $A_\sigma$. Extend linearly on each coefficient fiber. This constructs the entire chain map by a formula on generators, with finite sums and least vertices, rather than an infinite set of individually chosen fillings.

Construct $H:C_*^{\mathrm{sm}}\to C_{*+1}$ similarly. After lower degrees are defined, the chain $\sigma-JS\sigma-H(d\sigma)$ is a cycle in $A_\sigma$, with zero augmentation in degree zero. Cone it singularly at the chosen apex and call the result $H\sigma$. Its boundary is precisely that cycle, so $dH+Hd=I-JS$. Put $P=S\rho$. Then $$1-JP=(1-I\rho)+(I-JS)\rho=d(D+H\rho)+(D+H\rho)d.$$ Thus the displayed homotopy is actually right-linear and defined on all singular generators.

For an affine simplex $\tau$ of $L$, image preservation in step 2.1 and the carriers of step 3.1 put $PJ\tau$ in the simplicial chains of $\tau$ itself. On a vertex $PJ$ is the identity. Inducting on dimension, $d(PJ\tau-\tau)=0$. For a positive-dimensional geometric $n$-simplex, its top simplicial chain group is one fiber and its top boundary is injective: each codimension-one face occurs with coefficient the transported original coefficient, so zero boundary forces that coefficient zero. Hence $PJ\tau=\tau$. This proves $PJ=1$, including degenerate singular simplices, which were never discarded from the source complex.

For the manifold consequence, take the actual retraction $e:M\hookrightarrow L$ and $r:L\to M$ from [F2]. Triangulate each grid cube by its coordinate-order simplices: for each permutation of the axes take the successive vertices from its lower vertex by adding those coordinate edges in that order. These finitely many simplices cover the cube, and on shared faces the same ordering of the remaining coordinates gives the same triangulation. Pull the coefficient system to $L$ along $r$. With $F_*$ its finite simplicial complex, set $i_C=P\,C(e)$ and $r_C=C(r)J$. The homotopy of step 5.1 gives $r_Ci_C\simeq C(r)C(e)=1$, since $re=1$ literally. The coefficient maps have these same identities on fibers, so this is domination in right-$R$ chain complexes, not just ordinary homology.

Finally the singular modules on $M$ have actual formula-defined free bases. Take its finite convex ball/half-ball atlas. The finite intersection graph is connected; choose a finite spanning tree, one point for each tree-edge intersection, and coordinate-straight paths through these points joining the finitely many chart centers to the basepoint. For a point $x$, use the first chart containing it and append that chart's straight path from its center to $x$. This specifies a based path $\gamma_x$ for every point without pointwise selection. Transport the supplied base vector $1$ along $\gamma_x$ to obtain a basis of its fiber. Each singular generator then has its specified first-vertex basis. The differential and homotopies of the preceding steps respect those right-module structures. For disconnected finite complexes the first argument already works componentwise with finitely many vertex bases; empty complexes give zero maps. All manifold choices were finite atlas/tree data, and the only infinite constructions were recursive formulas on generators. This proves the full choice-free assertion.

Let $C_\bullet$ and $D_\bullet$ be chain complexes. A **chain map**
$f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ is a family of morphisms
$$f_n:C_n\to D_n$$
such that for every $n\in\mathbb Z$,
$$d^D_n\circ f_n=f_{n-1}\circ d^C_n.$$

Equivalently, each square
$$\begin{matrix} C_n&\xrightarrow{f_n}&D_n\\ d^C_n\downarrow&&\downarrow d^D_n\\ C_{n-1}&\xrightarrow{f_{n-1}}&D_{n-1} \end{matrix}$$
commutes.

Let $C_\bullet,D_\bullet$ be chain complexes in an abelian category
$\mathcal A$, and let $f,g:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ be chain maps. A **chain homotopy**
$s:f\simeq g$ is a graded morphism of degree $1$,
$$s_n:C_n\to D_{n+1},$$
such that for every $n\in\mathbb Z$,
$$f_n-g_n=d^D_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}d^C_n.$$

Equivalently, $f-g$ is the degree-$0$ boundary of the degree-$1$ family $s$ in
[[def-hom-complex-of-chain-complexes]].

A chain map $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ is a **chain homotopy equivalence** if
there exists a chain map $g:D_\bullet\to C_\bullet$ such that
$$g\circ f\simeq1_C,\qquad f\circ g\simeq1_D.$$

Such a map $g$ is called a **homotopy inverse** of $f$.

A left $R$-module $P$ is **projective** if it has the lifting property for epimorphisms: whenever $q:E\to M$ is a surjective module homomorphism and $f:P\to M$ is a module homomorphism, there exists a module homomorphism $\tilde f:P\to E$ such that $q\circ\tilde f=f$ ([[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

The lift need not be unique. Projectivity asks for a lift in every such square.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F$ be a function with domain $n$ all of whose
values are nonempty sets. Then the family of its values,
$\mathcal{F} = F[n] = \{\, F(i) : i \in n \,\}$, has a choice function
([[def-choice-function]]).

This is a theorem of ZF: its proof uses no form of the Axiom of Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$. The
natural number $n$ serves as the index set in the von Neumann sense,
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so "$F$ has domain $n$"
says precisely that the members of $\mathcal{F}$ are listed as
$F(0), \dots, F(n-1)$. The listing need not be injective, and $\mathcal{F}$ is the
set of values, so repetitions are harmless and are not counted.

The displayed statement and its proof use only a natural-number-indexed
function. They do not identify an arbitrary finite family with a particular
enumeration.

derivations.claim: Put $u=gf$ on $C$. Repeatedly substituting $dh=1-u-hd$ gives, for every integer $s\ge1$, $$dh^s=(-1)^sh^sd+\epsilon_s h^{s-1}-\sum_{\ell=0}^{s-1}(-1)^\ell h^\ell u h^{s-1-\ell},\qquad \epsilon_s=\begin{cases}1&s\text{ odd},\\0&s\text{ even}.\end{cases}$$ For $s=1$ this is the given equation. Multiplying the formula on the right by $h$ and substituting $dh$ in its first term proves the next case: the identity coefficient changes from $\epsilon_s$ to $\epsilon_s+(-1)^s=\epsilon_{s+1}$ and the last summand acquires index $s$. This is finite induction on a specified identity, with no choices.

Define $D_n=\bigoplus_{j=0}^nF_j$ for $n\ge0$, and $D_n=0$ for $n<0$. Define maps $\delta_n:D_n\to D_{n-1}$ by their finite blocks, with column $j$, row $k$, where $0\le j\le n$ and $0\le k\le n-1$: $$ (\delta_n)_{kj}=\begin{cases} 0&j\ge k+2,\\ (-1)^{n+k+1}\partial_j&j=k+1,\\ 1_{F_j}-f_jg_j&j=k,\ n+k\text{ odd},\\ f_jg_j&j=k,\ n+k\text{ even},\\ (-1)^{n+k}f_kh^{k-j}g_j&j<k. \end{cases}$$ All blocks have the displayed source and target, regardless of noncommutativity of $A$. Also define $\alpha_n:C_n\to D_n$ to have only its final component $f_n$, define $\beta_n:D_n\to C_n$ by the row $(h^ng_0,h^{n-1}g_1,\ldots,g_n)$, and let $s_n:D_n\to D_{n+1}$ be inclusion into the first $n+1$ summands. These are specified finite formulas in every degree. We next verify that $D$ is a chain complex and that the named maps have all claimed properties; these are not assumed from a matrix citation.

The final column of $\delta_n$ has only its final block $+\partial_n$. Therefore $\delta_n\alpha_n=\alpha_{n-1}d_n$, using $\partial f=fd$. To check $\beta_{n-1}\delta_n=d_n\beta_n$, consider column $j$. If $j=n$, the assertion is $g_{n-1}\partial_n=d_ng_n$. Otherwise put $t=n-j\ge1$. The superdiagonal contribution is $(-1)^t h^tdg_j$ (zero if $j=0$); the diagonal contribution is $\epsilon_t h^{t-1}g_j-(-1)^{t-1}h^{t-1}ug_j$. Reindexing the lower contributions by $\ell=n-1-k$ gives $-\sum_{\ell=0}^{t-2}(-1)^\ell h^\ell u h^{t-1-\ell}g_j$. The total is exactly $dh^tg_j$ by step 1.1. Thus both intertwining identities hold, without yet assuming $\delta^2=0$.

Directly in the blocks, $$\delta_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}\delta_n=1_{D_n}-\alpha_n\beta_n.$$ Indeed for rows $k<n$ the off-diagonal blocks cancel when $n$ is replaced by $n+1$, and the two diagonal blocks sum to $1$. In row $n$ only the first term is present: its blocks are $-f_nh^{n-j}g_j$ for $j<n$ and $1-f_ng_n$ for $j=n$. They are exactly the final row of $1-\alpha\beta$. For $n=0$ this is simply $\delta_1s_0=1-f_0g_0$. Also $\beta_n\alpha_n=g_nf_n$.

We prove $\delta_{n-1}\delta_n=0$ by induction on $n$. It holds at $n=1$ since $D_{-1}=0$. On the first $n$ summands of $D_n$, identified with $s_{n-1}D_{n-1}$, step 2.2 and the two intertwining identities give $$\begin{aligned} \delta_{n-1}\delta_ns_{n-1} &=\delta_{n-1}(1-\alpha\beta-s_{n-2}\delta_{n-1})\\ &=(1-\alpha\beta)\delta_{n-1}-\delta_{n-1}s_{n-2}\delta_{n-1}\\ &=s_{n-3}\delta_{n-2}\delta_{n-1}=0. \end{aligned}$$ The final equality uses the induction hypothesis, and negative-index terms mean zero. On the remaining summand $F_n$, the two final-column observations give $\partial_{n-1}\partial_n=0$. Thus the composite vanishes on every summand. This proves $\delta^2=0$. Now step 2.1 says that $\alpha,\beta$ are chain maps, and step 2.2 together with $1-\beta\alpha=dh+hd$ gives a chain homotopy equivalence $C\simeq D$.

Set $T=\bigoplus_{j=0}^mF_j$. For all $n\ge m$, $D_n$ is canonically $T$, because all subsequent summands are zero. For $n\ge m+1$, the square matrix $\delta_n:T\to T$ depends only on the parity of $n$. Write $p$ for its value when $n$ is even. The formulas show that its value when $n$ is odd is $1-p$: the off-diagonal blocks change sign and the diagonal blocks are complementary. Taking two consecutive such degrees in $\delta^2=0$ gives $p(1-p)=0=(1-p)p$, hence $p^2=p$. No assertion that the homotopy idempotent $fg$ itself is strictly idempotent has been made.

Choose the explicit even integer $N=2(m+1)$, and let $q=p:T\to T$. Define $E_n=D_n$ for $0\le n<N$, $E_N=qT\subseteq T=D_N$, and $E_n=0$ otherwise. Restrict $\delta_N$ to $qT$ at the top, and keep $\delta_n$ below it. The square-zero identities remain valid by step 3.1. The maps $J:E\to D$ are the evident inclusions. Define $I:D\to E$ to be identity below $N$, $q$ in degree $N$ and zero above $N$. At degree $N$, $\delta_Nq=\delta_N$ because $1-q=\delta_{N+1}$ and $\delta_N\delta_{N+1}=0$. At degree $N+1$, $q\delta_{N+1}=q(1-q)=0$. These are the only boundary degrees in checking that $I$ is a chain map; $J$ is a chain map by restriction, and $IJ=1_E$.

Define $t_n:D_n\to D_{n+1}$ to be zero for $n<N$ and the canonical identity $T\to T$ for $n\ge N$. Then $$1_D-JI=\delta t+t\delta.$$ Below $N$ both sides are zero. In degree $N$ the right side is $\delta_{N+1}=1-q$, which is the left side. Above $N$ it is the sum of the two complementary matrices $p$ and $1-p$, hence identity, as is the left side. Thus $I,J$ give a specified chain homotopy equivalence between $D$ and the bounded complex $E$.

The modules $E_n$ below $N$ are finite direct sums of the supplied finite free modules, so their concatenated bases are finite. The module $qT$ is generated by the finitely many vectors $q(e_i)$, where $(e_i)$ is that concatenated basis of $T$, and $T=qT\oplus(1-q)T$: write $x=qx+(1-q)x$, and apply $q$ to an element in the intersection to show it is zero. For completeness its projectivity is choice-free. Given a surjection $v:U\to V$ and a right-linear $w:qT\to V$, take, for each of the finitely many $e_i$, a lift in $U$ of $w(qe_i)$. Their simultaneous existence is [F3]. Extend this finite assignment right-linearly to a map $\widetilde w:T\to U$. Then $v\widetilde w=wq$, and restriction to $qT$ is the requested lift. The same proof with $q=1$ gives projectivity of the lower finite free modules. This verifies the actual lifting property, not the general claim that arbitrary free modules are projective in ZF.

Set $a=I\alpha$, $b=\beta J$. These are chain maps and $$1_C-ba=d(h+\beta t\alpha)+(h+\beta t\alpha)d,$$ since $1_C-\beta JI\alpha=(1_C-\beta\alpha)+\beta(1_D-JI)\alpha$. Similarly, using $IJ=1_E$ and step 2.2, $$1_E-ab=\delta_E(IsJ)+(IsJ)\delta_E.$$ Indeed $I(1_D-\alpha\beta)J=1_E-I\alpha\beta J$. These are the explicit required homotopies $H=h+\beta t\alpha$ and $L=IsJ$.

Every degree of $D$, every matrix product used to define its maps, and each component of the homotopies uses a finite sum and finitely many compositions of supplied maps. The single family indexed by all nonnegative degrees is defined by these formulas; it is not obtained by independently selecting a lift or basis in each degree. The only lifts selected in the entire projectivity verification are a finite list for one supplied lifting problem. If the two input complexes vanish below a common integer $b$, reindex $C'_n=C_{n+b}$, $F'_n=F_{n+b}$ with the same differentials and domination equations, apply the construction, and reindex the result back. No infinite recursion of choices and no unbounded-below input is involved. The proof therefore establishes exactly the stated ZF conclusion for the required bounded-below setting.

Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space and let $\mathcal L$ be a left $R$-module local system on $X$. Its **compactly supported cohomology with local coefficients** is
$$H_c^k(X;\mathcal L)=\varinjlim_{K\subseteq X\text{ compact}}H^k(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L).$$
For compact sets $K\subseteq K'$, the identity is a map of pairs $(X,X\setminus K')\to(X,X\setminus K)$; contravariance gives the displayed system's transition $H^k(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L)\to H^k(X,X\setminus K';\mathcal L)$. Thus the coefficient system is always the restriction of one ambient system, and no extension from $X\setminus K$ is being assumed.

Equivalently, an element is represented by $(K,a)$ with $K$ compact and $a\in H^k(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L)$. Two representatives $(K,a)$ and $(K',a')$ are equal precisely when their images agree for some compact $N\supseteq K\cup K'$. Compact union makes the support poset filtered, so this relation is transitive and addition is performed after transition to $K\cup K'$. This is the same explicit filtered-colimit construction as [[def-compactly-supported-singular-cohomology-of-a-locally-compact-space]], now applied to the relative local-cochain groups.

If $f:X\to Y$ is proper, $\mathcal K$ is a local system on $Y$, and $\theta:f^*\mathcal K\to\mathcal L$ is a coefficient morphism, then each compact $K\subseteq Y$ has compact inverse image and [[prop-local-coefficient-homology-and-cohomology-are-functorial-for-a-map-with-a-coefficient-morphism]] gives
$$H^k(Y,Y\setminus K;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H^k(X,X\setminus f^{-1}K;\mathcal L).$$
These maps commute with enlargement of supports and hence induce the proper pullback $f^*:H_c^k(Y;\mathcal K)\to H_c^k(X;\mathcal L)$. Identity and composite proper maps give identity and composite pullbacks because both assertions already hold before taking the colimit.

When $X$ is compact, $K=X$ is terminal and yields $H_c^k(X;\mathcal L)\cong H^k(X;\mathcal L)$. For $X=\varnothing$, for the zero system, and in negative degrees the group is zero. Local compactness permits the cofinal use of closures of relatively compact open sets exactly as in the published constant-coefficient definition. No simultaneous selection of supports or neighborhoods is made, so the construction is choice-free.

For $A\subseteq X$ and a local system $\mathcal L$ on $X$, restriction to $A$ gives natural exact sequences
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_{n-1}(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to\cdots$$
and

derivations.claim: Fix the coordinate center $0$. Transport along straight radii trivializes $\mathcal L$ with fiber $A=\mathcal L_0$; triangular straight homotopies show that these identifications intertwine every path transport, since the ball is contractible. A contraction induces the usual singular prism homotopy by triangulating each simplex times the interval into its finitely many standard prisms, carrying constant coefficients unchanged. Its boundary identity proves directly that a contractible space has cohomology $A$ in degree zero and zero in positive degrees, with no universal-coefficient theorem or chosen primitive family. It also computes homology as $A$ in degree zero and zero elsewhere. For two points the cochain complex splits as two such complexes, so its reduced degree-zero cohomology is $A$ by the difference of the two values.

The same coefficient calculation gives $\widetilde H^k(S^m;A)=A$ for $k=m$ and zero otherwise, for each $m\ge0$. Start with the two-point sphere from step 1.1. For $m\ge1$, cover $S^m$ by the complements of the two poles; both are contractible and their intersection retracts onto $S^{m-1}$. The reduced cohomology Mayer–Vietoris sequence in [F2] identifies each group with the preceding degree on that intersection. This is a finite induction. These identifications are normalized by evaluation on the oriented sphere cycle: split a triangulated sphere into its two oriented hemispheres; the connecting cochain evaluates on their sum as the preceding cochain evaluates on their common boundary. This follows from $(\delta a)(c)=a(\partial c)$ with the difference signs of Mayer–Vietoris. Starting with the oriented difference of the two points, induction proves that evaluation on the oriented fundamental sphere cycle is the resulting isomorphism to $A$, including its sign.

For $n\ge1$, closed concentric balls are cofinal among compact supports in $\mathbb R^n$. The complement of a closed radius-$r$ ball retracts radially onto any larger concentric sphere. Since the ambient space is contractible, its pair sequence in [F2] and step 2.1 identify $H^k(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R^n\setminus\overline B_r;A)$ with $A$ for $k=n$ and with zero otherwise. The isomorphism is evaluation on a positively oriented relative ball cycle: the pair connector and $(\delta a)(c)=a(\partial c)$ identify it with the sphere evaluation of step 2.1. Enlargement from $r$ to a larger radius preserves this normalization, since the two oriented sphere cycles bound the oriented intervening annulus and the relative ball cycles restrict to the same local orientation. Hence the direct limit in [F1] has exactly the asserted groups, without a choice of representatives at infinitely many radii. For $n=0$ the ball is a point and the same conclusion is step 1.1.

A finite triangulated coordinate ball enclosing the support, with boundary disjoint from it, represents the canonical support class by [F3]. In degree $n$, the cap formula sends a relative cocycle $\alpha$ and this oriented cycle $z$ to a zero-chain whose sum of coefficients is $\alpha(z)$: each retained back face is a vertex and each coefficient is the front evaluation on that simplex. derivations.claim: For compact $K,L\subset X$, write $C=C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathbb Z)$ and $A_K=C_*(X\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$, with analogous notation for $L$. Local cochains vanishing on $A_K$ are the relative local complex denoted $D_K$. Simplex by simplex, addition gives an onto map $D_K\oplus D_L\to D_{K\cup L}$: a simplex not entirely outside $K\cup L$ is not entirely outside at least one of $K,L$, so place its assigned coefficient in the first allowed summand. This is a degreewise lift, not asserted to commute with coboundaries. Its kernel consists of pairs $(a,-a)$ with $a$ vanishing on $A_K+A_L$. Thus there is a short exact cochain sequence with that kernel. The latter cochain complex computes the relative local cohomology supported in $K\cap L$. Indeed $X\setminus K$ and $X\setminus L$ are open and cover $X\setminus(K\cap L)$; [F2] replaces their small-chain sum by the full complement. To see the relative comparison on cochains explicitly, extend its small-chain homotopy $D$ to all ambient simplex generators by zero on simplices not contained in this complement. Then $1-\partial D-D\partial$ maps complement chains to their small-chain sum and fixes the sum, while $D$ vanishes on the sum. The resulting quotient maps are inverse up to the displayed chain homotopy; transporting coefficients along the same affine paths gives the identical local-cochain comparison. Taking cohomology gives the supported exact sequence.

Restrict to pairs $K\subset U$, $L\subset V$ compact. These unions are cofinal among compact supports in $X$. For any compact $Q\subset X$, choose finitely many relatively compact coordinate neighborhoods whose closures lie in one of $U,V$ and whose interiors cover $Q$. The union of the closures assigned to $U$, intersected with $Q$, is a compact $K\subset U$; the analogous construction gives $L\subset V$, with $Q=K\cup L$. Only one finite cover is selected. The intersections $K\cap L$ are cofinal for compact subsets of $U\cap V$, since one may take $K=L$ equal to any such compact set. Excision in [F2] identifies the groups supported in $K$, $L$ and $K\cap L$ with their groups in $U$, $V$ and $U\cap V$. Take the filtered colimit of the exact sequences of step 1.1. It is exact directly: a representative in a colimit kernel vanishes at one common larger pair of supports, where exactness supplies its lift; a zero representative of a lift also becomes zero at a common larger pair. With [F1] this gives exactly the displayed compact-support sequence and its extension maps.

For the cap assertion, use the support class of [F3] on $K\cup L$, whose restrictions are the two smaller support classes. Subdivide a finite representative orientation chain so that every simplex lies either in $U$ or outside $K$, and either in $V$ or outside $L$; the two open covers and the finite chain allow one common finite subdivision by [F2]. If $\alpha=\alpha_U+\alpha_V$ is a degree-$p$ supported cocycle lifted by the short exact sequence of step 1.1, then $\alpha_U\cap z$ is a chain in $U$ and $\alpha_V\cap z$ is a chain in $V$: the other simplices lie outside the corresponding support and their front evaluations vanish. Their sum is $\alpha\cap z$. The supported cohomology connector is represented by $\delta\alpha_U=-\delta\alpha_V$ in the intersection complex. The homology connector is represented by $\partial(\alpha_U\cap z)$. Since $\partial z$ lies outside $K\cup L$, [F4] gives $\partial(\alpha_U\cap z)=(-1)^{p+1}(\delta\alpha_U)\cap z$. To check the kernel-to-support comparison as well, put $\gamma=\delta\alpha_U$ and use $\rho=1-\partial D-D\partial$ from step 1.1. The actual cochain supported in $K\cap L$ is $\gamma\rho$. Since $\gamma$ is a cocycle, $\gamma\rho-\gamma=\delta\beta$ with $\beta=-\gamma D$. The identity [F4] shows that $(\gamma\rho)\cap z-\gamma\cap z$ is the boundary $(-1)^{p+1}\partial(\beta\cap z)$ in that intersection. These maps commute with enlargement of supports and hence induce the proper pullback $f^*:H_c^k(Y;\mathcal K)\to H_c^k(X;\mathcal L)$. Identity and composite proper maps give identity and composite pullbacks because both assertions already hold before taking the colimit.

When $X$ is compact, $K=X$ is terminal and yields $H_c^k(X;\mathcal L)\cong H^k(X;\mathcal L)$. For $X=\varnothing$, for the zero system, and in negative degrees the group is zero. Local compactness permits the cofinal use of closures of relatively compact open sets exactly as in the published constant-coefficient definition. No simultaneous selection of supports or neighborhoods is made, so the construction is choice-free.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and let $\mathcal L,\mathcal K$ be left $R$-module local systems on $X$. Their **objectwise tensor product** is

and

$$[M]^\mathrm{tw}_K\in H_n(M,M\setminus K;\mathcal O_M^R)$$
whose image at every $x\in K$ is the canonical local element: if $o_x$ is
either generator of the integral local group $\mathcal O_x$, it is represented
by a local relative cycle for $o_x$ carrying coefficient $o_x\otimes1_R$.

$o_x\otimes(o_x\otimes1_R)$, the first in local integral homology and the
second in the stalk $\mathcal O_x^R$. Changing $o_x$ to $-o_x$ changes both

with these prescribed local images at all interior points. Its pair boundary is the canonical twisted class of $A$ for the outward-normal-first identification $\mathcal O_M^R|_A\cong\mathcal O_A^R$.

$$\cdots \to A_{n-1} \to A_n \to A_{n+1} \to A_{n+2} \to A_{n+3} \to \cdots$$
and
$$\cdots \to B_{n-1} \to B_n \to B_{n+1} \to B_{n+2} \to B_{n+3} \to \cdots$$
be long exact sequences in an abelian category, together with a morphism of
these sequences. If the four comparison maps at $A_{n-1},A_n,A_{n+2},A_{n+3}$
are isomorphisms, then the comparison map $A_{n+1} \to B_{n+1}$ is an

2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and

derivations.claim: For every open $W\subset M$, define $D_W:H_c^p(W;\mathcal L)\to H_{n-p}(W;\mathcal L)$ by the supportwise cap of [F1], using the restricted orientation. If $W=U\cup V$ and all three maps for $U,V,U\cap V$ are isomorphisms in every degree, the exact ladder [F3] and five lemma [F4] make $D_W$ an isomorphism in every degree. The five-term window centered on degree $p$ has the surrounding compact-support terms in degrees $p$ and $p+1$ on the intersection and on the two pieces; their homology comparisons are the assumed isomorphisms. Multiplying a connecting map by the specified sign preserves exactness. Thus this finite gluing implication is valid without a chosen splitting.

Let $O$ be any open subset of one coordinate ball. In coordinates enumerate all bounded open boxes with rational endpoints whose closures lie in $O$, using the fixed elementary enumeration of finite rational tuples. They cover $O$: each point has a sufficiently small coordinate box with closure in $O$, and density supplies rational endpoints on either side of its coordinates. A box, and a nonempty intersection of finitely many boxes, is a coordinate ball; its local coefficient system is trivialized by the straight contraction inside the ambient coordinate chart, so [F2] applies. Prove duality for every finite union of these boxes by induction on their number. For the last box $B$ and preceding union $A$, the intersection $A\cap B$ is a union of fewer boxes, namely the nonempty intersections with $B$. The induction hypothesis applies to that union as well as to $A$, and step 1.1 proves duality on $A\cup B$. Empty intersections and the empty union have zero groups.

Let $O_j$ be the union of the admissible boxes among the first $j$ tuples in the fixed rational enumeration; inadmissible tuples contribute nothing. Every compact subset of $O$ is contained in some $O_j$, since finitely many of the boxes cover it and their indices have a finite maximum. Excision [F4] identifies a relative class supported on such a compact set with its class in that $O_j$; any equality of compact-support classes is witnessed on one larger compact support by [F1], hence in some common later stage. The stage maps are isomorphisms by step 2.1; surjectivity and injectivity at a common stage therefore make $D_O$ an isomorphism. This argument uses an explicitly enumerated family inside one supplied chart, rather than selecting a countable chart family on the manifold.

Compactness supplies a finite cover $B_1,\ldots,B_m$ of $M$ by coordinate balls, each with a specified chart; selecting that finite list requires only finite choice. Induct on the number of balls. Since $M$ is compact, its support $M$ is terminal and $H_c^p(M;\mathcal L)=H^p(M;\mathcal L)$; its support orientation class is the integral orientation class by [F1]. This is exactly the displayed map.

Compact disconnected manifolds have finitely many components, since their open components cover them; the same finite construction already applies without choosing data on an infinite component family. Local compactness permits the cofinal use of closures of relatively compact open sets exactly as in the published constant-coefficient definition. Let
$$\cdots \to A_{n-1} \to A_n \to A_{n+1} \to A_{n+2} \to A_{n+3} \to \cdots$$
and
$$\cdots \to B_{n-1} \to B_n \to B_{n+1} \to B_{n+2} \to B_{n+3} \to \cdots$$

Let $\mathcal L$ be a left $R$-module local system on an arbitrary space $X$. For a singular simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$, write $v_i=\sigma(e_i)$ and $\gamma_{01}^\sigma(t)=\sigma(1-t,t,0,\ldots,0)$.

The **intrinsic singular local chain group** is
$$C_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)=\bigoplus_{\sigma:\Delta^n\to X}\mathcal L_{v_0}.$$
Write an element of the $\sigma$-summand as $m\sigma$. Its boundary is
$$\partial(m\sigma)=T_{\gamma_{01}^\sigma}(m)(\sigma\delta_0)+\sum_{i=1}^n(-1)^im(\sigma\delta_i),$$
and the boundary of a zero-simplex is zero. The exceptional zeroth face transports its coefficient from the old first vertex $v_0$ to the new first vertex $v_1$; all other faces keep $v_0$.

The **intrinsic singular local cochain group** is the product
$$C^n_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)=\prod_{\sigma:\Delta^n\to X}\mathcal L_{v_0},$$
so a cochain $\varphi$ assigns $\varphi(\sigma)\in\mathcal L_{v_0}$ to every simplex, with no finite-support requirement. Its positive coboundary, consistent with [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]], is
$$(\delta\varphi)(\sigma)=T_{\gamma_{01}^\sigma}^{-1}\bigl(\varphi(\sigma\delta_0)\bigr)+\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}(-1)^i\varphi(\sigma\delta_i).$$
Now the exceptional face value is transported back from $v_1$ to $v_0$.

For $A\subseteq X$, restrict $\mathcal L$ along the inclusion and set
$$C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)=C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)/C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(A;\mathcal L),\qquad C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)=\ker\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)\to C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(A;\mathcal L)\bigr).$$

For a connected CW complex with chosen basepoint $x$, universal cover $\widetilde X$, $\pi=\pi_1(X,x)$, and base fiber $M=\mathcal L_x$ carrying $g m=T_{\bar g}m$, the equivalent universal-cover models are
$$C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R)\otimes_{R[\pi]}M,\qquad \operatorname{Hom}_{R[\pi]}\bigl({}_{R[\pi]}C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R),M\bigr).$$
The first tensor product is the balanced construction of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] using the right action of [[def-right-group-ring-action-on-the-chains-of-a-universal-cover]]. For the second, convert that right chain module to a left one by
$$g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}.$$
Thus an equivariant cochain has the correctly typed rule
$$\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c),$$
not a module-Hom between one right and one left module.

The intrinsic/tensor identification sends $\widetilde\sigma\otimes m$ to the simplex $\sigma=p\widetilde\sigma$ with coefficient obtained by transporting $m$ along the path represented by $\widetilde\sigma(e_0)$. If $\widetilde\sigma$ is replaced by $\widetilde\sigma\cdot g$, that path is changed by the loop $g^{-1}$ and the coefficient becomes the transport of $gm$, exactly the balanced relation. The analogous statement for cochains proves the displayed equivariance rule. These maps respect the two boundary formulas term by term.

The **cellular local chain and cochain groups** of a connected CW complex are
$$C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;\mathcal L)=C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R)\otimes_{R[\pi]}M,\qquad C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X;\mathcal L)=\operatorname{Hom}_{R[\pi]}\bigl({}_{R[\pi]}C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R),M\bigr).$$
For a CW pair, quotient by the lifted subcomplex before tensoring and use the corresponding relative cellular complex before applying equivariant Hom. For a disconnected CW complex, take the direct sum of chain complexes and the degreewise product of cochain complexes over its components. Universal-cover coordinates of this componentwise description require a supplied basepoint in each component; the intrinsic complexes require no simultaneous basepoint choice and remain the definition when no such family is supplied.

The next lemma proves square-zero and independence of supplied lift bases. Empty spaces and negative degrees give zero groups, the zero local system gives the zero complexes, and constant systems reduce to the ordinary formulas because every transport is the identity.

derivations.claim: For a singular simplex $\sigma:[v_0,\ldots,v_n]\to M$, put its coefficient in $\mathcal R_{\sigma(v_0)}$ and take the direct sum of those right modules over all singular simplices. For $n\ge1$ define $d(c\sigma)=T_{01}(c)\,\sigma[1,\ldots,n]+\sum_{i=1}^n(-1)^i c\,\sigma[0,\ldots,\widehat i,\ldots,n]$, and let the degree-zero differential be zero. Every face map is right-linear because transport is, so this defines right-$R$ linear differentials without assuming that $R$ is commutative. To check $d^2=0$, pair the two terms deleting vertices $i<j$. Their signs are $(-1)^{i+j-1}$ and $(-1)^{i+j}$. If $i>0$, both coefficients are $c$. If $i=0<1<j$, both coefficients are $T_{01}(c)$. If $(i,j)=(0,1)$, the coefficients are $T_{12}T_{01}(c)$ and $T_{02}(c)$, which agree because the two-edge path is endpoint-fixed homotopic to the direct edge in the simplex and transport is a groupoid functor. Thus every pair cancels. This includes degenerate simplices and degree one, where the next differential is zero. These are the underlying abelian local chains of [F1], now equipped with their verified right-$R$ structure.

Choose a finite cover by coordinate balls $U_1,\ldots,U_m$ with charts onto convex Euclidean balls, including a ball centered at $o$. This uses compactness and only a finite selection. Their intersection graph is connected: otherwise the unions belonging to different graph components would be disjoint nonempty open sets partitioning connected $M$. For each edge choose one point in the intersection, a finite selection; join it to each chart center by its straight coordinate segment. Choose a spanning tree by the finite index order and concatenate these segments to get paths from $o$ to every chart center. For $x\in M$, take the least-index chart containing it and follow its center path by the straight segment to $x$; at $o$ use the constant path. Denote this explicitly prescribed path by $\gamma_x$. This defines paths for all points from one finite list of charts and edge points, rather than selecting an infinite family of paths.

Transport the supplied basis $1\in\mathcal R_o$ along $\gamma_x$ to obtain a basis at each $x$. Thus [F1] makes every $C_j$ the free right $R$-module on its actual singular $j$-simplices. Write $e_x$ for the degree-zero basis and $e_\sigma$ for the degree-one basis of a path $\sigma:x\to y$. The degree-one boundary is $d_1e_\sigma=e_y g_\sigma-e_x$, where $g_\sigma\in H$ is the transition unit obtained by transporting first along $\gamma_x$, then along $\sigma$, and back along $\gamma_y$. For $x\ne o$, the path $\gamma_x$ is itself one singular one-simplex; denote its basis element by $p_x$. These basis elements are distinct because their terminal points are distinct, and $d_1p_x=e_x-e_o$. Put $p_o=0$.

Change the degree-zero basis to $e_o$ and $b_x=e_x-e_o$ for $x\ne o$. This is invertible even with infinitely many vertices: the inverse is $e_x=b_x+e_o$, and every vector has finite support. Let $Q_1$ be free on the $p_x$, $Q_0$ free on the $b_x$, and $Q_j=0$ in other degrees, with differential $p_x\mapsto b_x$. Let $C'_1$ be free on the remaining $q_\sigma$, $C'_0=Re_o$, and $C'_j=C_j$ for $j\ge2$. The differential of a degree-two chain has zero $p_x$ coefficient for every $x$: applying $d_1$ would otherwise give a nonzero corresponding $b_x$ coefficient, contrary to $d_1d_2=0$ proved in step 1.1. Thus $d_2$ lands in $C'_1$, and higher differentials already stay in $C'$. This proves the claimed direct sum of complexes. Its contractible summand has the explicit homotopy $b_x\mapsto p_x$, zero on all other degrees. Dualizing this actual homotopy gives the cochain equivalences for any coefficient module; no exactness assertion about an infinite product or choice of primitives is needed.

The image of $d'_1$ is the right ideal generated by the elements $g_\sigma-1$. All transition units belong to $H$, so this ideal is contained in $\sum_{h\in H}(h-1)R$. Conversely every $h\in H$ is realized by transport along a based loop at $o$. That loop is one singular one-simplex and is not one of the removed $p_x$, whose endpoints differ. Its reduced boundary is $e_o(h-1)$. Thus every generator of the displayed ideal occurs, and equality follows.

If $H=\langle t\rangle$ is cyclic, $t^k-1$ is a right multiple of $t-1$ for every integer $k$: use the finite geometric sum for $k>0$, zero for $k=0$, and $t^{-k}-1=-t^{-k}(t^k-1)$ for negative powers. Since powers of $t$ commute with $t-1$, this last expression is also a right multiple. The ideal is therefore $(t-1)R$, including $H=\{1\}$ with zero ideal. The other two sufficient conditions for principality are literal. All basis changes and homotopies were explicit finite-support formulas, and the only initial choices were finite. This proves the stated choice scope.

Use the finite-atlas paths of [F1] to transport the supplied base vector $1$ to a frame $e_x$ in every fiber. Two paths to $x$ give frames $e_x$ and $e'_x=e_xv$ where $v$ is unitary, because their difference is a based loop. Define $h_x(e_xa,e_xb)=\bar a b$. In the second frame the coordinates are $v^{-1}a,v^{-1}b$, and
$$\overline{v^{-1}a}\,v^{-1}b=\bar a(\bar v)^{-1}v^{-1}b=\bar a b.$$
Thus this definition is path-independent and every transport preserves $h$. The finite-atlas rule supplies all the paths by a formula, so no infinite family of choices is required. The resulting frames are unitary and their transition units are unitary.

Use the paths from [F1] to put a specified basis on every fiber, and let $u_{01}$ be the transition unit along the first edge of a singular simplex. In this gauge its right-chain boundary has first term $e_{\partial_0\sigma}u_{01}$ and its remaining terms $(-1)^i e_{\partial_i\sigma}$ for $i>0$. A right-linear cochain $f$ consequently has coboundary first term $f(e_{\partial_0\sigma})u_{01}$, with the same remaining signed terms. Intrinsic local cochains use inverse first-edge transport. Thus these are exactly the cochain formulas for the coefficient system whose transport is right multiplication by $u_{01}^{-1}$; that transport commutes with left multiplication by $R$. Sending $f$ to its values on these supplied simplex basis elements is a bijection, in every degree, with the intrinsic cochains, and the displayed formulas show that it commutes with coboundaries. No values in an infinite product are lifted or chosen.

Intrinsically send $\bar v$ to the right-linear functional $w\mapsto h(v,w)$. In a unitary frame this is $J:\overline R\to R$, $J(\bar a)=\bar a$, where the bar on the right is the ring involution. It is left-linear: $J(r\cdot\bar a)=\overline{a\bar r}=r\bar a$. It commutes with transport, since $\overline{ua}=\bar a\bar u=\bar a u^{-1}$. Hence it identifies the conjugate chain-coefficient local system with the dual system of step 1.2. Conjugation changes neither underlying abelian-group cycles nor boundaries and is involutive, so the homology of that dual system identifies with $\overline{H_*(C_*)}$. When $M$ is oriented and closed, apply [F2] to the actual dual local system from step 1.2, viewed as a local system of abelian groups with a commuting left-$R$ action. Its cap isomorphism gives precisely the displayed cohomology-to-conjugate-homology identification.

For $K$ coefficients, every right-linear $f:C_j\to K$ extends uniquely to the right-$K$ linear map $C_j\otimes_RK\to K$, $c\otimes k\mapsto f(c)k$. Balancing proves that formula well-defined; its inverse is restriction to $c\otimes1$. These maps commute with the differentials and left $K$ actions. $$H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W;\mathcal L),\qquad H^p(W;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W,A;\mathcal L).$$
The maps commute with every coefficient action commuting with transport, including noncommutative ring actions on the underlying abelian-group systems. No choice principle, smoothness, triangulation or finite CW structure is assumed.

Let $(M,o)$ be a compact connected based Hausdorff manifold, let $R$ be an involutive unital ring, and supply a rank-one right-$R$ local system $\mathcal R$ with an identification $\mathcal R_o=R$. Assume every based-loop monodromy is left multiplication by a unit $u$ satisfying $\bar u=u^{-1}$. Equip the base fiber with the standard Hermitian form $h_o(a,b)=\bar a b$. Transport extends this to a path-independent parallel Hermitian form $h$ on $\mathcal R$. Put $C_*=C_*(M;\mathcal R)$. For a right $R$-module $P$, write $\overline P$ for its conjugate left module, with $r\cdot\bar p=\overline{p\bar r}$.

The left-$R$ cochain complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R)$ is the intrinsic cochain complex of the left-$R$ local system with fiber $R$ and transport $a\mapsto au^{-1}$. Relative to the supplied parallel Hermitian form, that local system is naturally isomorphic to $\overline{\mathcal R}$ by $\bar v\mapsto[w\mapsto h(v,w)]$. The identifications are independent of unitary fiber frames; an arbitrary change of Hermitian structure is not asserted to preserve them. If $M$ is oriented, boundaryless and of dimension $n$, cap duality therefore gives
$$H^p(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))\cong\overline{H_{n-p}(C_*)}.$$
If $R\subseteq K$ is an embedding into an involutive division ring extending the involution, the same conclusion is valid for $K$, with $C_*\otimes_R K$ in the homology target. If $R$ is involution-stable in $K$, the complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K/R)$ is the corresponding intrinsic left-$R$ cochain complex with fiber $K/R$ and transport by right multiplication by $u^{-1}$. These identifications require no choice principle and commute with the coefficient maps $R\to K\to K/R$.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and let $\mathcal L,\mathcal K$ be left $R$-module local systems on $X$. Their **objectwise tensor product** is
$$(\mathcal L\otimes_R\mathcal K)_x=\mathcal L_x\otimes_R\mathcal K_x,\qquad T_\gamma(\ell\otimes k)=T_\gamma\ell\otimes T_\gamma k.$$
The tensor relations make the displayed transport well defined; identity and composition hold on elementary tensors, and $T_{\bar\gamma}\otimes T_{\bar\gamma}$ is its inverse. Thus this is again a local system.

A **local-coefficient pairing** is a natural transformation $b:\mathcal L\otimes_R\mathcal K\to\mathcal N$, equivalently bilinear maps $b_x:\mathcal L_x\times\mathcal K_x\to\mathcal N_x$ satisfying $T_\gamma b_x(\ell,k)=b_y(T_\gamma\ell,T_\gamma k)$ for every path class $\gamma:x\to y$.

For a simplex $\sigma:[v_0,\ldots,v_{p+q}]\to X$, let $\lambda_{0p}^\sigma$ be its affine edge path from $v_0$ to $v_p$. For $\varphi\in C^p(X;\mathcal L)$ and $\psi\in C^q(X;\mathcal K)$ define
$$(\varphi\smile_b\psi)(\sigma)=b_{v_0}\left(\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p]),T^{\mathcal K}_{\overline{\lambda_{0p}^\sigma}}\psi(\sigma[p,\ldots,p+q])\right).$$
The reverse transport is necessary because the back-face value lies over $v_p$ while the output cochain value must lie over $v_0$. The Alexander--Whitney face calculation, with naturality of $b$ on each triangular transport comparison, gives
$$\delta(\varphi\smile_b\psi)=\delta\varphi\smile_b\psi+(-1)^p\varphi\smile_b\delta\psi.$$

Here forward transport is necessary because the retained back face begins at $v_p$. The published front/back face cancellation, with the same naturality squares, yields
$$\partial(\varphi\cap_b c)=(-1)^p\left(\varphi\cap_b\partial c-\delta\varphi\cap_b c\right).$$

$$H^p(X,A;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH_n(X,A;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X;\mathcal N),$$
and
$$H^p(X;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH_n(X,A;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X,A;\mathcal N).$$

If a cohomology class is represented with compact support $K$, cup with any ordinary class remains supported in $K$, while the cap of a class in $H^p(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L)$ with a class in $H_n(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal K)$ is an absolute class. $$[M]^\mathrm{tw}_K\in H_n(M,M\setminus K;\mathcal O_M^R)$$
whose image at every $x\in K$ is the canonical local element: if $o_x$ is

derivations.claim: On the dual coefficient fibers and their conjugates, the natural evaluation pairing is the ring-valued pairing $(a,\bar b)\mapsto a\bar b$ in a unitary frame. The needed cup interchange is an explicit finite cochain identity. Since $\alpha,\beta$ are relative, $H$ vanishes on every simplex in $\partial W$. If $z$ is the finite relative orientation cycle, then $\langle\delta H,z\rangle=\langle H,\partial z\rangle=0$. derivations.claim: First construct a compatible metric from finite data. Compactness supplies finitely many coordinate balls $V_i$ whose closures lie in larger coordinate balls with charts $\varphi_i$; take their coordinate images concentric balls of radii $r_i<R_i$. A continuous radial function $\chi_i$ equals one on $\overline V_i$, decreases linearly to zero before the larger chart boundary, and is zero elsewhere on $M$. The finitely many functions $\chi_i$ and $\chi_i\varphi_i$, extended by zero, are continuous because their coordinate supports are compactly contained in the charts. Their combined map $F$ into a finite Euclidean space is injective: for $x$, choose $i$ with $x\in V_i$, so $\chi_i(x)=1$; equality $F(x)=F(y)$ forces $\chi_i(y)=1$ and $\varphi_i(x)=\varphi_i(y)$, hence $x=y$. A continuous injection of a compact space into a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image: images of closed subsets are compact and hence closed. Therefore $d(x,y)=|F(x)-F(y)|$ is a compatible metric. All choices so far are finite.

Choose a finite cover of $M$ by contractible coordinate balls. It has a positive Lebesgue number $\lambda$: for a finite open cover the functions $x\mapsto d(x,M\setminus U)$, with the empty-complement case assigned a positive constant, are continuous; their finite maximum is everywhere positive and has a positive minimum on compact $M$. A sufficiently small number below that minimum makes every set of diameter less than $\lambda$ lie in some member, by taking a point in the set and using the corresponding distance bound. Choose $0<\epsilon<\lambda/10$. There is a finite cover by smaller coordinate balls $B_j$ of $d$-diameter less than $\epsilon$, because one can shrink a coordinate neighborhood inside a metric ball of radius less than $\epsilon/2$ and then take a finite subcover. Choose $0<\delta<\epsilon$ that is a Lebesgue number for this second finite cover. Any pair of points of distance less than $\delta$ can therefore be joined inside one $B_j$ by its straight coordinate path, of diameter less than $\epsilon$.

Compactness gives a finite $\delta/4$-net of anchors $a_0=o,a_1,\ldots,a_s$, with the basepoint added first. For each unordered distinct anchor pair of distance less than $\delta$, put an edge in a finite graph and map it to the straight coordinate path in the least-index $B_j$ containing that pair; the reverse orientation uses the reversed path. Map each vertex to its anchor. For any $x\in M$, let $a(x)$ be the least-index anchor at distance less than $\delta/4$. Join $x$ to $a(x)$ by the straight path in the least-index $B_j$ containing them. These connectors have diameter less than $\epsilon$ and are defined by finite lists and the chart formulas, without choosing a family of paths. At $o$ take the constant connector.

Let $\ell$ be any based loop in $M$. Uniform continuity on its compact interval gives a finite subdivision such that each segment has image diameter less than $\delta/4$. Write its successive endpoints as $x_i$ and anchors as $a_i=a(x_i)$. Then $d(a_i,a_{i+1})<3\delta/4$, so the selected graph has an edge between successive distinct anchors; repeated anchors give the constant path. The loop formed by this edge, the original loop segment and the two endpoint connectors is contained in a set of diameter less than $4\epsilon$: each connector and edge has diameter less than $\epsilon$, and its initial or terminal point lies within $\delta/4$ of an endpoint of the original short segment. This entire small loop therefore lies in one of the contractible coordinate balls of step 2.1. Contract it there. Gluing these finitely many homotopies, with adjacent connectors cancelling, shows that $\ell$ is based homotopic to the resulting graph edge loop at $a_0=o$. Thus the fundamental-group map of the component of this finite graph containing $a_0$ is onto.

Choose a spanning tree of that finite graph component by its finite vertex order. For every oriented edge outside the tree, follow the tree path from the base vertex to its initial vertex, traverse the edge, and return along the tree path from its terminal vertex. These finitely many loops generate all graph edge loops: insert the corresponding tree paths at successive vertices of an edge loop; the intervening inverse tree paths cancel, and a tree-edge loop contracts by deleting immediate reversals. Step 4.1 then makes their images generate $\pi_1(M,o)$. All graph data, covers, nets and tree paths were finite; a loop uses its own one finite subdivision and finite homotopy construction. No infinite family of generators, partitions or primitives was selected. This proves the statement without AC.
