citations.quote:
Let $L$ be a finite geometric simplicial complex with an ordered vertex set, and let $\mathcal R$ be a local system of rank-one free right modules over an arbitrary unital ring $R$. Its finite simplicial chain complex $F_*(L;\mathcal R)$ and intrinsic singular chain complex $C_*(L;\mathcal R)$ admit $R$-linear chain maps
$$P:C_*(L;\mathcal R)\to F_*(L;\mathcal R),\qquad J:F_*(L;\mathcal R)\to C_*(L;\mathcal R)$$
with $PJ=1$ and an explicitly constructed chain homotopy $JP\simeq1$. Choices of bases at its finitely many vertices make $F_*$ bounded finite-free.

Consequently, for every compact connected Hausdorff topological manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, and every such local system supplied with a base-fiber identification with $R$, its nonnegative singular chain complex is free with a formula-specified basis and is $R$-linearly chain-homotopy dominated by a bounded finite-free complex. No choice principle, triangulation of $M$, or assertion of finite CW type for $M$ is assumed.

Work in ZF. Let $A$ be any associative unital ring and let $C$ be a chain complex of unital right $A$-modules with $C_n=0$ for $n<0$. Supply a chain complex $F$ with $F_n=0$ outside $0\le n\le m$, each $F_n$ supplied as a finite free right $A$-module, chain maps $f:C\to F$ and $g:F\to C$, and right $A$-linear maps $h_n:C_n\to C_{n+1}$ such that
$$1_C-gf=d_Ch+hd_C.$$
Then there is a chain complex $E$ of finitely generated projective right $A$-modules, zero outside $0\le n\le N$ for some finite $N$, together with explicitly constructed chain maps $a:C\to E$, $b:E\to C$ and chain homotopies
$$1_C-ba=dH+Hd,\qquad 1_E-ab=dL+Ld.$$
The modules of $E$ below its top degree can be taken finite free, and its top module is the image of an explicit idempotent on $\bigoplus_{j=0}^mF_j$.

Neither freeness nor projectivity nor finite generation of the modules of $C$ is required. Thus the result applies in particular to the nonnegative singular or cellular free chain complexes with specified bases. More generally it applies after reindexing whenever $C$ and $F$ have a common finite lower bound. It makes no assertion for inputs unbounded below and no assertion that $E$ is finite free or that any underlying space has finite CW type. No form of the Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Let $W$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological $n$-manifold with boundary $A$ and a supplied boundary collar $c:A\times[0,1)\to W$. Let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. Cap with the integral relative orientation class $z=[W,A]$ gives isomorphisms in every integer degree:
$$H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W;\mathcal L),\qquad H^p(W;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W,A;\mathcal L).$$
The maps commute with every coefficient action commuting with transport, including noncommutative ring actions on the underlying abelian-group systems. No choice principle, smoothness, triangulation or finite CW structure is assumed.

Let $M$ be a compact oriented boundaryless Hausdorff topological $n$-manifold and let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. Cap with its integral orientation class induces isomorphisms
$$H^p(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;\mathcal L)$$
for every integer $p$, without a choice principle. The maps respect any coefficient-ring action commuting with transport, and in particular apply to local systems of modules over a noncommutative ring by forgetting to abelian groups and retaining that action. No smoothness, triangulation or prescribed finite CW structure is assumed.

Let $(M,o)$ be a compact connected based Hausdorff manifold, let $R$ be an involutive unital ring, and supply a rank-one right-$R$ local system $\mathcal R$ with an identification $\mathcal R_o=R$. Assume every based-loop monodromy is left multiplication by a unit $u$ satisfying $\bar u=u^{-1}$. Equip the base fiber with the standard Hermitian form $h_o(a,b)=\bar a b$. Transport extends this to a path-independent parallel Hermitian form $h$ on $\mathcal R$. Put $C_*=C_*(M;\mathcal R)$. For a right $R$-module $P$, write $\overline P$ for its conjugate left module, with $r\cdot\bar p=\overline{p\bar r}$.

The left-$R$ cochain complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R)$ is the intrinsic cochain complex of the left-$R$ local system with fiber $R$ and transport $a\mapsto au^{-1}$. Relative to the supplied parallel Hermitian form, that local system is naturally isomorphic to $\overline{\mathcal R}$ by $\bar v\mapsto[w\mapsto h(v,w)]$. The identifications are independent of unitary fiber frames; an arbitrary change of Hermitian structure is not asserted to preserve them. If $M$ is oriented, boundaryless and of dimension $n$, cap duality therefore gives
$$H^p(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))\cong\overline{H_{n-p}(C_*)}.$$
If $R\subseteq K$ is an embedding into an involutive division ring extending the involution, the same conclusion is valid for $K$, with $C_*\otimes_R K$ in the homology target. If $R$ is involution-stable in $K$, the complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K/R)$ is the corresponding intrinsic left-$R$ cochain complex with fiber $K/R$ and transport by right multiplication by $u^{-1}$. These identifications require no choice principle and commute with the coefficient maps $R\to K\to K/R$.

Assume AC. Let $G$ be a discrete group, let $A=\mathcal N G\subseteq\mathcal B(\ell^2(G))$ have its canonical faithful normal trace $\tau$, and give matrices the unnormalized trace $\tau_r((a_{ij}))=\sum_{i=1}^r\tau(a_{ii})$. For a projection $p\in M_r(A)$ put $\dim_A(pA^r)=\tau_r(p)$; for any right $A$-module take the supremum of dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules. These dimensions are independent of the projective representation. If $L\subseteq pA^r$ is any submodule and $q$ is the projection onto its Hilbert closure in $p\ell^2(G)^r$, then $q\in M_r(A)$, $q\le p$, and
$$\dim_A L=\tau_r(q),\qquad \dim_A(pA^r/L)=\tau_r(p)-\tau_r(q).$$
In particular a Hilbert-dense submodule has dimension-zero quotient. Modules of dimension zero are closed under submodules, quotients, extensions and filtered colimits. For any matrix $B\in M_{r,s}(A)$, its kernel and Hilbert-closed image are projection modules, its algebraic image is isomorphic to its support projection module, and
$$\tau_s(P_{\ker B})+\tau_r(P_{\overline{\operatorname{im}B}})=s.$$

Work under the standing AC convention for finite von Neumann modules. Let $A=\mathcal N G$ with its finite trace, and let all Hilbert modules below be ranges of projections on finite sums of $\ell^2(G)$. For a bounded self-adjoint module operator $J$ define its positive and negative inertia by the traces of $\mathbf1_{(0,\infty)}(J)$ and $\mathbf1_{(-\infty,0)}(J)$, and its signature by their difference. Each inertia is the supremum of dimensions of closed module subspaces on which the form $\langle Jx,x\rangle$ is strictly positive or strictly negative, respectively. If $T:H_0\to H_1$ is bounded, injective and has dense image, then $T^*JT$ and $J$ have the same inertia. If $J$ is invertible, $V\subseteq H$ is closed, and $V^{\perp_J}\subseteq V$, then the form on $H$ and its restriction to $V$ have equal signatures. Kernels contribute zero. These statements include ordinary real signatures by complexification and the trivial-group trace.

Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold with supplied boundary collar, and let $R$ be an involutive unital ring. Supply a based rank-one right-$R$ local system $\mathcal R$, a base-fiber identification with $R$, unitary monodromy and its parallel standard Hermitian form. For $p\in H_2(W;\mathcal R)$ let $a_p\in H^2(W,\partial W;\mathcal R^\vee)$ be the inverse cap-duality image of $\bar p$, using the form to identify the intrinsic dual system with $\overline{\mathcal R}$. Define
$$\lambda(p,q)=\langle j(a_p),q\rangle,$$
where $j$ forgets the relative condition and the last pairing is intrinsic cochain evaluation. Then
$$\lambda(p,q)=\overline{\lambda(q,p)}$$
for all $p,q$. In particular $\lambda(\ell_i,d_j)=\delta_{ij}$ implies $\lambda(d_j,\ell_i)=\delta_{ij}$. No choice axiom, triangulation or geometric transversality of surfaces in dimension four is required.

Let $W,X$ be compact oriented topological four-manifolds with supplied boundary collars and decompositions $\partial W=A\sqcup D$, $\partial X=A\sqcup B$. Glue their copies of $A$ by a supplied orientation-reversing identification, obtaining $Y=W\cup_A X$ with $\partial Y=D\sqcup B$. Supply one ambient rank-one right-$R$ local system on $Y$, where $R$ is an involutive unital ring. On each connected component supply a base-fiber identification with $R$ and unitary monodromy, and use its transported standard Hermitian form. Use its restrictions and the induced orientations on $W,X$.

For the intersection pairings defined by inverse relative cap duality, passage to absolute cohomology and evaluation,
$$\lambda_Y(i_*p,i_*q)=\lambda_W(p,q)\qquad(p,q\in H_2(W;R)).$$
In particular all isotropic and dual-pair identities for homology classes in $W$ persist under their inclusion in $Y$. The result applies to topological manifolds and requires no geometric surface transversality or choice principle.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

For $A\subseteq X$ and a local system $\mathcal L$ on $X$, restriction to $A$ gives natural exact sequences
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_{n-1}(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to\cdots$$
and
$$\cdots\to H^n(X,A;\mathcal L)\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\xrightarrow{\delta}H^{n+1}(X,A;\mathcal L)\to\cdots.$$
The homology connector sends a relative cycle represented by $c$ to $[\partial c]$. The cohomology connector sends a cocycle $a$ on $A$ to $[\delta\widetilde a]$, where $\widetilde a$ is its extension by zero to simplices not contained in $A$. Naturality uses the variances of the preceding functoriality proposition.

Let $M$ be a boundaryless $n$-manifold, $R$ a commutative unital ring, and $K\subseteq M$ compact. There is a unique class
$$[M]^\mathrm{tw}_K\in H_n(M,M\setminus K;\mathcal O_M^R)$$
whose image at every $x\in K$ is the canonical local element: if $o_x$ is
either generator of the integral local group $\mathcal O_x$, it is represented
by a local relative cycle for $o_x$ carrying coefficient $o_x\otimes1_R$.
Equivalently its two typed factors are
$o_x\otimes(o_x\otimes1_R)$, the first in local integral homology and the
second in the stalk $\mathcal O_x^R$. Changing $o_x$ to $-o_x$ changes both
factors and leaves the class fixed. These classes commute with restriction
when the compact support shrinks.

If $M$ is compact with boundary $A$, the boundary orientation system from [[def-orientation-local-system-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]] has a unique relative class
$$[M,A]^\mathrm{tw}\in H_n(M,A;\mathcal O_M^R)$$
with these prescribed local images at all interior points. Its pair boundary is the canonical twisted class of $A$ for the outward-normal-first identification $\mathcal O_M^R|_A\cong\mathcal O_A^R$.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and let $\mathcal L,\mathcal K$ be left $R$-module local systems on $X$. Their **objectwise tensor product** is
$$(\mathcal L\otimes_R\mathcal K)_x=\mathcal L_x\otimes_R\mathcal K_x,\qquad T_\gamma(\ell\otimes k)=T_\gamma\ell\otimes T_\gamma k.$$
The tensor relations make the displayed transport well defined; identity and composition hold on elementary tensors, and $T_{\bar\gamma}\otimes T_{\bar\gamma}$ is its inverse. Thus this is again a local system.

A **local-coefficient pairing** is a natural transformation $b:\mathcal L\otimes_R\mathcal K\to\mathcal N$, equivalently bilinear maps $b_x:\mathcal L_x\times\mathcal K_x\to\mathcal N_x$ satisfying $T_\gamma b_x(\ell,k)=b_y(T_\gamma\ell,T_\gamma k)$ for every path class $\gamma:x\to y$.

For a simplex $\sigma:[v_0,\ldots,v_{p+q}]\to X$, let $\lambda_{0p}^\sigma$ be its affine edge path from $v_0$ to $v_p$. For $\varphi\in C^p(X;\mathcal L)$ and $\psi\in C^q(X;\mathcal K)$ define
$$(\varphi\smile_b\psi)(\sigma)=b_{v_0}\left(\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p]),T^{\mathcal K}_{\overline{\lambda_{0p}^\sigma}}\psi(\sigma[p,\ldots,p+q])\right).$$
The reverse transport is necessary because the back-face value lies over $v_p$ while the output cochain value must lie over $v_0$. The Alexander--Whitney face calculation, with naturality of $b$ on each triangular transport comparison, gives
$$\delta(\varphi\smile_b\psi)=\delta\varphi\smile_b\psi+(-1)^p\varphi\smile_b\delta\psi.$$
Hence cocycles give cup products in cohomology. The same vanishing-on-front-face argument as for ordinary relative cups gives $H^p(X,A;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH^q(X,B;\mathcal K)\to H^{p+q}(X,A\cup B;\mathcal N)$ under the usual excisive-triad comparison.

For $\varphi\in C^p(X;\mathcal L)$ and a local chain generator $m\sigma\in C_n(X;\mathcal K)$, define the **cohomology-first cap product** by zero when $p>n$ and otherwise by
$$\varphi\cap_b(m\sigma)=T^{\mathcal N}_{\lambda_{0p}^\sigma}\left(b_{v_0}(\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p]),m)\right)\sigma[p,\ldots,n].$$
Here forward transport is necessary because the retained back face begins at $v_p$. The published front/back face cancellation, with the same naturality squares, yields
$$\partial(\varphi\cap_b c)=(-1)^p\left(\varphi\cap_b\partial c-\delta\varphi\cap_b c\right).$$
Consequently cap descends to the same relative quotient patterns as [[def-relative-cap-product]], with the chain coefficient system changed from $\mathcal K$ to $\mathcal N$ in the target. In particular,
$$H^p(X,A;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH_n(X,A;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X;\mathcal N),$$
and
$$H^p(X;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH_n(X,A;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X,A;\mathcal N).$$

If a cohomology class is represented with compact support $K$, cup with any ordinary class remains supported in $K$, while the cap of a class in $H^p(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L)$ with a class in $H_n(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal K)$ is an absolute class. Enlargement of $K$ commutes with the formulas, giving the compact-support cup and supportwise cap operations used in duality. Constant systems and multiplication recover the published operations. Empty spaces, zero systems or rings, $p=0$, $p=n$, and $p>n$ follow from the displayed formulas. Only finite faces of a supplied simplex occur, so no AC is used.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff topological manifold and $o\in M$. There is a finite based graph mapped continuously into $M$ such that its induced fundamental-group map is onto. Consequently $\pi_1(M,o)$ has a finite generating list, without a choice principle. No triangulation or smooth structure on $M$ is assumed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] over $R$ to each of the finitely many compact manifolds in a proposed finite diagram, obtaining $C(M;R)\simeq E(M)$ with bounded finite-projective $E$, actual chain maps $a:C\to E$, $b:E\to C$, and actual homotopies for $ba\simeq1_C$, $ab\simeq1_E$. Realize each projective term as $eR^r$ for a supplied finite idempotent $e$, using [F1]'s explicit presentation. Its conjugate right dual is $e^*R^r$, after the finite dual-coordinate identification. Every map or homotopy between two such finite projective terms is a finite rectangular matrix: compose it with the source idempotent and include its target in the ambient finite free module. This assertion includes dual maps; it does not identify the dual of an infinite singular direct sum with a direct sum.

For an inclusion $u:C(B)\to C(M)$ use the finite model map $u_E=a_Mub_B$ and its mapping cone, with differential $d(y,x)=(d_My+u_Ex,-d_Bx)$. This cone is bounded finite-projective and compares to the actual singular cone. For example a comparison to the singular cone is $(y,x)\mapsto(b_My-H_Mub_Bx,b_Bx)$ when $1-b_Ma_M=dH_M+H_Md$: substituting gives a chain map because $ub_B-b_Mu_E=d(H_Mub_B)+(H_Mub_B)d$. Its component maps induce homology isomorphisms, so the cone comparison is a homology isomorphism by the exact mapping-cone sequence. For the pair, the singular inclusion is a split injection in every degree, using the actual subset of singular generators lying in $B$. The map from its cone to the quotient $C(M,B)$ is a homology isomorphism, with kernel the contracted cone of the identity of $C(B)$. Under [A1] the comparison cones are chain contractible: a bounded-below acyclic complex of projectives splits first onto its lowest term, leaving a projective kernel, and then recursively onto that kernel. Free singular terms are projective here by choosing preimages of their basis elements using AC. Thus these are actual chain homotopy comparisons, not just homology identifications.

The same construction applies to a finite gluing graph of embedded compact pieces whose distinct seams join different pieces and are disjoint closed whole boundary components. Take collar-enlarged open neighborhoods $U_v$ of the pieces with no triple intersections and their disjoint seam overlaps $U_e$. The small singular chain sequence is $$0\to\bigoplus_e C(U_e)\to\bigoplus_v C(U_v)\to C^{\mathrm{sm}}(X)\to0.$$ Its first map is the two inclusions with opposite signs. It is degreewise split by assigning a small simplex to the least piece containing it; a duplicated simplex is exactly in one seam overlap. The supplied collar deformations retract $U_v$ onto $M_v$ and $U_e$ onto $N_e$, with their actual coefficient comparisons; the displayed exact sequence is the open-neighborhood sequence before those homotopy replacements. Small subdivision and its homotopy [F5] compare the last term with all singular chains. Taking finite models and the finite matrix of signed inclusion maps therefore gives a bounded finite-projective cone model for the entire diagram, by step 2.1. Dualizing these actual chain homotopy comparisons gives cochain comparisons too. The first-vertex free bases identify the scalar-extended singular complex literally with the singular complex of the extended $A$ fiber. Tensoring with $A$ preserves the comparisons because their homotopy identities are actual identities, requiring no flatness assumption. On finite projectives the dual coefficient comparison is $\overline{\operatorname{Hom}_R(E,R)}\otimes_R A\cong\overline{\operatorname{Hom}_R(E,A)}$, verified directly on the idempotent coordinates; thus no infinite product is interchanged with tensor.

Transfer cap with one finite relative fundamental representative $z$ using these chain comparisons. The absolute cochain cap lands in relative chains, and relative cochain cap lands in absolute chains. They are chain maps with the cap signs of [F5]: in the chain reindexing of a degree-$p$ dual cochain use differential $(-1)^{p+1}\delta$, so $\partial(\bar\alpha\cap z)=(-1)^{p+1}\overline{\delta\alpha}\cap z$ after the appropriate relative quotient. Conjugate the intrinsic left duals to right modules via [F2]. For example the absolute-to-relative map on finite models is the composite of the dual of $a_M$, cap with $z$, and the relative comparison back to $E(M,\partial M)$. Its induced homology is an isomorphism by [F2] and steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1. Both ends are bounded finite-projective, so its mapping cone is bounded acyclic finite-projective and is contractible: split its lowest term and continue through only finitely many degrees. All resulting maps and homotopies are finite matrices over $R$. This proves a finite-projective cap chain homotopy equivalence, before any Hilbert completion.

Each finite $R$ matrix acts boundedly on finite sums of $\ell^2(G)$, with norm bounded by the finite sums of absolute values of its group coefficients. An idempotent $e$ has closed Hilbert range, since it is the kernel of $1-e$; its orthogonal range projection $p$ lies in a matrix algebra over $A$ by [F3]. The identities $ep=p$, $pe=e$ give $eA^r=pA^r$. Hence the finite projective complexes and all cap maps and their inverses and homotopies from step 4.1 complete to bounded Hilbert-module chain maps. Bounded homotopies send closures of boundaries into closures of boundaries and induce inverse maps on completed reduced homology. Thus completed cap duality is a bounded isomorphism, without a closed-range assertion for any differential.

In a completed degree term $p\ell^2(G)^r$, let $p_Z$ project onto $\ker d_i$ and $p_B$ onto $\overline{\operatorname{im}d_{i+1}}$. These are matrix projections in $A$, $p_B\le p_Z\le p$, and the algebraic matrix kernel is exactly $p_ZA^r$: check columns for one inclusion and use $d_ip_Z=0$ for the other. Harmonic projection gives an algebraic homology surjection onto $P_i=(p_Z-p_B)A^r$ with kernel $p_BA^r/\operatorname{im}d_{i+1}$, of dimension zero by [F3]. Inclusion of harmonic algebraic cycles splits that surjection. The map $P_i\to(p_Z-p_B)\ell^2(G)^r$, sending each operator column to its value on $\delta_e$, is injective: an operator annihilating $\delta_e$ annihilates all its right translates. Its image is dense because group-ring columns are Hilbert dense. This gives exactly the algebraic/projective/completed dictionary in the Statement, with no false surjectivity onto the completed Hilbert module.

All pair and finite-graph homology and cohomology sequences from step 3.1 are algebraically exact after tensoring with $A$: their finite cone sequences are degreewise split and their actual comparisons are homotopy equivalences. Their maps on harmonic parts are bounded, since inclusions, cone connectors and degreewise projections are finite matrices followed by orthogonal harmonic projections. Write each algebraic term as $P\oplus T$ as in step 6.1. Every map $T\to P'$ is zero, since its image is zero-dimensional whereas every nonzero vector in a finite projection module generates a positive-dimensional submodule by [F3]. For consecutive maps $f,g$, let $K_A=\ker g_P$, a finite algebraic projection module whose Hilbert closure is the kernel $K_H$ of the completed map. Lift $K_A$ as harmonic algebraic cycles into the middle homology. Its actual $g$ image lies in the target $T'$, so $K_A/\ker(g|_{K_A})$ is zero-dimensional. The quotient formula [F3] makes that kernel dense in $K_H$. Algebraic exactness puts it in the actual preceding image; projecting a preimage off its $T$ part does not change its harmonic image. Thus $\operatorname{im}f_P$ contains this dense kernel and is contained in $K_A$. The closure of the completed preceding image is precisely $K_H$. This proves weak exactness, and proves only weak exactness, without assuming images closed.

Riesz duality of the completed finite projective complex identifies its completed reduced cohomology with the Hilbert dual of completed reduced homology: conjugate adjoint differentials have harmonic space the orthogonal complement of their boundary closures. Compose inverse relative cap, restriction, and this identification to obtain the bounded middle intersection operator $J_M$. The cochain cap/evaluation definition agrees on algebraic $A$ homology by step 3.1 and the same simplex formula, and [F4] makes its extension Hermitian. Thus $J_M$ is self-adjoint. Its Hilbert radical is exactly $\ker J_M$, a closed projection submodule. Removing that radical leaves its orthogonal complement, but its restricted operator need not be bounded below; signature is defined by the positive and negative spectral projections, which discard only the zero spectral projection. If $M$ is closed, restriction has no relative condition, so cap duality from step 5.1 and Riesz duality make $J_M$ boundedly invertible. This is the only place below where invertibility is asserted.

The cap boundary, restriction and support/excision identities persist in these completed models. Restriction and cone connectors are finite matrix maps by steps 1.1 and 3.1, and the actual cap equivalences are finite matrices by step 4.1. For the identities needed here, work directly on singular cochains with the $A$ coefficient fiber: [F2,F5] give the cap-boundary identities on the finite orientation chain, and [F4] gives the support/excision identities, with the prescribed standard form. Step 3.1 identifies this actual cohomology and homology with the finite $A$ complexes, so the identities hold on their harmonic algebraic parts. These are dense by step 6.1 and all the maps just named are bounded by step 5.1, hence the identities hold on the Hilbert completions. No assertion that an arbitrary homology identity supplies a chain homotopy is needed. A change of finite-projective model is handled by the finite chain maps $a'b$ and their actual comparison homotopies; they induce bounded inverse harmonic maps. Both models compute the same singular $A$ cap/evaluation form, so these harmonic maps preserve it on the dense algebraic parts and then everywhere. Inertia is invariant under this bounded congruence by [F3], proving model independence.

Let $X$ now be a closed oriented four-manifold decomposed into a finite graph of compact topological pieces with disjoint closed seams as in step 3.1. Put $H=\mathscr H_2(X)$ and let $j:\bigoplus_v\mathscr H_2(M_v)\to H$ sum the actual inclusions, with $U=\overline{\operatorname{im}j}$. Its closed intersection operator $J_X$ is invertible by step 7.2. Under cap and Riesz duality, $U^{\perp_{J_X}}$ is the kernel of cohomology restriction from $X$ to the pieces, since evaluation on a piece is pairing with its inclusion. Weak graph Mayer–Vietoris exactness from step 7.1 identifies this kernel with the closure of the connecting image from $\bigoplus_e\mathscr H^1(N_e)$. The cap boundary identity of step 8.1 identifies its dual image, up to the fixed seam orientation signs, with the closure of the inclusion image from $\bigoplus_e\mathscr H_2(N_e)$. Cap is boundedly invertible on $X$ and on each closed three-dimensional seam, so these are actual equal closed submodules. Each seam inclusion factors through a piece, hence that image lies in $U$. Therefore $U^{\perp_{J_X}}\subseteq U$, establishing coisotropy with image closures retained throughout.

The pullback form $j^*J_Xj$ is the orthogonal sum of the pieces' relative intersection forms. Same-piece terms are [F4]'s actual collared inclusion identity. For a cross term, take a piece's inverse relative-cap class. Excision identifies it with a class on $X$ relative to the union of the other pieces: remove their closed cores off the seams and retract the remaining collars, exactly as in [F4]'s support comparison. Its cap is the inclusion image of the original piece's class by the local orientation identity. Its restriction to every other piece is zero, so its evaluation on every other piece's class is zero. This proves cross-term vanishing by relative cochains, without a geometric transverse-intersection assertion. Apply the same argument directly with $A$ coefficient fibers; steps 6.1 and 8.1 extend it continuously to the completed harmonic modules. Orientation reversal negates inverse cap and hence the corresponding piece operator.

Discard $\ker j$, a null summand of $j^*J_Xj$. On its Hilbert orthogonal complement, $j$ is injective with dense image in $U$, without any assertion that this image is closed. Dense congruence in [F3] identifies the pullback signature with the signature of $J_X|_U$. Coisotropic reduction in [F3] and step 9.1 identify this last signature with the signature on all of $H$. Step 10.1 and finite additivity of spectral trace therefore prove $$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X)=\sum_v\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(M_v).$$ The boundary piece operators may have nonclosed ranges and radicals; the argument uses invertibility only for the closed $J_X$, and their zero spectral projections contribute zero.

For the stated possibly partial-boundary gluing $W=W_0\cup_NW_1$, take its closed double $X=W\cup_{\partial W}(-W)$. Extend the coefficient system by the fold map $X\to W$. The reflection swapping the two copies reverses orientation and preserves the folded system, so bounded cap naturality and model independence give $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X)=-\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X)$, hence zero. View the same $X$ as the finite graph of pieces $W_0,W_1,-W$, with seams $N$ and the remaining boundary components of $W_0,W_1$. These seams are disjoint closed whole components, with no triple intersections. Step 11.1 gives $0=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_0)+\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_1)-\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W)$, the required formula. Empty remaining boundary or disconnected pieces produce a finite disjoint union of the same constructions; empty seams give ordinary direct sums. Apply the identical proof to the trivial coefficient group to obtain ordinary complex signature additivity; complexification of a finite real symmetric form preserves both inertia dimensions, giving the ordinary real formula.

Finally take a possibly uncountable target $G$. Include the glued manifolds and their doubles among the finitely many spaces considered. A component with boundary is a retract of its closed double by the collar fold map, so its fundamental group is a quotient of that closed double's group. Thus [F6], applied to closed compact components, makes all the needed fundamental groups finitely generated, so the subgroup $H$ generated by the images of those finitely many generating lists is countable; enumerate its elements by finite words and take the first word for each element. Construct the entire finite-projective diagram first over $\mathbb CH$ and extend its finite matrices to $\mathbb CG$. For each right coset $H\gamma$, its subspace $\ell^2(H\gamma)$ is invariant for every left-$H$ matrix; the unitary $\delta_h\mapsto\delta_{h\gamma}$ identifies the restriction with the same $\ell^2(H)$ matrix. Kernel, closure, harmonic and positive/negative spectral projections are therefore the identical operators on these blocks, by functional calculus. Their canonical trace is the sum of identity-coordinate diagonals, so the $G$ trace equals the $H$ trace on every relevant projection, regardless of the number of cosets. This proves the stated dimension and signature equality and compatibility with the countable convention. Full AC was the standing Hilbert and projective-comparison hypothesis; all completed maps were finite matrices, and no smoothing, finite CW inference, ordinary-versus-$L^2$ closed index equality or analytic rho foundation entered the proof.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $A$ and $C$ be groups, and let

$$\alpha,\beta:C\to A$$

be injective group homomorphisms ([[def-group-homomorphism]]). Let $F(\{t\})$
be the free group on one generator and form the free product
$A\ast F(\{t\})$ ([[def-free-product-of-a-family-of-groups]],
[[def-free-group]]). The **HNN extension** of $A$ with associated edge maps
$\alpha,\beta$ is

$$\frac{A\ast F(\{t\})}{\left\langle\!\left\langle t\alpha(c)t^{-1}\beta(c)^{-1}:c\in C\right\rangle\!\right\rangle}.$$

Equivalently, in **relative-presentation notation**, it is

$$\left\langle A,t\ \middle|\ t\alpha(c)t^{-1}=\beta(c)\text{ for every }c\in C\right\rangle.$$

Thus the conjugacy relations are

$$t\,\alpha(c)\,t^{-1}=\beta(c)\qquad(c\in C).$$

If $A=\langle X\mid R\rangle$ is presented as in
[[def-group-presentation]], choose words $u_c,v_c\in F(X)$ representing
$\alpha(c),\beta(c)$ for each $c\in C$. The corresponding ordinary group
presentation is

$$\left\langle X,t \,\middle|\, R,\ t u_c t^{-1}v_c^{-1}\text{ for every }c\in C\right\rangle.$$

Different choices of $u_c,v_c$ differ by consequences of $R$, so they give
the same quotient. The relative notation avoids making any word-lift choice.

The new generator $t$ is the **stable letter**.

In an HNN extension, the canonical map from the base group $A$ to the presented
group is injective. Equivalently, a base-group element represents the identity
in the HNN extension only when it is already the identity in $A$.

Let

$$G=\left\langle A,t \,\middle|\, t\,\alpha(c)\,t^{-1}=\beta(c)\text{ for }c\in C\right\rangle$$

be an HNN extension. Let $H$ be a group, let $f:A\to H$ be a group
homomorphism, and let $h\in H$ satisfy

$$h\,f(\alpha(c))\,h^{-1}=f(\beta(c))\qquad(c\in C).$$

Then there is a unique group homomorphism

$$\overline f:G\to H$$

whose restriction to $A$ is $f$ and whose value on the stable letter is
$\overline f(t)=h$.

For $n\ge0$, let $B_n(G)$ be the free abelian group on
$(g_0,\ldots,g_n)\in G^{n+1}$, with diagonal left action
$h(g_0,\ldots,g_n)=(hg_0,\ldots,hg_n)$. For $n\ge1$, put
$$d_n=\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^id_i:B_n(G)\longrightarrow B_{n-1}(G),$$
where $d_i$ deletes the $i$th vertex. In degree zero use the augmentation
$\varepsilon:B_0(G)\to\mathbb Z$, $\varepsilon(g_0)=1$, with trivial action
on $\mathbb Z$. Thus the augmented complex is
$\cdots\to B_1(G)\to B_0(G)\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}\mathbb Z\to0$; no
undefined object $B_{-1}$ or differential $d_0$ is used.

Assume DC and the supplied projective-resolution convention for derived group homology. For every left $G$-module $M$, $H_n(G;M)$ is naturally the homology of $C_n(G;M)=(\overline B_n(G)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M)_G$, with diagonal left action and alternating vertex-deletion differential. Equivalently it is computed by $\overline B^{\rm right}(G)\otimes_{\mathbb ZG}M$, where $b\cdot g=g^{-1}b$.

derivations.claim: Put $B=K\times K$. First adjoin $u$ with $u(g,1)u^{-1}=(1,g)$, an HNN extension between the two injective copies of $K$ in $B$. Next adjoin $t$ with $t(g,1)t^{-1}=(g,g)$; these associated maps remain injective after the first extension. By [F1], $B$ embeds after both adjunctions. Eliminating $(1,g)$ using the first relation leaves precisely the displayed presentation of $m(K)$: commutation between the two factors gives $[h,ugu^{-1}]=1$, and the diagonal relation becomes $tgt^{-1}=gugu^{-1}$. Conversely those relations define the commuting homomorphisms $(g,h)\mapsto g uhu^{-1}$ and satisfy both HNN relations, so the two presentation maps are inverse on generators. Thus $k_K:K\to m(K)$ is injective.

We give the chain constructions needed for integral acyclicity, rather than using a field Kunneth splitting. The tuples of [F2] form a simplicial set $BK$: inserting $1$ gives degeneracies and the stated faces satisfy $d_i d_j=d_{j-1}d_i$ for $i<j$, by associativity, including the two end faces. Hence the alternating boundary squares to zero by pairing these faces. A tuple specifies a simplicial map from the standard simplicial simplex $\Delta^n$: a face edge from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$ is labelled by the product $g_{i+1}\cdots g_j$, with the empty product $1$. This uniquely describes all faces and degeneracies. Products obey $B(K\times L)=BK\times BL$ exactly. We use these unnormalized simplicial chains also for the finite standard simplex models below.

A homomorphism $f:K\to L$ extends to $m(f)$ by applying $f$ to the old generators and sending $u,t$ to the respectively named generators. Every defining relation is preserved. Uniqueness on generators gives $m(1)=1$, $m(fg)=m(f)m(g)$ and $m(f)k_K=k_Lf$. Iterating gives a functorial sequence of injections $G_r\to G_{r+1}$. Its colimit may be represented as the disjoint union of the pairs $(r,g)$ modulo equality after transport to a common later stage; multiplication at a common stage is well-defined, and the stage maps are injective. This defines $A$ and the natural injective $\iota$.

For simplices $x,y$ of common dimension $n$, define the Alexander-Whitney map by $$D(x,y)=\sum_{i=0}^n x[0,\ldots,i]\otimes y[i,\ldots,n].$$ Define the shuffle $E(x\otimes y)$, for dimensions $p,q$, as the sum over the monotone lattice paths from $(0,0)$ to $(p,q)$ of their product simplices, with sign $(-1)^v$, where $v$ counts pairs consisting of a vertical step before a horizontal step. The coordinate simplex maps interpret a path vertex $(a,b)$ by the corresponding vertices of $x,y$, allowing repeated vertices. These formulas are natural. For $D$, the tensor boundary terms inside each front or back face reproduce the corresponding faces of $(x,y)$; the extra terms cutting at $i$ and $i+1$ cancel with opposite signs. Thus $dD=Dd$. For $E$, a face deleting the junction of steps of different types occurs in exactly the two paths interchanging those steps, with opposite signs. The remaining faces delete a vertex between two horizontal steps or between two vertical steps, or a first or last path vertex. These are exactly the shuffles of $dx\otimes y+(-1)^p x\otimes dy$, with the displayed signs, including paths with a zero-length coordinate. Consequently $dE=Ed$. Both maps agree with inverse identification of vertices in degree zero.

For $v\in L$, write $\mu_v(h)=vhv^{-1}$. The homomorphism $\mu_v$ is chain homotopic to the identity on $C(L)$ by the finite formula $$S_v[h_1,\ldots,h_j]=\sum_{i=0}^j(-1)^i[h_1,\ldots,h_i,v^{-1},\mu_v(h_{i+1}),\ldots,\mu_v(h_j)].$$ Indeed faces wholly before the inserted entry cancel with $S_vd$, as do those wholly after it with the shifted sign. The two faces crossing the inserted entry in adjacent summands cancel because $h_i v^{-1}=v^{-1}\mu_v(h_i)$. The only unpaired end faces are $\mu_v[h_1,\ldots,h_j]$ and $-[h_1,\ldots,h_j]$. Hence $dS_v+S_vd=\mu_v-1$, also in degree zero where both sides vanish. These formulas commute with any homomorphism taking $v$ to its specified image.

There is a specified natural homotopy $P$ with $dP+Pd=1-ED$ and $P_0=0$. Here are its model fillings. A simplex of $\Delta^n\times\Delta^n$ is a weakly increasing sequence of pairs in $\{0,\ldots,n\}^2$. Prepending $(0,0)$ defines a cone $c$; direct deletion gives $dc+cd=1-v\epsilon$, with $v\epsilon$ the augmentation projection onto that vertex, zero in positive degrees. Having defined $P$ below degree $n$, take the universal diagonal simplex $a_n$ in this product, set $z=(1-ED)a_n-P da_n$, and define $P a_n=cz$. For $n>0$, $dz=0$ by the lower identity and step 2.2; for $n=0$ set $P a_0=0$ since $z=0$. Thus $dP a_n=z$. For arbitrary $(x,y)$ push this fixed model chain forward by their uniquely specified simplex maps and extend linearly. The same rule defines its values on faces, so the identity holds on every generator. Composition of the simplex maps proves naturality. This construction does not require simplices to be nondegenerate, and every output is finite.

Suppose $\phi:\Pi\to K$ has a specified partial chain homotopy $Q$ with $dQ+Qd=\phi-e$ through degree $n-1$, where $n\ge1$, $e$ is the trivial homomorphism and $Q_0=0$. On $C(B\Pi\times B\Pi)$ put $L_1(x,y)=x\otimes[\ ]$, $L_2(x,y)=[\ ]\otimes y$ and $L=D-L_1-L_2$. Each is a chain map: the endpoint maps drop the other coordinate and tensor with the zero-cycle $[\ ]$. For positive degree $j$, $L$ has only tensor bidegrees $(i,j-i)$ with $1\le i\le j-1$. In degree zero $L=-[\ ]\otimes[\ ]$, which is killed by $Q\otimes\phi$ because $Q_0=0$. Therefore on degrees at most $n$ the signed tensor differential gives $$d((Q\otimes\phi)L)+(Q\otimes\phi)Ld=((\phi-e)\otimes\phi)L.$$ The terms involving the differential of the second factor cancel; the first factor only uses the stipulated identity below $n$.

In step 3.2 let $U=\phi\times\phi$ and $V=e\times\phi$, as maps from $\Pi\times\Pi$ to $K\times K$. Set $$T=P(U-V)+E(Q\otimes\phi)L.$$ By naturality of $D$ and step 3.1, the boundary of the first summand is $(1-ED)(U-V)$. By step 3.2 the second boundary is $E((\phi-e)\otimes\phi)L$. Subtracting the $L$ contributions leaves the two endpoint terms: $E((\phi-e)\otimes\phi)L_1=\phi\times e-e\times e$ and $E((\phi-e)\otimes\phi)L_2=0$, since $\phi$ and $e$ agree on the vertex. Thus $$dT+Td=\phi\times\phi-\phi\times e-e\times\phi+e\times e$$ through degree $n$. Also $T_0=0$, using $P_0=Q_0=0$. All identities concern actual unnormalized chains; a trivial homomorphism is not replaced by the zero chain map.

Let $k=k_K$, and let $F:K\times K\to m(K)$ be $F(g,h)=k(g)u k(h)u^{-1}$, a homomorphism since its two factor images commute. On $\Pi$ let $i(g)=(g,1)$, $j(g)=(1,g)$, and $\delta(g)=(g,g)$. Put $a=F(\phi\times\phi)i=k\phi$, $b=F(\phi\times\phi)j=\mu_u a$, and $c=F(\phi\times\phi)\delta=\mu_t a$. The last two equalities are precisely the mitosis relations. Composing step 4.1 with $F$ and $\delta$ gives $d(FT\delta)+(FT\delta)d=c-a-b+e$. Step 2.3 gives boundaries $c-a$ for $S_ta$ and $b-a$ for $S_ua$. Consequently the explicit formula $$R=-FT\delta+S_ta-S_ua$$ satisfies $dR+Rd=a-e=k\phi-e$ through degree $n$. In degree zero, the two conjugation terms are $[t^{-1}]-[u^{-1}]$, independent of the single input vertex, while $FT\delta$ is zero there. To arrange zero degree-zero homotopy, replace $S_ta-S_ua$ in this formula by its difference from $(S_t-S_u)e$. Its boundary is unchanged, since $\mu_t e=\mu_u e=e$. Thus the required normalized formula is $$R=-FT\delta+(S_t-S_u)(a-e),\qquad R_0=0.$$ This supplies a full explicit one-degree improvement, with its sign checked by the three displayed boundary identities.

For $n=0$ the identity and trivial homomorphisms $G\to G$ agree on $C_0(G)=\mathbb Z$, so $Q^0=0$ is a partial homotopy through degree zero. Given $Q^{n-1}$ between the trivial map and $G\to G_{n-1}$, apply step 5.1 with $\Pi=G$, $K=G_{n-1}$, and $\phi$ that inclusion, obtaining $Q^n$. Each $Q^n_0=0$, so the induction applies at every stage. All constructions use finite sums, fixed simplex cones, named stable letters, and composition of natural maps. The formulas for $P,S,T,R$ therefore commute with a homomorphism on the original group; no choices of null-homology primitives are made in this induction.

If $z\in C_j(G_r)$ is a cycle with $j>0$, apply step 6.1 to $G_r$ with $n=j$. Its image in $C_j(G_{r+j})$ differs from $e(z)$ by $dQ^jz$. The latter trivial-image cycle lies in the image of $C_*(1)$. This unnormalized point complex has one generator $e_l$ in each degree, with $de_l=e_{l-1}$ for positive even $l$ and zero for odd $l$. Its positive-degree contraction is $b e_l=e_{l+1}$ for odd $l$ and zero for positive even $l$, with $b e_0=0$; it satisfies $db+bd=1$ in positive degrees. Thus $e(z)$ bounds and so does the transported $z$. This handles identity entries without discarding degenerate simplices.

Every bar chain in $A(G)$ is a finite sum of tuples involving finitely many group elements. All those elements belong to a common stage, and injectivity of the stage maps means that an equation $dz=0$ in the union is already the identical equation in that stage's free bar complex. Step 7.1 then fills it at a later stage. Hence the positive integral bar homology of $A(G)$ vanishes; the unique vertex makes $H_0=\mathbb Z$. The identification [F2] yields the stated group homology. Countability follows because a group generated by a countable set has countably many finite words, each mitosis adds just two generators, and a countable union of countable explicitly generated groups is countable under [A1]. The trivial group, finite groups, arbitrary cardinalities and degree zero are all covered by the same constructions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological manifold with supplied boundary collar, and supply a based homomorphism on each component to a discrete group $G$, with compatible paths when maps or gluings are considered. Use $R=\mathbb CG$, with involution conjugating complex scalars and sending $g$ to $g^{-1}$, and its based right regular local system with standard parallel Hermitian form. Let $A=\mathcal NG$ have the canonical group trace. Then its singular coefficient complex has an actual bounded finite-projective $R$ chain-homotopy model. Absolute, relative and finite whole-component gluing diagrams admit such models and finite matrix comparison maps.

After extending these finite projective matrices to $\ell^2(G)$, write $\mathscr H_i(M)$ for completed reduced homology, with boundaries replaced by their Hilbert closures. If $p_Z,p_B$ are the cycle and boundary-closure projections in a finite ambient projection module, the corresponding algebraic reduced module is $P_i=(p_Z-p_B)A^r$, and
$$H_i(M;A)\twoheadrightarrow P_i\hookrightarrow\mathscr H_i(M)=(p_Z-p_B)\ell^2(G)^r.$$
The first map has dimension-zero kernel, and the second is injective with dense image and need not be onto. Pair and whole-component Mayer–Vietoris sequences are weakly exact on the completed modules. Oriented cap duality gives bounded mutually inverse maps on their completed reduced homology and cohomology, with the cap-boundary and restriction identities. These structures and the resulting spectral signature do not depend on the finite-projective model.

For a four-manifold the middle intersection form is the bounded Hermitian form defined by inverse relative cap duality, restriction and evaluation. Its Hilbert radical is the kernel of its self-adjoint operator. Its signature is the trace of the positive spectral projection minus the trace of the negative projection; no closed range or bounded inverse is required for a manifold with boundary. For a closed four-manifold its middle intersection operator is boundedly invertible.

Let $W_0,W_1$ be compact oriented topological four-manifolds, let $N$ be a union of entire closed boundary components, and glue the two marked copies of $N$ by an orientation-reversing identification and the supplied collars. Put $W=W_0\cup_N W_1$ and supply one compatible regular coefficient system on $W$. Other boundary components may remain. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_0)+\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_1),\qquad\operatorname{sign}(W)=\operatorname{sign}(W_0)+\operatorname{sign}(W_1).$$
Orientation reversal changes the corresponding sign. No finite CW type, triangulation, smoothing of a topological four-manifold, equality of ordinary and $L^2$ signatures on arbitrary closed manifolds, or analytic eta-to-defect comparison is asserted or assumed. For an arbitrary possibly uncountable $G$, the finite-matrix construction has the same dimensions and signatures as its countable coefficient image, so it agrees with the countable-group convention.

Work under the standing AC convention for finite von Neumann modules. Let $A=\mathcal N G$ with its finite trace, and let all Hilbert modules below be ranges of projections on finite sums of $\ell^2(G)$. For a bounded self-adjoint module operator $J$ define its positive and negative inertia by the traces of $\mathbf1_{(0,\infty)}(J)$ and $\mathbf1_{(-\infty,0)}(J)$, and its signature by their difference. Each inertia is the supremum of dimensions of closed module subspaces on which the form $\langle Jx,x\rangle$ is strictly positive or strictly negative, respectively. If $T:H_0\to H_1$ is bounded, injective and has dense image, then $T^*JT$ and $J$ have the same inertia. If $J$ is invertible, $V\subseteq H$ is closed, and $V^{\perp_J}\subseteq V$, then the form on $H$ and its restriction to $V$ have equal signatures. Kernels contribute zero. These statements include ordinary real signatures by complexification and the trivial-group trace.

derivations.claim: Use [F1] for $Y,X$ and $(Y,X)$ with $R=\mathbb CG$ and $A=\mathcal NG$. Write $V=\mathscr H^2(X)$ for completed reduced cohomology. Transport the middle intersection form of $X$ to $V$ by its bounded cap isomorphism, and denote it by $Q$. It is a bounded Hermitian form with boundedly invertible operator, since $X$ is closed. Let $r:\mathscr H^2(Y)\to V$ be restriction and $\delta:V\to\mathscr H^3(Y,X)$ the completed connecting map of the pair. These are bounded maps of finite Hilbert $A$ modules. Set $U=\overline{\operatorname{im}r}$, an actual closed submodule; no assertion that $\operatorname{im}r$ is closed is made.

Cap duality on $Y$ and Riesz duality give a bounded nondegenerate scalar sesquilinear pairing $\mathscr H^2(Y)\times\mathscr H^3(Y,X)\to\mathbb C$: take evaluation of the first class on the cap of the second with $[Y,X]$, followed by the canonical trace, initially on algebraic harmonic parts. Riesz and the bounded cap isomorphism extend this pairing to the Hilbert completions and identify either factor boundedly with the Hilbert dual of the other. No $A$-valued pairing is asserted on arbitrary $\ell^2$ vectors. The boundary identity identifies $Q(ra,b)$ with this pairing of $a$ and $\delta b$, up to the fixed conjugation convention, for all $a\in\mathscr H^2(Y)$ and $b\in V$. Concretely, for an actual degree-two boundary cocycle $\beta$ extend it to a cochain $\widetilde\beta$ on $Y$. The relative cocycle $d\widetilde\beta$ represents $\delta\beta$, and the cohomology-first cap formula gives $\partial(\widetilde\beta\cap[Y,X])=\beta\cap[X]-(d\widetilde\beta)\cap[Y,X]$. Thus $i_*\mathrm{PD}_X\beta=\mathrm{PD}_{Y,X}\delta\beta$ in absolute homology. Pairing with $a$ proves the asserted identity on algebraic harmonic parts. Such parts are dense, all displayed maps and pairings are bounded, and [F1] transfers this actual identity to the completed modules. This uses cochains and the finite orientation chain, with no geometric transverse intersections in dimension four or five.

By step 2.1 and nondegeneracy of the perfect pairing, $Q(ra,b)=0$ for every $a$ if and only if $\delta b=0$. Continuity replaces $\operatorname{im}r$ by its closure without changing this annihilator, giving $U^{\perp_Q}=\ker\delta$. Weak exactness of the actual pair sequence in [F1] gives $\ker\delta=\overline{\operatorname{im}r}=U$. Therefore $U$ is a closed self-annihilating, hence coisotropic, submodule, and $Q|_U$ is identically zero. These are equalities of Hilbert-closed submodules; no algebraic exactness has been promoted to closed-range exactness.

Apply [F2] to the invertible closed-boundary form $Q$ and $U$. Its signature is the signature of the zero restriction, namely zero. The bounded cap change of coordinates preserves inertia, so this is precisely $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X)$. Apply the same argument to the trivial group: its complex Hermitian intersection form is the complexification of the real symmetric form, with equal positive and negative multiplicities, and hence gives the ordinary signature zero. All arguments allow finite disconnected boundaries and empty boundary; in the latter case the middle module is zero.

A disjoint union is an orthogonal direct sum of the finite-projective complexes and forms; orientation reversal negates cap and the form. Thus $X=X_1\sqcup(-X_0)$ in step 4.1 yields the two asserted bordism-invariance equalities. For an embedded coefficient subgroup $G\hookrightarrow K$, construct the same finite models over $\mathbb CG$ and extend the matrices to $\mathbb CK$. Every left-$G$ matrix decomposes on $\ell^2(K)=\bigoplus_{G\gamma}\ell^2(G\gamma)$ into identical copies of its $\ell^2(G)$ operator. Kernel, harmonic and positive/negative projections have the same identity-coordinate diagonal trace. By [F1] this preserves the signatures on both ends and on $X$, for arbitrary cardinalities of $K$. No equality between ordinary and $L^2$ signatures on arbitrary closed four-manifolds and no TOP bordism realization theorem was assumed.
