citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. There is an explicit functor $A$ from groups to groups and a natural transformation $\iota:\mathrm{id}\to A$ such that each $\iota_G:G\to A(G)$ is injective and
$$H_j(A(G);\mathbb Z)=0\quad(j>0),\qquad H_0(A(G);\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z.$$
One may take $A(G)$ to be the increasing union of the iterated mitoses $G_0=G$, $G_{r+1}=m(G_r)$, where
$$m(K)=\langle K,u,t\mid [h,ugu^{-1}]=1,\ t g t^{-1}=gugu^{-1}\ (g,h\in K)\rangle.$$
For every $n\ge0$ there is a specified partial chain homotopy, in degrees at most $n$, between the trivial homomorphism and $G\hookrightarrow G_n$ on integral unnormalized bar chains. It is zero in degree zero, has finite values on every basis simplex, and is natural in $G$. In particular every integral positive-degree bar cycle from any stage bounds after finitely many further mitoses. If $G$ is countable, $A(G)$ is countable.

Assume DC and the supplied projective-resolution convention for derived group homology. For every left $G$-module $M$, $H_n(G;M)$ is naturally the homology of $C_n(G;M)=(\overline B_n(G)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M)_G$, with diagonal left action and alternating vertex-deletion differential. Equivalently it is computed by $\overline B^{\rm right}(G)\otimes_{\mathbb ZG}M$, where $b\cdot g=g^{-1}b$.

Assume AC. For a discrete group $G$, Milnor's $BG$ is connected and

$$ \pi_1(BG)\cong G,\qquad \pi_n(BG)=0\quad(n>1). $$

Consequently any connected CW model of $BG$ is an Eilenberg--Mac Lane space $K(G,1)$.

For a well-pointed topological group $G$ of CW type, the diagonal action on Milnor's $EG$ is free, $EG$ is contractible, and

$$ p:EG\longrightarrow BG $$

is a numerable principal $G$-bundle. The numeration satisfies the library's support-subordinate convention, not merely cozero containment.

The embeddings

$$e\left(\sum_i t_i g_i\right)=\sum_i t_i g_i\text{ in slot }2i,\qquad o\left(\sum_i t_i g_i\right)=\sum_i t_i g_i\text{ in slot }2i+1$$

are $G$-equivariantly homotopic to the identity. If $a,b:T\to EG$ are
continuous equivariant maps, then
$(1-t)e(a(-))+t\,o(b(-))$ is a continuous equivariant homotopy.

For $G=S^1$ or $G=\mathbb Z/2$, the selected compact-group topology identifies $BG$ with the standard weak CW colimit of the finite projective quotients $\mathbb{CP}^N$ or $\mathbb{RP}^N$, respectively.

Assume AC, used only through embeddings, tubular neighbourhoods, approximation
and classifying maps. For every $n\ge0$ the collapse construction induces
isomorphisms of abelian groups
$$\Omega_n^{O}\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\pi_n(M\mathrm O),\qquad \Omega_n^{SO}\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\pi_n(M\mathrm{SO}),$$
where the right-hand sides are the stable homotopy groups of the Thom
prespectra of the universal real and oriented bundles. A collapse at any sufficiently large embedding rank represents the stable
image, and the inverse sends a class represented by a map transverse to the zero section to
the unoriented bordism class of the preimage with its pulled-back normal bundle,
with the orientation-induced refinement in the oriented case. The isomorphisms
are compatible with disjoint union, with products, and with null-cobordism in
that a null-cobordant manifold has zero stable class.

Assume AC, inherited from embeddings, bundle classification, controlled approximation and transversality. Every class in $\Omega_n^{O}$ (respectively $\Omega_n^{SO}$) is represented
by a closed smooth $n$-manifold $M$, and for every $r\ge n+1$ the construction
of the collapse lemma gives an element $\alpha(M)\in\pi_n(M\mathrm O)$
(respectively $\pi_n(M\mathrm{SO})$) depending only on the bordism class; the
resulting map $\Omega_n^{O}\to\pi_n(M\mathrm O)$,
$\Omega_n^{SO}\to\pi_n(M\mathrm{SO})$ is a well-defined homomorphism of abelian
groups, and it is surjective in each degree, so that every stable Thom class is
represented by an embedded closed manifold.

Assume AC. Let $R$ be a commutative PID and $X,Y$ any spaces. For $n\ge0$ there is a natural short exact sequence
$$0\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H_p(X;R)\otimes_RH_q(Y;R)\xrightarrow{\times}H_n(X\times Y;R)\xrightarrow{\gamma}\bigoplus_{p+q=n-1}\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(H_p(X;R),H_q(Y;R))\longrightarrow0.$$
All indices are nonnegative, and an empty sum is zero. The left map is the singular cross product. Naturality is covariant in maps of both spaces; no choice of a splitting is part of this sequence.

For a CW pair $(X,A)$ with $A\ne\varnothing$, every abelian group $G$ and every $i\ge0$, the ordinary quotient map induces an isomorphism
$$q_*:H_i(X,A;G)\longrightarrow H_i(X/A,\{*\};G),\qquad *=q(A).$$
These isomorphisms are natural in continuous maps of such pairs. No choice principle is required. The proof does not assume an open neighborhood of $A$ in $X$ already supplied with a retraction.

Let $(X,A)$ and $(Y,B)$ be CW pairs with supplied characteristic maps, and let $f:(X,A)\to(Y,B)$ be continuous and cellular on $A$. If $X\setminus A$ has finitely many cells, then, without any choice principle, $f$ is homotopic rel $A$ through maps of pairs to a cellular map $g$, meaning $g(X^n)\subseteq Y^n$ for every $n\ge0$. Assuming the Axiom of Choice, the same conclusion holds for an arbitrary set of relative cells.

If two cellular maps of pairs are homotopic rel $A$, they have a cellular homotopy rel $A$: the homotopy can be taken cellular as a map $X\times I\to Y$ for the product CW structure, with its prescribed end maps. This conclusion is choice-free for a finite relative source and uses AC for an arbitrary relative source. Here cellular homotopy refers to the cylinder map; it does not require every time slice to be cellular on $X$.

Let $X,Y$ be CW complexes with supplied characteristic maps and a common CW subcomplex $A$. Let $f:X\to Y$ be cellular and equal to the identity on $A$. Form the ordinary quotient
$$W=(Y\sqcup(X\times I))/\big((x,0)\sim f(x),\ (a,t)\sim a\text{ for }a\in A\big).$$
Then $W$ is a CW complex. Its embedded endpoint copies $j(X)$, $j(x)=[x,1]$, and $k(Y)$ are subcomplexes meeting in their common $A$. Its cells are those of $Y$, those of the free-end $X\setminus A$, and one $(r+1)$-cell $e^r\times(0,1)$ for every $r$-cell of $X\setminus A$.

The map $r:W\to Y$, $r([x,s])=f(x)$ and $r(k(y))=y$, is a strong deformation retraction in the sense that the included $Y$ is fixed throughout its deformation. The deformation also fixes $A$, and $r$ induces a bijection on components and isomorphisms on all positive homotopy groups at every basepoint of $W$.

When $A$ is empty this is the ordinary mapping cylinder. If $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then $W$ is finite; more precisely the cells outside $j(X)$ are the cells of $Y\setminus A$ and the listed prism cells. These statements require no choice principle.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $(X,A,a)$ be an $(n-1)$-connected CW pair, with $A$ nonempty and simply connected and with supplied characteristic maps. Without any choice principle,
$$H_i(X,A;\mathbb Z)=0\quad(0\le i<n),\qquad h:\pi_n(X,A,a)\xrightarrow{\cong}H_n(X,A;\mathbb Z).$$
Here $h$ is the actual relative Hurewicz homomorphism with the boundary-oriented disk convention. The weak model used in the proof need not have a chosen homotopy inverse.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every weak homotopy equivalence $f:X\to Y$ between CW complexes is a homotopy equivalence. If $X,Y$ are finite CW complexes, the same conclusion holds without any choice principle.

For every based pair $(X,A,x_0)$, the natural sequence
$$\cdots\longrightarrow\pi_n(A)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(X)\xrightarrow{j_*}\pi_n(X,A)\xrightarrow{\partial}\pi_{n-1}(A)\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,A)\xrightarrow{\partial}\pi_0(A)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(X)$$
is exact at each term with an incoming and outgoing arrow. Exactness means that the incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element under the outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $x_0$ throughout. No terminal surjectivity onto $\pi_0(X)$ is claimed. Arrows are homomorphisms where both group structures have been established.

For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$

Assume AC. Every compact closed oriented smooth three-manifold $X$ admits a compact oriented smooth four-manifold $W$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $j:\partial W\to X$. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. Consequently $\Omega_3^{SO}=0$ integrally, with a single copy of each input manifold.

More precisely, if $X=M\cup C$ is an actual closed manifold obtained by attaching specified smooth caps $C$ to a compact oriented three-manifold $M$ along specified collared boundary parametrizations, the identification $j$ retains these marked submanifolds, their parametrizations and any decorations by pullback. No extension of a boundary diffeomorphism across a cap or filling is required. The assertion is existence; a simultaneous choice of fillings for a set of inputs may use AC and is not asserted canonical.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every compact smooth manifold, with boundary
allowed, has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. If its boundary is a
supplied finite CW manifold, the collar may be retained in a finite relative CW
model.

Assume AC. Let $Y$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological five-manifold with supplied boundary collar, and let $X=\partial Y$ have its boundary orientation. Supply a based homomorphism $\psi:\pi_1Y\to G$ on each component, where $G$ is an arbitrary discrete group, with the standard unitary regular coefficient systems. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X,\psi|_X)=0,\qquad \operatorname{sign}(X)=0.$$
In particular, when $X=X_1\sqcup(-X_0)$, the ordinary and $L^2$ signatures of these closed oriented four-manifolds agree across this actual coefficient-extending TOP bordism. The equality is unchanged under embedding the target group in a larger group. This theorem asserts bordism invariance and does not assert existence of a bordism between arbitrary closed coefficient manifolds.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological manifold with supplied boundary collar, and supply a based homomorphism on each component to a discrete group $G$, with compatible paths when maps or gluings are considered. Use $R=\mathbb CG$, with involution conjugating complex scalars and sending $g$ to $g^{-1}$, and its based right regular local system with standard parallel Hermitian form. Let $A=\mathcal NG$ have the canonical group trace. Then its singular coefficient complex has an actual bounded finite-projective $R$ chain-homotopy model. Absolute, relative and finite whole-component gluing diagrams admit such models and finite matrix comparison maps.

After extending these finite projective matrices to $\ell^2(G)$, write $\mathscr H_i(M)$ for completed reduced homology, with boundaries replaced by their Hilbert closures. If $p_Z,p_B$ are the cycle and boundary-closure projections in a finite ambient projection module, the corresponding algebraic reduced module is $P_i=(p_Z-p_B)A^r$, and
$$H_i(M;A)\twoheadrightarrow P_i\hookrightarrow\mathscr H_i(M)=(p_Z-p_B)\ell^2(G)^r.$$
The first map has dimension-zero kernel, and the second is injective with dense image and need not be onto. Pair and whole-component Mayer–Vietoris sequences are weakly exact on the completed modules. Oriented cap duality gives bounded mutually inverse maps on their completed reduced homology and cohomology, with the cap-boundary and restriction identities. These structures and the resulting spectral signature do not depend on the finite-projective model.

For a four-manifold the middle intersection form is the bounded Hermitian form defined by inverse relative cap duality, restriction and evaluation. Its Hilbert radical is the kernel of its self-adjoint operator. Its signature is the trace of the positive spectral projection minus the trace of the negative projection; no closed range or bounded inverse is required for a manifold with boundary. For a closed four-manifold its middle intersection operator is boundedly invertible.

Let $W_0,W_1$ be compact oriented topological four-manifolds, let $N$ be a union of entire closed boundary components, and glue the two marked copies of $N$ by an orientation-reversing identification and the supplied collars. Put $W=W_0\cup_N W_1$ and supply one compatible regular coefficient system on $W$. Other boundary components may remain. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_0)+\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_1),\qquad\operatorname{sign}(W)=\operatorname{sign}(W_0)+\operatorname{sign}(W_1).$$
Orientation reversal changes the corresponding sign. No finite CW type, triangulation, smoothing of a topological four-manifold, equality of ordinary and $L^2$ signatures on arbitrary closed manifolds, or analytic eta-to-defect comparison is asserted or assumed. For an arbitrary possibly uncountable $G$, the finite-matrix construction has the same dimensions and signatures as its countable coefficient image, so it agrees with the countable-group convention.

Every element of $G\ast_KH$ has a unique normal form $s_1\cdots s_nk$ relative to fixed transversals. A normal word of positive length is nonidentity. The represented group and these conclusions are independent of the chosen transversals.

derivations.claim: We first identify the actual classifying-space homology used below. For a group $H$, use a CW $K(H,1)$ model from [F1], with universal cover $E$. Lift its CW cells to $E$; the higher homotopy groups agree with those of $BH$ and the fundamental group is zero, so [F4] and Whitehead make $E$ contractible. The singular complex $C_*(E;\mathbb Z)$ is a free $\mathbb ZH$ complex: deck action is free on singular simplices, since a deck transformation fixing one simplex fixes its first vertex. Choose orbit representatives under [A1]. Its augmented complex is exact by contractibility. Taking deck coinvariants identifies it with singular chains of $BH$: every simplex lifts, and two lifts differ by a unique deck transformation, consistently on faces. Comparing this free resolution of $\mathbb Z$ with the bar resolution gives the same coinvariant homology. Explicitly lift the identity in degree zero and recursively lift each boundary of a free basis vector through the next differential of the exact resolution. This gives augmentation-preserving chain maps in both directions. The same recursion on their difference from the identity supplies chain homotopies. Tensoring with the trivial module retains these actual identities. Therefore $H_*(BH;\mathbb Z)=H_*(H;\mathbb Z)$; in particular $K=BA(H)$ is connected and integrally acyclic. All free-basis lifts are permitted by [A1].

We need the labelled version of smooth collapse, and give its extension explicitly. For a CW space $K$ set $K_+=K\sqcup\{*\}$. A closed oriented smooth $n$-manifold with a map $f:M\to K$ gives a based map $S^{n+q}\to T_q\wedge K_+$: embed $M$, take the normal tube and its oriented classifying map as in [F2], and on a normal vector over $x$ retain the additional label $f(x)$. Collapse the tube exterior to the basepoint. Here $T_q$ is the Thom space of the universal oriented $q$-plane bundle and sufficiently large $q\ge\max(2,n+1)$ is allowed. Independence of the embedding, tube, normal metric and classifying homotopy follows from the same explicit tube comparisons and stabilization in [F2], with the label retained on each tracked base point of $M$. A smooth bordism carrying a map to $K$ embeds neatly with product boundary collars by [F2]; collapsing its tube and retaining its label gives a based homotopy after a common stabilization. The normal-first convention of [F2] gives negative incoming and positive outgoing boundary orientations.

Now take connected integrally acyclic $K$. At a finite oriented Grassmannian stage let $T$ be its Thom space, with rank $q\ge2$. It is a finite based CW space with one basepoint zero-cell and all other cells in dimensions at least $q$: trivialize the oriented bundle over each base characteristic disk and collapse its sphere boundary, which shifts that disk's cell dimension by $q$. The ordinary product of a finite CW space with a CW space has the product CW structure. For this topology assertion, product with each compact disk preserves the quotient test for the characteristic-map presentation of $K$ by the ordinary compact-domain exponential law, iterated from the interval. The finite characteristic-disk quotient onto the Hausdorff finite complex $T$ is a closed map with compact fibers; its product with $K$ is still closed by the compact-fiber tube argument, hence quotient. Together these two tests are exactly the product-cell weak topology. The quotient $(T\times K)/(\{*\}\times K)=T\wedge K_+$ is therefore CW with all nonbasepoint cells of dimension at least $q$. Both it and $T$ are simply connected, by cellularly moving each loop into its single-vertex one-skeleton.

Maps to these $K(H,1)$ spaces realize group homomorphisms and classify them up to based homotopy on the smooth domains used here. Indeed replace a compact smooth domain by its finite CW model [F5]. Send a maximal tree to the basepoint and the remaining one-cells to loops representing the stipulated generator images. The relator condition extends this map across its two-cells; vanishing $\pi_jK(H,1)$ for $j>1$ extends it across every higher cell. A homotopy between maps with the same based fundamental-group homomorphism is built by the same relative cell induction on the cylinder; its obstruction on each cell lies in the corresponding zero higher homotopy group, with the one-cell case fixed by equality in $\pi_1$. Transport along the actual CW homotopy equivalence gives the map on the smooth domain. The same construction gives maps $Bf$ for group homomorphisms and their compositional compatibility up to specified based homotopies. On a boundary collar these homotopies can be inserted to make the restrictions exactly the specified maps.

Conversely let $g:S^{n+q}\to T_q\wedge K_+$ be based. The Thom projection $p_T$, induced by $K_+\to S^0$, is continuous. Its zero preimage is compact and lies in the open set where $g$ has uniquely defined Thom and $K$ coordinates. Its Thom coordinate has compact image in a finite Grassmannian Thom space. On a compact buffer about the zero preimage apply [F2]'s controlled Euclidean smoothing/retraction and arbitrarily small transverse perturbation to that coordinate, keeping the $K$ coordinate unchanged. Cutoffs have support in this product-coordinate open set; on the compact outer buffer the Thom coordinate stays away from zero, so sufficiently small perturbations create no extra zeros. Off the buffer retain $g$. The result is based and has a compact smooth transverse zero preimage $P$ and its continuous retained map to $K$. The identical construction on a homotopy, constant on endpoint collars and protecting the basepoint track, gives a smooth normal bordism of the endpoint preimages with its retained $K$ map. Thus stable homotopies give actual labelled bordisms.

Projection $T\times K\to T$ induces an integral homology isomorphism by [F3]: the Kunneth terms from $K$ are only its $H_0=\mathbb Z$, with no Tor contribution. The restriction $\{*\}\times K\to\{*\}$ is also an integral homology isomorphism. Their pair sequences imply an isomorphism on relative homology. The quotient comparison in [F3] thus shows that the actual projection $p:T\wedge K_+\to T$ is an integral reduced homology isomorphism, also an ordinary degree-zero isomorphism since both spaces are connected. To see it is a homotopy equivalence, replace it by its cellular CW mapping cylinder. The simply connected pair has zero relative integral homology by its pair sequence. Its relative degree one is zero by the homotopy pair sequence; if it is $(r-1)$-connected for $r\ge2$, the first relative Hurewicz isomorphism [F4] makes its degree-$r$ homotopy zero. Induction makes all relative homotopy groups zero. The homotopy sequence and Whitehead [F4] give a homotopy equivalence. It is based: its source basepoint is a CW subcomplex, so the inverse and its homotopies can be adjusted along their basepoint tracks, whose loops are null in the simply connected spaces.

These assignments are inverse, including surjectivity with the label. Near $P$, write the smooth Thom coordinate as $(b(x,v),a(x,v))$ on a small normal tube. Its normal derivative $A_x$ is invertible. As in [F2], transport the bundle along $b(x,tv)$ by its finite Grassmannian orthogonal projections and linearize $a$ to $A_xv$; a uniform $o(\|v\|)$ bound makes this homotopy zero-free off $P$. Simultaneously replace the continuous label $k(x,v)$ by $k(x,(1-s\chi(v))v)$, where the tube cutoff is one on a smaller tube and zero near its boundary. This homotopy is defined entirely in the product-coordinate region. On that smaller tube its final label is $k(x,0)$. Compactness bounds the nonzero Thom radius away from zero outside a still smaller tube. A radial Thom map, homotopic to the identity, expands every radius at least this bound to the collapsed boundary; the resulting map is exactly the normally classified collapse of $P$ with label $k|_P$, up to the metric/tube comparisons in [F2]. Its normal orientation gives the original orientation on a collapsed $M$. Stabilization adds the same positive first normal coordinate as in [F2] and leaves the labels unchanged. Consequently labelled oriented smooth bordism is identified with the stable colimit of $\pi_{n+q}(T_q\wedge K_+)$, with an actual labelled bordism witnessing equality of any two classes. No topology or smoothness of $K$ beyond its CW topology was used for perturbing the Thom coordinate.

The section $s:T\to T\wedge K_+$ using a fixed point of $K$ has $ps=1$. Step 2.3 makes $p$ an isomorphism on all based homotopy groups, so $s_*$ is its unique inverse. For a labelled collapse of a fixed compact $M$, choose one finite Grassmannian Thom stage $T$ containing its classifying tube map. Apply step 2.3 to this $T$ and the whole acyclic $K$. Since $p_*$ is injective and $p s=1$, the labelled collapse and the constant-labelled version of its unlabelled collapse represent the same homotopy class already at this finite stage. The homotopy may have labels escaping finite subcomplexes near a basepoint preimage, which is harmless: its Thom projection remains in this same finite $T$, and step 2.2 perturbs only that projection on a compact zero buffer. Thus the equality passes to the same stable collapse group without any global compact-label claim. By step 2.2 this equality is witnessed by an actual compact smooth $(n+1)$-bordism over $K$, between $(M,f)$ and the same oriented $M$ with constant map. In this argument finite stage projection is applied to a collapsed tube, whose label lies in the compact image $f(M)$, so no compact image bound at a basepoint singularity is assumed.

For a closed smooth four-manifold $Z$ with group map $\theta:\pi_1Z\to G$, map it to $BA(G)$ using $\iota_G\theta$ and step 2.1. This classifying space is integrally acyclic by step 1.1. Step 4.1 gives an actual smooth five-bordism over $BA(G)$ from this coefficient manifold to $Z$ with constant map. By [F6], its $L^2$ signatures agree. With constant coefficients the completed finite matrices are those of ordinary complex chains tensored with the regular Hilbert module, so each positive or negative scalar eigenspace contributes its ordinary multiplicity times the trace of $1$, equal to one. The constant-map $L^2$ signature is therefore the ordinary signature of $Z$. Group-subgroup induction [F6] identifies the original $G$ signature with its $A(G)$ signature, proving the first assertion for arbitrary $G$, without an analytic index theorem.

Fix a connected smooth $M^3$, put $\Pi=\pi_1M$, and choose its map $M\to BA(\Pi)$ induced by $\iota_\Pi$. Step 4.1 gives a smooth four-bordism over $BA(\Pi)$ from $M$ to $M$ with constant map. The latter end bounds a compact smooth four-manifold by [F5], whose constant map extends that end. Glue this actual filling with the bordism, respecting its collars and orientation, to obtain one fixed smooth $W_M$ with $\partial W_M=M$ and a map $\psi_M:\pi_1W_M\to A(\Pi)$ restricting to $\iota_\Pi$. For any $\phi:\Pi\to G$ compose with $A(\phi)$; functoriality gives $A(\phi)\iota_\Pi=\iota_G\phi$. Thus the same smooth $W_M$ is a valid bounding extension into $A(G)$ for every $G,\phi$, establishing existence with injective $G\to A(G)$.

Compare any two smooth bounds $W_1,W_2$ for the same $(M,\phi)$, over target enlargements $j_i:G\hookrightarrow\Gamma_i$. Form $L=\Gamma_1*_G\Gamma_2$; [F7] embeds both targets into $L$. Their maps agree on the based boundary, and the collar gluing and van Kampen property supply the map on the smooth closed four-manifold $Z=W_1\cup_M(-W_2)$. If a boundary restriction was given only up to based homotopy, insert its actual cylinder homotopy first; its two maps then agree literally. Induction in [F6] preserves each signature under its target inclusion. Additivity and orientation reversal give the difference of their defects as $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_L(Z)-\operatorname{sign}(Z)$, zero by step 5.1. This proves independence of both the smooth bound and the extending enlargement/map. Replacing $G$ by a group containing it preserves the value by using the same extension into an amalgamated target. No surjectivity of $\phi$ is involved.

A smooth $W$ bounding $rM$ may be compared in the same amalgamated target to the disjoint union of $r$ copies of $W_M$. Glue their $r$ matched boundary components. The result is a closed smooth four-manifold, possibly disconnected, with a compatible target map; its signature defect is zero by step 5.1 componentwise. Additivity in [F6] gives $\operatorname{defect}(W)=r\operatorname{defect}(W_M)$. If coefficient identifications on different components involve based paths, choose the corresponding paths when applying van Kampen; equivalently use the graph-of-spaces fundamental group and send its additional connecting generators to these specified group elements. Thus division by $r$ yields exactly the same value.

Fix a finite-projective coefficient chain model for the fixed smooth $W_M$ over $R=\mathbb C\pi_1W_M$, using [F6], and fix an idempotent presentation $E_2=eR^N$ of its degree-two term. Here $N$ is fixed with $W_M$, before $G$ or $\phi$ is chosen. Under any coefficient homomorphism $R\to\mathbb CA(G)$ the actual chain comparison maps and homotopy identities extend by tensoring. First-vertex singular frames identify that extended singular complex with the actual target local-coefficient complex; this uses a chain homotopy equivalence, not flatness of the homomorphism. The extended idempotent has Hilbert-closed range in $\ell^2(A(G))^N$ and dimension at most $N$. Reduced degree-two homology and its positive/negative spectral subspaces consequently have dimension at most $N$, giving $|\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_{A(G)}W_M|\le N$. Extend the same matrices along the ordinary augmentation $R\to\mathbb C$; their ordinary degree-two homology has dimension at most $N$ too, giving $|\operatorname{sign}W_M|\le N$. Thus $|\rho_{\mathrm{sm}}(M,\phi)|\le2N$ independently of $G,\phi$. Model independence in [F6] identifies the signatures with the original geometric ones. No target-dependent choice of bordism or finite CW model of a TOP manifold enters this bound.

All subgroup changes and arbitrary cardinalities are covered by [F6]'s identical coset matrix blocks; no countability or finite-image substitution was made. The only manifold bordisms constructed here were obtained by smooth transverse preimages in step 2.2. Hence the result proves smooth bounding-defect independence and uniformity, while making no inference for a nonsmooth TOP bound or for an analytic eta invariant.
